4. Wash the residue with distilled water.
5. Dry it between sheets of filter paper.
method_templates.watch_out: Both starting chemicals must be solutions. Nitrates and sodium salts are safe choices because they are always soluble.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Drawing a dot-and-cross diagram for a covalent molecule
method_templates.method:
1. Count the outer electrons of each atom.
2. Work out how many more each atom needs for a full shell: that is the number of bonds it makes.
3. Draw overlapping outer shells and put one dot and one cross in the overlap for each bond.
4. Add the remaining outer electrons as pairs that are not shared.
5. Check every atom has a full outer shell (hydrogen has 2).
method_templates.watch_out: A double bond has two shared pairs in the overlap; a triple bond has three.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning to find the concentration of a carbonate solution by collecting gas
method_templates.method:
1. Measure 25 cm³ of the carbonate solution into a conical flask.
2. Add excess dilute acid and connect a gas syringe at once.
3. Record the gas volume when it stops rising.
4. Moles of CO₂ = volume in dm³ ÷ 24.
5. Moles of carbonate = moles of CO₂.
6. Concentration = moles ÷ 0.025 dm³.
method_templates.watch_out: State the assumption that no gas escapes before the syringe is connected.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing the oxidation of an alcohol to a carboxylic acid
method_templates.method:
1. Reagent: acidified potassium manganate(VII).
2. Condition: warm.
3. Observation: purple solution turns colourless.
4. Product: the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms, and water.
method_templates.watch_out: Say "acidified". Give the colour before and after.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining the conditions chosen for the Haber process
method_templates.method:
1. Temperature: lower gives a higher yield but the reaction is too slow; higher is fast but the yield is too low. 450 °C is the compromise.
2. Pressure: higher gives a higher yield, but very high pressure costs too much. 200 atm is used.
3. Iron catalyst speeds up the reaction.
4. Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.
method_templates.watch_out: Each answer needs both sides: yield and rate for temperature, yield and cost for pressure.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Drawing a dot-and-cross diagram for an ionic compound
method_templates.method:
1. Write the electron arrangement of each atom and decide how many electrons the metal gives away.
2. Work out how many of each ion are needed so the charges cancel.
3. Draw each ion in square brackets with its charge outside.
4. Metal ion: show an empty outer shell (or the full shell below). Non-metal ion: eight outer electrons, with the gained ones drawn as the other symbol.
5. Write the number of each ion in front of its bracket.
method_templates.watch_out: No shared electrons and no overlapping shells in an ionic diagram.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning: comparing how well two catalysts work
method_templates.method:
1. Measure the same volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide into a flask.
2. Add a fixed mass of the first catalyst. Join a gas syringe at once and start the stopwatch.
3. Record the gas volume at regular time intervals.
4. Repeat with the same mass of the second catalyst at the same temperature.
5. Plot volume against time for both.
6. The steeper starting gradient is the better catalyst.
method_templates.watch_out: Change only the catalyst. Both runs end at the same final volume; the gradient is what differs.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Identifying the anion in an unknown solution
method_templates.method:
1. Chloride: add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate; white precipitate.
2. Sulfate: add dilute nitric acid, then barium nitrate; white precipitate.
3. Nitrate: add sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil, warm; gas turns moist red litmus blue.
4. Carbonate: add dilute acid; gas gives white precipitate with limewater.
method_templates.watch_out: For a negative test write "no visible change", then move to the next test.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Total pressure at a depth in a liquid
method_templates.method:
1. Pressure due to the liquid = depth × density × g.
2. Use depth in m and density in kg/m³.
3. Add atmospheric pressure to get the total pressure at that depth.
method_templates.watch_out: If the question asks for the pressure due to the liquid only, do not add atmospheric pressure.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Sketching the current–time graph for a magnet falling through a coil
method_templates.method:
1. Entering the coil: draw one pulse.
2. Fully inside: current is zero.
3. Leaving: draw a pulse on the opposite side of the axis.
4. Make the second pulse taller and narrower, because the magnet is now faster.
method_templates.watch_out: The two pulses are not the same size; the magnet speeds up as it falls.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Finding the missing product in a cracking equation
method_templates.method:
1. Write the big alkane on the left and the known products on the right.
2. Subtract carbon atoms to get the carbons in the missing product.
3. Subtract hydrogen atoms the same way.
4. Check: carbons and hydrogens balance on both sides.
5. CnH2n means the missing product is an alkene.
method_templates.watch_out: Multiply by the number of moles of each product before subtracting.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a more reactive metal protects iron from rusting
method_templates.method:
1. State that the other metal is more reactive than iron.
2. Say it corrodes (loses electrons) in place of the iron.
3. Say the iron stays protected as long as some of that metal remains.
method_templates.watch_out: This works even when the coating is scratched. A barrier such as paint, grease or tin works only while it keeps out oxygen and water.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Recording readings in a results table
method_templates.method:
1. Head each column with quantity / unit, e.g. t / s.
2. Put no units inside the cells.
3. Write every raw reading to the precision of the instrument.
4. Keep the same number of decimal places down a column.
5. List the values you chose in rising order.
method_templates.watch_out: A ruler reading of exactly 12 cm is written 12.0 cm; a stopwatch reading keeps both decimal places.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing what happens at one electrode
method_templates.method:
1. Name the ions that move to that electrode.
2. Say which ion is discharged.
3. Say whether it gains electrons (cathode, reduction) or loses electrons (anode, oxidation).
4. Write the half-equation with state symbols.
5. State what is seen: a gas given off or a metal deposited.
method_templates.watch_out: Anode = positive electrode, takes electrons from anions. Cathode = negative electrode, gives electrons to cations.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why energy is lost between trophic levels
method_templates.method:
1. Only about a tenth of the energy at one level reaches the next.
2. Much is lost as heat from respiration.
3. Some stays in uneaten parts.
4. Some leaves in faeces and excreted waste.
5. So a shorter food chain passes on more of the producers' energy.
method_templates.watch_out: Energy flows one way and is not recycled. Carbon is cycled; energy is not.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Electrolysis of a molten mixture of salts
method_templates.method:
1. List the positive ions and the negative ions present. There is no water, so no H⁺ or OH⁻.
2. Negative electrode: the ion of the least reactive metal is discharged first.
3. Positive electrode: the simple halide ion is discharged, not sulfate.
4. Write a half-equation for each.
method_templates.watch_out: Molten means no hydrogen or oxygen from water.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Finding the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons
method_templates.method:
1. Protons = proton (atomic) number.
2. Neutrons = nucleon (mass) number – proton number.
3. Atom: electrons = protons.
4. Ion: take away electrons for a positive charge, add them for a negative charge.
method_templates.watch_out: The larger of the two numbers is the nucleon number, wherever it is printed.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Charging a metal sphere by induction
method_templates.method:
1. Bring a charged rod near the sphere without touching it.
2. Earth the sphere (touch it) while the rod stays near.
3. Electrons flow to or from the earth.
4. Remove the earth connection first.
5. Then remove the rod.
6. The sphere is left with the charge opposite to the rod.
method_templates.watch_out: If the rod is taken away before the earth connection, the sphere ends up neutral.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Drawing a dot-and-cross diagram of a simple molecule
method_templates.method:
1. Find the number of outer-shell electrons of each atom.
2. Work out how many more each atom needs for a full shell.
3. Overlap the shells and place that many shared pairs in the overlap.
4. Use dots for one element and crosses for the other.
5. Add the unshared outer electrons.
6. Label each atom with its symbol and count every shell.
method_templates.watch_out: Count each atom's outer shell at the end: 8 (2 for hydrogen). No electron may be lost or added compared with the free atoms.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning: finding the water of crystallisation in a hydrated salt
method_templates.method:
1. Weigh an empty crucible, then weigh it with the hydrated salt.
2. Heat strongly, cool and weigh again.
3. Repeat heating, cooling and weighing until the mass stays the same.
4. Mass lost = mass of water. Final mass − crucible = mass of anhydrous salt.
5. Turn both masses into moles.
6. Divide moles of water by moles of salt to get x.
method_templates.watch_out: One heating is not enough. Say "heat to constant mass" to show all the water has gone.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why graphite conducts electricity and is soft
method_templates.method:
1. Each carbon atom is bonded to three others, in layers.
2. One outer electron per atom is not used in bonding.
3. These electrons are mobile and carry charge: graphite conducts.
4. Only weak forces act between the layers.
5. The layers slide over each other easily: graphite is soft and slippery.
method_templates.watch_out: In diamond each carbon is bonded to four others, so no electrons are free and it does not conduct.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a villus is adapted for absorption
method_templates.method:
1. Microvilli on the cells: larger surface area.
2. Wall one cell thick: short distance to diffuse.
3. Many blood capillaries carry glucose and amino acids away: keeps a steep concentration gradient.
4. A lacteal carries fats away.
method_templates.watch_out: Each feature needs its effect on the rate of absorption. A list of features alone scores half.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a population evolved a feature by natural selection
method_templates.method:
1. Mutation gave variation: some individuals had the feature, some did not.
2. Name the selection pressure from the question (fire, disease, predator).
3. Those with the feature survived; the others died.
4. The survivors reproduced and passed the allele to their offspring.
5. Over many generations, most of the population has the feature.
method_templates.watch_out: Use the context's own words in every step. A general account with no mention of the organism or the pressure scores poorly.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining which substance is oxidised or reduced using oxidation states
method_templates.method:
1. Find the oxidation state of the element before and after.
2. Increase: oxidised. Decrease: reduced.
3. Write the sentence with the numbers and the species: "the oxidation state of iron increases from 0 in Fe to +3 in FeCl₃".
4. Do the same for the other substance.
method_templates.watch_out: Name the element, both numbers and both species. "It gains oxygen" is not enough when no oxygen is involved.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how silica is removed in the blast furnace
method_templates.method:
1. Limestone decomposes in the heat to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
2. Calcium oxide (basic) reacts with silica (acidic).
3. The product is molten calcium silicate, called slag.
4. Slag floats on the molten iron and is run off separately.
method_templates.watch_out: Three marks: decomposition of limestone, reaction with silica, slag removed. Write both equations if you can.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a fatty diet leads to a heart attack
method_templates.method:
1. Fat and cholesterol are deposited on the inner wall of the coronary arteries.
2. The lumen narrows and the wall hardens.
3. Less blood flows, or a clot blocks the artery.
4. Heart muscle gets less oxygen and glucose.
5. It cannot release enough energy and that part of the muscle dies.
method_templates.watch_out: Name the coronary arteries and say what the muscle is short of: oxygen and glucose for respiration.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deducing an order of reactivity from displacement results
method_templates.method:
1. For each metal, count how many of the other metals it displaces from their solutions or oxides.
2. The metal that displaces the most is the most reactive.
3. A metal that displaces none is the least reactive.
4. Write the order and check it against every result in the table.
method_templates.watch_out: "No reaction" is a result: the metal added is less reactive than the metal in the compound.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning an experiment to compare how fast two metal samples rust
method_templates.method:
1. Use pieces of the same size and shape.
2. Weigh each piece.
3. Place each in the same volume of the same water in a stoppered test tube, at the same temperature.
4. Leave for the same number of days.
5. Dry and weigh again.
6. The larger increase in mass has rusted more.
method_templates.watch_out: State what is kept the same and what is measured. "See which rusts more" is not a measurement.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Transformer calculation with an efficiency below 100%
method_templates.method:
1. Find the secondary voltage from Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.
2. Input power = Vp × Ip.
3. Output power = efficiency × input power.
4. Secondary current = output power ÷ Vs.
method_templates.watch_out: VpIp = VsIs holds only for an ideal transformer. The turns ratio still gives the voltage.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Drawing a best-fit line through plotted points
method_templates.method:
1. Plot each point as a small, sharp cross.
2. Lay a clear ruler so the points are spread evenly on both sides along the whole line.
3. Draw one thin line.
4. Circle and label any point far from the line; leave it out of the fit.
5. For a curve, draw one smooth freehand curve.
method_templates.watch_out: Do not join point to point, and do not force the line through the origin.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why an alloy is harder than the pure metal
method_templates.method:
1. Pure metal: atoms of the same size sit in regular layers.
2. The layers slide over each other easily when a force is applied.
3. Alloy: atoms of a different size disrupt the regular arrangement.
4. The layers can no longer slide easily, so the alloy is harder.
method_templates.watch_out: Say "different size" and "layers cannot slide easily". Both phrases carry marks.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing how the electrolyte changes during electrolysis
method_templates.method:
1. Write which two ions are discharged.
2. Write which two ions are left behind.
3. Name what the left-behind ions make: H⁺ left means more acidic; OH⁻ left means more alkaline.
4. If a coloured ion such as Cu²⁺ is removed, say the colour fades.
method_templates.watch_out: If only H⁺ and OH⁻ are discharged, water is being removed, so the solution becomes more concentrated.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Setting up an electroplating cell
method_templates.method:
1. Make the object to be plated the cathode (join it to the negative terminal).
2. Make the plating metal the anode (positive terminal).
3. Use a solution of a salt of the plating metal as the electrolyte.
4. State the changes: the anode gets smaller, the object gains a metal coat, the solution keeps its colour and concentration.
method_templates.watch_out: If the object does not get coated, the connections are the wrong way round. Reverse them.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Setting up a cell to electroplate an object
method_templates.method:
1. Make the object the cathode (negative terminal).
2. Make the plating metal the anode (positive terminal).
3. Use a solution of a salt of the plating metal as the electrolyte.
4. Anode: metal atoms lose electrons and go into solution.
5. Cathode: metal ions gain electrons and coat the object.
method_templates.watch_out: The object is always the cathode. Swap the terminals and the object dissolves instead.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how air is breathed in (and out)
method_templates.method:
1. Diaphragm muscle contracts and flattens.
2. External intercostal muscles contract, internal ones relax.
3. Ribs move up and out.
4. Volume of the thorax increases.
5. Pressure in the lungs falls below air pressure.
6. Air is forced in.
For breathing out, reverse every step.
method_templates.watch_out: Keep the order: muscles, ribs, volume, pressure, air. Air moves because of the pressure change.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Finding out whether an organism with the dominant trait is homozygous or heterozygous (test cross)
method_templates.method:
1. Cross it with a homozygous recessive organism.
2. Look at many offspring.
3. All offspring show the dominant trait: the organism is homozygous dominant.
4. About half show the recessive trait: the organism is heterozygous.
5. Show both cases with a Punnett square.
method_templates.watch_out: An organism showing the recessive trait needs no test cross. Its genotype can only be homozygous recessive.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Finding the direction of the induced current when a magnet moves near a coil
method_templates.method:
1. Note which pole faces the coil and whether it moves in or out.
2. Moving in: the near end of the coil becomes the SAME pole, to repel it.
3. Moving out: the near end becomes the OPPOSITE pole, to attract it.
4. Use the right-hand grip rule (thumb to the N end) to get the current direction.
method_templates.watch_out: Changing the pole OR the direction of motion reverses the current; changing both leaves it the same.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Calculating percentage change in mass or length of tissue
method_templates.method:
1. Change = final value − starting value.
2. Divide the change by the STARTING value.
3. Multiply by 100.
4. Keep the sign: + for a gain, − for a loss.
5. Round to match the precision of the data.
method_templates.watch_out: A loss must carry a minus sign; the sign has its own mark.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describe flue gas desulfurisation with equations
method_templates.method:
1. Say the waste gas from the power station is passed through calcium carbonate (limestone) or calcium oxide.
2. Write: CaCO3 + SO2 -> CaSO3 + CO2 (or CaO + SO2 -> CaSO3).
3. Say calcium sulfite is then oxidised by air: 2CaSO3 + O2 -> 2CaSO4.
4. State the result: sulfur dioxide is removed, so less acid rain.
method_templates.watch_out: This works because sulfur dioxide is acidic. It does not remove carbon monoxide.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Choosing how to prepare a salt
method_templates.method:
1. Decide whether the salt is soluble.
2. Insoluble salt: precipitation, by mixing two solutions that each supply one of its ions.
3. Soluble salt of sodium, potassium or ammonium: titration of acid with alkali.
4. Any other soluble salt: add excess insoluble metal, oxide or carbonate to the acid.
method_templates.watch_out: All starting substances for sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble, so excess cannot be filtered off.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Choosing a suitable fuse rating
method_templates.method:
1. Find the normal working current: I = P ÷ V.
2. Look at the fuse ratings offered.
3. Pick the one just above the working current.
4. Example: 5 kW at 240 V draws about 21 A, so use the 25 A fuse.
method_templates.watch_out: A rating below the working current blows in normal use; one far above gives no protection.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Sketching the new product–time curve after a change in conditions
method_templates.method:
1. Decide if the rate changes: faster means a steeper start.
2. Find the limiting reactant.
3. Ask if its number of moles has changed.
4. Unchanged: the curve levels off at the same height, only sooner or later.
5. Changed: scale the final height by the same factor.
6. Start at the origin.
method_templates.watch_out: Changing the reactant in excess changes the slope only, never the final height.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Reading peak voltage and frequency from an oscilloscope trace
method_templates.method:
1. Peak voltage = squares from the centre line to the top of the wave × volts per square.
2. Period = squares across one full wave × time per square.
3. Change ms to s.
4. Frequency = 1 ÷ period.
method_templates.watch_out: Count from the centre line, not from trough to crest.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Checking whether a liquid is pure
method_templates.method:
1. Measure its boiling point.
2. Pure: it boils at one fixed temperature.
3. Impure: it boils over a range of temperatures.
method_templates.watch_out: A fixed boiling point means pure; a range means impure.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predicting the products when an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes
method_templates.method:
1. List four ions: two from the compound, plus H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
2. Cathode: the ion of the less reactive metal (or H⁺) is discharged.
3. Anode: OH⁻ is discharged, giving oxygen and water.
4. Exception: a concentrated chloride, bromide or iodide gives the halogen at the anode.
5. Write the half-equations.
method_templates.watch_out: Sulfate and nitrate ions are never discharged, however concentrated the solution is.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Concentration from a thermometric titration graph
method_templates.method:
1. Draw the two best-fit straight lines on the temperature graph.
2. Read the volume where they cross. This is the volume that just neutralises the acid.
3. Moles of acid = concentration × volume in dm³.
4. Use the ratio to get moles of alkali.
5. Concentration of alkali = moles ÷ the volume from the graph in dm³.
method_templates.watch_out: The volume at the crossing point is the titre. Do not use the last volume added.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describe the reactions in the blast furnace with equations
method_templates.method:
1. Coke burns in hot air: C + O2 -> CO2. This gives the heat.
2. Carbon dioxide meets more coke: CO2 + C -> 2CO.
3. Carbon monoxide reduces the ore: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2.
4. Limestone breaks down: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
5. Calcium oxide removes sand: CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (slag).
6. Molten iron sinks; slag floats on it.
method_templates.watch_out: Three raw materials go in at the top (haematite, coke, limestone); hot air goes in near the bottom.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Identifying the stage of mitosis from a diagram
method_templates.method:
1. Chromosomes short and visible, nuclear membrane disappearing: prophase.
2. Chromosomes lined up in a single row at the equator: metaphase.
3. Chromatids pulled apart to opposite poles: anaphase.
4. Two new nuclei forming, cytoplasm starting to divide: telophase.
method_templates.watch_out: In meiosis I the chromosomes line up in PAIRS at the equator, and whole chromosomes (not chromatids) are pulled apart.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Energy delivered by a cell given current and time
method_templates.method:
1. Change the time to seconds.
2. Charge Q = I × t.
3. Energy W = Q × V, using the e.m.f. or the p.d. given.
4. Answer in joules.
method_templates.watch_out: Use e.m.f. for the whole circuit and p.d. for a single component.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing how to check that a substance is pure
method_templates.method:
1. Measure its melting point (or boiling point).
2. Pure: it melts or boils at one fixed temperature.
3. Impure: it melts or boils over a range of temperatures.
method_templates.watch_out: Say "at a fixed temperature". "It has a high melting point" does not show purity.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Finding the rate of an enzyme reaction from a product against time graph
method_templates.method:
1. Draw the best-fit curve.
2. At the time asked, draw a tangent to the curve.
3. Build a large triangle on the tangent.
4. Rate = rise ÷ run.
5. Give the unit: the y-unit per the x-unit (e.g. % per min).
method_templates.watch_out: The triangle must be shown on the graph. No unit, no full marks.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deducing a reactivity order from reduction of metal oxides
method_templates.method:
1. "Carbon (or metal R) removes oxygen from the oxide of P": carbon (or R) is more reactive than P.
2. "Does not remove oxygen": it is less reactive than that metal.
3. Write each fact as an inequality.
4. Join them into one order.
method_templates.watch_out: The metal whose oxide carbon cannot reduce is the MOST reactive one.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Mass ↔ moles
method_templates.method:
1. Write the formula of the substance as it exists (O₂ for oxygen gas).
2. Find its Mr.
3. Change the mass to grams.
4. Moles = mass ÷ Mr. Mass = moles × Mr.
method_templates.watch_out: Decide between the atom and the molecule before finding Mr: nitrogen gas is 28, nitrogen atoms are 14.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predict whether a halogen displacement happens and what is seen
method_templates.method:
1. Order of reactivity: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine.
2. A reaction happens only if the halogen added is ABOVE the halide in the solution.
3. The colour seen is that of the halogen set free: bromine reddish-brown, iodine brown.
4. Write the ionic equation, for example Cl2 + 2I- -> 2Cl- + I2.
5. If the halogen added is BELOW the halide, there is no reaction: the mixture just keeps the colour of the halogen that was added (e.g. iodine solution added to potassium bromide stays brown). Do not write 'colourless'.
method_templates.watch_out: The halide solution itself is colourless at the start.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deducing the structure of a substance from a table of properties
method_templates.method:
1. Conducts when solid: metal (or graphite).
2. High melting point, does not conduct as a solid but does when molten or aqueous: giant ionic.
3. Very high melting point, never conducts, insoluble: giant covalent.
4. Low melting point, never conducts: simple molecular.
method_templates.watch_out: Check conductivity in every state given before deciding.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning tests to identify several unlabelled colourless solutions
method_templates.method:
1. Take a small sample of each solution in separate test-tubes.
2. Add the first reagent to all; state what is seen in the one that reacts and name it.
3. Test the remaining solutions with the next reagent.
4. Carry on until every solution has its own positive result.
5. For any gas, give its test and result.
method_templates.watch_out: Each solution needs a positive test. "The one left over must be X" does not score.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Recording what happens when a solid is heated
method_templates.method:
1. Record the colour of the solid before heating.
2. Record any colour change, melting, or liquid at the mouth of the tube.
3. Test any gas given off and name it.
4. Record the colour again after cooling.
method_templates.watch_out: Heat until there is no further change before writing the final colour.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explain how a catalytic converter cuts pollutants from a car exhaust
method_templates.method:
1. Name the three pollutants going in: carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen, unburnt hydrocarbons.
2. Say carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons are oxidised to carbon dioxide (and water).
3. Say oxides of nitrogen are reduced to nitrogen.
4. Give one equation: 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2.
method_templates.watch_out: The products are harmless to breathe, but carbon dioxide is still a greenhouse gas.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Finding resistance at a point on a curved I–V graph
method_templates.method:
1. Go to the given p.d. (or current) on the graph.
2. Read off the matching current (or p.d.).
3. Resistance = that p.d. ÷ that current.
4. Repeat at a second point to show how the resistance changes.
method_templates.watch_out: Do not use the gradient of the curve or of a tangent.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Recording titration results and finding the average titre
method_templates.method:
1. Record every burette reading to 2 decimal places.
2. Titre = final reading − initial reading.
3. Repeat until two titres are within 0.20 cm³ of each other.
4. Tick those results.
5. Average only the ticked titres.
method_templates.watch_out: The rough titration is not included in the average.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing the menstrual cycle with oestrogen and progesterone
method_templates.method:
1. Days 1–5: both hormones low, uterine lining breaks down (menstruation).
2. Days 6–13: a follicle grows and makes oestrogen; the lining is repaired and thickens.
3. Day 14: ovulation, an egg is released.
4. Days 15–28: progesterone keeps the lining thick and full of blood vessels.
5. No fertilisation: progesterone falls, the lining breaks down, the cycle restarts.
method_templates.watch_out: Oestrogen repairs the lining; progesterone maintains it. Do not swap them.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how a blood clot forms
method_templates.method:
1. Blood vessels are damaged; platelets gather at the wound.
2. Soluble fibrinogen in the plasma is changed to insoluble fibrin threads.
3. The threads form a mesh across the wound.
4. The mesh traps blood cells and forms a clot.
5. The clot seals the wound: less blood is lost and bacteria are kept out.
method_templates.watch_out: FibrinoGEN is the soluble one in the plasma; fibrin is the insoluble thread.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Testing for a cation with aqueous sodium hydroxide or aqueous ammonia
method_templates.method:
1. Use about 1 cm depth of the solution.
2. Add the reagent a few drops at a time and shake.
3. Record whether a precipitate forms and its colour.
4. Add the reagent until in excess.
5. Record whether the precipitate dissolves, and the colour of the solution formed.
method_templates.watch_out: Two observations are needed: at a few drops and in excess. Adding too much at once can hide the precipitate.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Writing equations for complete and incomplete combustion
method_templates.method:
1. Complete (plenty of oxygen): products are carbon dioxide and water.
2. Incomplete (limited oxygen): products are carbon monoxide or carbon (soot), and water.
3. Balance C first, then H, then O.
method_templates.watch_out: Water is formed in both cases.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Telling apart an alkene, an alcohol and a carboxylic acid by chemical tests
method_templates.method:
1. Add aqueous bromine to each. Reddish-brown turns colourless: the alkene.
2. Add a carbonate to the other two. Effervescence, gas gives a white precipitate with limewater: the carboxylic acid.
3. Warm the last one with acidified potassium manganate(VII). Purple turns colourless: the alcohol.
method_templates.watch_out: For each test give the result for the liquids that do NOT react as well: "stays reddish-brown", "no effervescence".

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Finding an unknown bond energy from ΔH
method_templates.method:
1. Call the unknown bond energy x.
2. Write the total for bonds broken and the total for bonds formed, with x in the right place.
3. Set: bonds broken − bonds formed = ΔH (keep the sign of ΔH).
4. Solve for x.
method_templates.watch_out: Count how many of the unknown bond there are; the total may be 2x, not x.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Separating a soluble solid from an insoluble solid
method_templates.method:
1. Add excess water and stir until the soluble solid has dissolved.
2. Filter. The insoluble solid is the residue.
3. Wash the residue with distilled water and dry it.
4. Heat the filtrate to evaporate water until crystals of the soluble solid form.
method_templates.watch_out: The order is always dissolve, filter, evaporate.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Planning an experiment on the effect of temperature on catalase
method_templates.method:
1. Set water baths at 5 or more temperatures.
2. Use the same mass of tissue and the same volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide each time.
3. Leave both in the bath to reach the temperature before mixing.
4. Mix and measure the oxygen collected in a fixed time.
5. Use fresh tissue each time. Repeat and find the mean.
6. Plot volume against temperature.
method_templates.watch_out: Give one safety step with its reason: hydrogen peroxide is corrosive, so wear goggles and gloves.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a catalyst speeds up a reaction
method_templates.method:
1. Say the catalyst lowers the activation energy.
2. Say more of the colliding particles now have enough energy to react.
3. Say the frequency of effective collisions increases, so the rate is faster.
4. If asked about the end: the catalyst is chemically unchanged and its mass is the same.
method_templates.watch_out: A catalyst does not make particles move faster or collide more often.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning: finding the percentage of a metal in its oxide ore by reduction with carbon
method_templates.method:
1. Weigh a sample of the ore in a crucible.
2. Mix with excess carbon powder.
3. Heat strongly with the lid off until no more change is seen.
4. Cool and weigh the metal left.
5. Percentage = mass of metal ÷ mass of ore × 100.
method_templates.watch_out: Leave the crucible uncovered so the extra carbon burns away as carbon dioxide and is not weighed with the metal.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how the body responds when it gets too hot
method_templates.method:
1. Temperature receptors in the skin, and the hypothalamus, detect the rise.
2. The hypothalamus sends nerve impulses to effectors.
3. Arterioles in the skin dilate: more blood flows near the surface, more heat lost.
4. Sweat glands make more sweat: evaporation removes heat.
5. Metabolic rate falls: less heat released.
6. Body temperature returns to normal.
method_templates.watch_out: For a cold day, reverse every step and add shivering: muscle contractions release heat.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predicting the products when a molten ionic compound is electrolysed
method_templates.method:
1. Write the two ions in the compound.
2. The positive ion (metal) goes to the cathode and gains electrons: the metal forms.
3. The negative ion (non-metal) goes to the anode and loses electrons: the non-metal forms.
4. Write each half-equation and balance the electrons.
method_templates.watch_out: Molten means only two ions. There is no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing and explaining a rate of photosynthesis against carbon dioxide concentration graph
method_templates.method:
1. Rising part: as carbon dioxide concentration rises, the rate rises. Quote values.
2. Reason: carbon dioxide is the limiting factor here.
3. Flat part: the rate stays almost constant. Quote where it levels off.
4. Reason: carbon dioxide is no longer limiting; another factor (light or temperature) now limits the rate.
method_templates.watch_out: If the table gives time taken, a SHORTER time means a FASTER rate.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how a d.c. motor keeps turning
method_templates.method:
1. Current in the coil in a magnetic field: each side feels a force.
2. The currents in the two sides are opposite, so the forces are opposite: one up, one down.
3. This pair of forces turns the coil.
4. Every half turn the split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil.
5. So the coil keeps turning the same way.
method_templates.watch_out: Name the split-ring commutator and say WHEN it reverses the current.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Comparing the thermal stability of metal carbonates
method_templates.method:
1. Heat the same number of moles of each carbonate in the same way.
2. Pass the gas into limewater, or measure its volume each minute.
3. Slower carbon dioxide production means a more stable carbonate.
4. More stable carbonate means a more reactive metal.
method_templates.watch_out: Carbonates of very reactive metals such as sodium and potassium do not decompose on heating.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how burning fossil fuels damages buildings
method_templates.method:
1. Fossil fuels contain sulfur, so burning gives sulfur dioxide.
2. Sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen and rainwater.
3. This forms acid rain.
4. Acid rain corrodes limestone and metal structures.
method_templates.watch_out: Name the gas and name what is corroded; "pollution damages buildings" scores nothing.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing how ethanol is made by fermentation
method_templates.method:
1. Mix glucose solution with yeast.
2. Keep it at about 37 °C.
3. Keep air out.
4. Glucose turns into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
5. Separate the ethanol by fractional distillation.
method_templates.watch_out: Fermentation only gives a dilute solution (about 15 %), because the yeast dies in more ethanol.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Calculating an Rf value
method_templates.method:
1. Measure from the start line to the centre of the spot.
2. Measure from the start line to the solvent front.
3. Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent.
4. Give the answer as a decimal with no unit.
method_templates.watch_out: Rf is always less than 1, because the solvent travels furthest.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Volume of gas left after air is passed over heated copper
method_templates.method:
1. Copper removes only the oxygen.
2. Oxygen is about 21% of air.
3. Volume removed = 21% of the starting volume.
4. Volume left = starting volume − volume removed.
5. Read volumes only after cooling to room temperature.
method_templates.watch_out: The question usually asks for the gas REMAINING, not the oxygen used up.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Choosing a scale for a graph axis
method_templates.method:
1. Take largest value minus smallest value on that axis.
2. Divide by the number of big squares available.
3. Round UP to an easy step: 1, 2 or 5 (times a power of ten).
4. Label the axis as quantity / unit.
5. Number every big square.
method_templates.watch_out: The plotted points should cover more than half the grid each way. The axis need not start at zero.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Why the catalytic converter reaction is redox
method_templates.method:
1. Write 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
2. Carbon goes from +2 in CO to +4 in CO₂: oxidised.
3. Nitrogen goes from +2 in NO to 0 in N₂: reduced.
4. Both happen in the same reaction, so it is redox.
method_templates.watch_out: Quote the oxidation state before AND after for each element.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Finding the poles of a solenoid or the field around a straight wire
method_templates.method:
1. Mark the direction of conventional current.
2. Straight wire: right thumb along the current; curled fingers show the field circles.
3. Solenoid: curl right fingers the way the current goes round the turns; the thumb points to the N pole.
4. Draw field lines out of N and into S.
method_templates.watch_out: The two grips are different: thumb is current for a wire, thumb is N pole for a coil.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why a reaction stopped, given amounts of both reactants
method_templates.method:
1. Convert each reactant to moles (mass ÷ Mr, or concentration × volume in dm³).
2. Compare with the mole ratio in the equation.
3. Name the reactant that is used up and the one in excess.
4. State that the reaction stopped because that reactant was all used up.
method_templates.watch_out: Show the mole numbers. "The reactants ran out" does not say which one.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing selective breeding (artificial selection)
method_templates.method:
1. Choose parents that show the wanted trait.
2. Breed them together (cross two varieties if each has one wanted trait).
3. Pick the offspring that show the trait best.
4. Breed these with each other.
5. Repeat over many generations until all offspring show the trait.
method_templates.watch_out: Humans do the choosing. Do not write that the environment selects.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how the eye focuses on a near (or distant) object
method_templates.method:
1. Near: ciliary muscles contract.
2. Suspensory ligaments slacken.
3. Lens becomes thicker and more convex.
4. Light is bent more and focused on the retina.
Distant: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments pulled taut, lens thinner, light bent less.
method_templates.watch_out: The ligaments do not contract or relax; they slacken or become taut. Contracting ciliary muscles give SLACK ligaments.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning how to find the percentage purity of a soluble salt with an insoluble impurity
method_templates.method:
1. Weigh the impure sample.
2. Add excess water and stir until no more dissolves.
3. Filter.
4. Wash the residue with water and dry it.
5. Weigh the dry residue: this is the impurity.
6. Mass of salt = sample − impurity. Divide by the sample mass and multiply by 100.
method_templates.watch_out: The residue must be washed and fully dry before weighing, or the impurity looks heavier than it is.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deciding the electrodes and electron flow in a simple cell
method_templates.method:
1. Find the two metals in the reactivity series.
2. The more reactive metal is the negative electrode. It loses electrons and dissolves.
3. Electrons flow through the wire from the more reactive metal to the less reactive one.
4. At the less reactive metal, ions from the solution gain electrons (hydrogen gas in an acid).
5. The further apart the two metals, the larger the voltage.
method_templates.watch_out: Two electrodes of the same metal give no voltage.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Naming a blood vessel from the organ it joins
method_templates.method:
1. Find the organ: lungs = pulmonary, liver = hepatic, kidney = renal, heart muscle = coronary.
2. Decide the direction: away from the heart is an artery, towards the heart is a vein.
3. Put the two together, such as renal vein.
method_templates.watch_out: Artery or vein is set by direction, not by oxygen. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predicting the products of electrolysing an aqueous solution with inert electrodes
method_templates.method:
1. List every ion present, including H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
2. Cathode: send the positive ions there. The ion of the less reactive element is discharged (H⁺ unless the metal is below hydrogen).
3. Anode: send the negative ions there. OH⁻ is discharged, unless the solution is a concentrated halide.
4. Write the half-equation at each electrode.
5. State what is seen and what happens to the solution.
method_templates.watch_out: Sulfate and nitrate ions are never discharged. A concentrated chloride gives chlorine; a dilute one gives oxygen.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how ADH changes the urine after water loss or a large drink
method_templates.method:
1. State the change in water potential of blood plasma (falls after sweating; rises after drinking).
2. The hypothalamus detects it.
3. The pituitary gland releases more (or less) ADH.
4. The collecting duct walls become more (or less) permeable to water.
5. More (or less) water is reabsorbed into the blood.
6. Urine: less and more concentrated (or more and dilute).
7. Water potential returns to normal.
method_templates.watch_out: More ADH = more water reabsorbed = LESS urine. Keep the direction consistent through every step.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing the path of water from soil to leaf
method_templates.method:
1. Soil water has a higher water potential than root hair cell sap, so water enters by osmosis.
2. It passes from cell to cell across the root by osmosis.
3. It enters the xylem.
4. It is drawn up the xylem mainly by transpiration pull, helped by root pressure and capillary action.
5. In the leaf it moves by osmosis to the mesophyll cells.
method_templates.watch_out: Use water potential for water movement between cells; concentration gradient is for the water vapour leaving the leaf.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Following a reaction that gives off a gas by loss of mass
method_templates.method:
1. Put the flask with the reactants on an electronic balance.
2. Plug the mouth loosely with cotton wool.
3. Record the mass at regular times.
4. Plot mass against time.
5. The curve falls steeply, then less steeply, then goes flat when the reaction stops.
method_templates.watch_out: The mass lost is the mass of gas that escaped. The curve flattens above zero.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Sketching the curve for a repeat experiment with one condition changed
method_templates.method:
1. Decide the steepness: higher concentration, higher temperature, smaller pieces or a catalyst give a steeper start.
2. Decide the final height: work out the moles of the reactant that runs out.
3. Same moles, same final height. Half the moles, half the height.
4. Start at the origin, draw the curve, level off, and label it.
method_templates.watch_out: Steepness and final height are two separate decisions. Make both every time.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Drawing the product of an addition reaction of an alkene
method_templates.method:
1. Draw the alkene.
2. Change the C=C to a single C–C bond.
3. Add one atom or group to each of the two carbons (H and H, Br and Br, or H and OH).
4. Check each carbon has four bonds.
5. There is only one product.
method_templates.watch_out: Conditions: hydrogen needs nickel and 200 °C; steam needs phosphoric(V) acid, 300 °C, 60 atm; bromine needs none.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Read a heating or cooling curve
method_templates.method:
1. Sloping parts: one state only, temperature changing.
2. Flat parts: a change of state, two states present.
3. Read the temperature of the lower flat part: melting (freezing) point.
4. Read the upper flat part: boiling (condensation) point.
5. Name the state in each sloping part from its place between these two.
method_templates.watch_out: A sharp, level flat part means a pure substance. A sloping change over a range means a mixture.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing what is seen in a displacement reaction
method_templates.method:
1. Say what happens to the metal added: it dissolves or gets smaller.
2. Give the colour and state of the metal that forms, e.g. a reddish-brown or grey solid deposit.
3. Give the colour change of the solution, from its starting colour to its final colour.
method_templates.watch_out: Three things to state: the metal added, the new solid, the solution.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing and explaining a displacement reaction between a metal and a salt solution
method_templates.method:
1. Compare the two metals in the reactivity series.
2. Describe the solid: name the colour of the metal deposited.
3. Describe the solution: colour at the start and colour at the end.
4. Explain: the more reactive metal displaces the less reactive metal from its salt solution.
5. Write the equation.
method_templates.watch_out: No reaction if the metal added is less reactive. Then write "no visible change".

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Planning an experiment to compare the energy given out by two fuels
method_templates.method:
1. Measure a fixed volume of water into a beaker or can and record its temperature.
2. Weigh the burner with fuel.
3. Burn the fuel under the water, stirring, then put out the flame.
4. Record the highest water temperature and weigh the burner again.
5. Repeat with the other fuel, using the same volume of water and the same mass burned.
6. Larger temperature rise: more energy given out.
method_templates.watch_out: Measure the temperature of the water, not of the fuel or the flame.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Choosing the method of extraction from a metal's position in the reactivity series
method_templates.method:
1. Find the metal in the reactivity series.
2. Above zinc (very reactive): electrolysis of the MOLTEN compound.
3. Zinc down to copper: heat the oxide with carbon.
4. Give the reason: the more reactive the metal, the harder its compound is to break down.
method_templates.watch_out: Carbon cannot reduce the oxides of very reactive metals such as sodium.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Comparing rates from a graph of product against time
method_templates.method:
1. Look at the gradient at the start: the steeper curve is the faster reaction.
2. Follow one curve: where it gets less steep, the reaction is slowing down.
3. Where the curve goes flat, the reaction has stopped.
4. Compare the heights of the flat parts: the higher one made more product.
method_templates.watch_out: Steepness tells you the rate. Final height tells you the amount made. They are separate answers.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Finding the probability of a child with a given trait and a given sex
method_templates.method:
1. Draw the genetic diagram for the trait.
2. Read off the probability of the trait (e.g. 1 in 4).
3. The probability of a boy, or of a girl, is 1 in 2.
4. Multiply the two probabilities.
method_templates.watch_out: "A boy with blood group O" needs both probabilities multiplied, not just the trait.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining the effect of concentration or pressure on rate
method_templates.method:
1. Higher concentration (or pressure) means more reacting particles per unit volume.
2. Particles collide more often.
3. The frequency of effective collisions increases.
4. The rate of reaction increases.
method_templates.watch_out: Write "frequency of effective collisions", not just "more collisions".

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Find the percentage of oxygen in air by passing air over heated copper
method_templates.method:
1. Note the starting volume of air in the syringes.
2. Pass the air back and forth over the hot copper until the volume stops falling.
3. Let the apparatus cool to room temperature, then read the final volume.
4. Volume of oxygen = starting volume - final volume.
5. Percentage = volume of oxygen / starting volume x 100.
method_templates.watch_out: The copper turns black (copper(II) oxide). The gas left is mostly nitrogen, about four fifths of the start.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explain the result of a rusting experiment with nails in different test tubes
method_templates.method:
1. For each tube, list what the nail can reach: oxygen? water?
2. Boiled water under a layer of oil: no oxygen, no rust.
3. Dry air with a drying agent: no water, no rust.
4. Air and water together: rust.
5. Salt or acid in the water: rusts faster.
6. Conclude that rusting needs both oxygen and water.
method_templates.watch_out: Say why each tube is set up: boiling drives out dissolved air, oil keeps air from getting back in.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Work out the formula of a compound from the groups of its elements
method_templates.method:
1. Read the group number of each element.
2. Metals in Groups I, II, III form ions of charge 1+, 2+, 3+.
3. Non-metals in Groups V, VI, VII form ions of charge 3-, 2-, 1-.
4. Balance the charges to zero.
5. Put brackets round a group ion such as NO3 if you need more than one.
method_templates.watch_out: A Group II nitrate is M(NO3)2, not MNO3.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Writing the substitution reaction of an alkane with chlorine
method_templates.method:
1. State the condition: ultraviolet light.
2. One hydrogen atom is replaced by one chlorine atom.
3. The other product is hydrogen chloride: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
4. With more chlorine, repeat: CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄, each time with HCl.
method_templates.watch_out: A mixture of chloroalkanes forms, so more than one organic product is possible.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Comparing water loss from the two surfaces of a leaf with cobalt chloride paper
method_templates.method:
1. Tape a piece of dry blue cobalt chloride paper to the upper surface and another to the lower surface.
2. Time how long each takes to turn fully pink.
3. The side that turns pink sooner loses more water vapour.
4. Link it to stomata: the lower surface usually has more.
method_templates.watch_out: Seal the paper fully with tape and handle it dry, or moisture from the air or fingers turns it pink.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deduce the monomer from a section of an addition polymer chain
method_templates.method:
1. Look only at the carbon backbone.
2. Cut it into pairs of carbons, starting from one end.
3. Check each pair carries the same side groups: that pair is the repeat unit.
4. Remove the two end bonds and put a double bond between the two carbons.
5. Name or draw this alkene as the monomer.
method_templates.watch_out: The monomer has a C=C; the polymer does not.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Stating a source of error in an experiment
method_templates.method:
1. Name the thing in this set-up that you could not control.
2. Say which reading it affects.
3. Say how: the reading is larger or smaller than the true value.
4. Example: heat lost to the air while the hot object was moved, so the measured temperature rise is too small.
method_templates.watch_out: Parallax error, zero error and "human error" are not accepted; they can be prevented.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Put metals in order of reactivity from a table of observations
method_templates.method:
1. Check cold water first: metals that react are the most reactive.
2. Next, those that react only with steam.
3. Next, those that react only with dilute acid; rank by how fast the bubbles form.
4. Metals with no reaction with acid go last.
5. Use displacement or 'oxide reduced by carbon' to settle close pairs.
method_templates.watch_out: Compare like with like: same acid, same concentration, same size of metal piece.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Using time taken (disappearing cross) to compare rates
method_templates.method:
1. Mix the same volumes each time, changing only one concentration.
2. Time until the cross can no longer be seen.
3. Shorter time means faster reaction.
4. Link the trend to the concentration: lower concentration, fewer particles per unit volume, less frequent effective collisions, longer time.
method_templates.watch_out: Time and rate move in opposite directions.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Working out the oxidation state of an element in a compound or ion
method_templates.method:
1. An uncombined element is 0.
2. Put in the known values: oxygen −2, hydrogen +1, Group 1 metals +1.
3. Let the unknown be x and multiply each value by the number of atoms.
4. Set the sum equal to 0 for a compound, or to the charge for an ion.
5. Solve for x and write the sign.
method_templates.watch_out: For an ion the sum equals the charge of the ion, not zero.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Writing an ionic equation for a precipitation reaction
method_templates.method:
1. Write the balanced chemical equation with state symbols.
2. Split every aqueous substance into its ions.
3. Leave solids, liquids and gases whole.
4. Cross out ions that appear unchanged on both sides.
5. Write what is left, and check atoms and charges balance.
method_templates.watch_out: The precipitate is never split into ions.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Ranking metals from simple-cell voltages
method_templates.method:
1. For each cell, note which metal is the negative electrode: that one is more reactive.
2. Use the size of the voltage as the gap between the two metals.
3. Place the metals on one line, using a shared metal to join the cells.
4. Read off the order, and add or subtract gaps to get the voltage of a new pair.
method_templates.watch_out: A negative reading means the metals are connected the other way round: the second one is more reactive.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predicting which metal carbonate decomposes most easily on heating
method_templates.method:
1. Place the metals in the reactivity series.
2. The more reactive the metal, the more stable its carbonate to heat.
3. The carbonate of the least reactive metal decomposes at the lowest temperature, giving the oxide and carbon dioxide.
method_templates.watch_out: The carbonates of the very reactive metals such as sodium do not decompose in a Bunsen flame.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Interpreting the colour of hydrogencarbonate indicator
method_templates.method:
1. Red = carbon dioxide at the normal level in air.
2. Yellow = more carbon dioxide (more acidic).
3. Purple = less carbon dioxide.
4. Link to the process: yellow means respiration is faster than photosynthesis; purple means photosynthesis is faster.
method_templates.watch_out: Give the colour before and after, then what it shows about carbon dioxide.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Total e.m.f. of cells joined in series
method_templates.method:
1. Check which way each cell faces.
2. Cells facing the same way: add their e.m.f.s.
3. A cell facing the other way: subtract its e.m.f.
4. The current flows the way the larger total pushes it.
method_templates.watch_out: Two equal cells facing each other give zero e.m.f. and no current.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Reading a limiting-factor graph with several curves (rate against light intensity)
method_templates.method:
1. On the rising part of a curve, the factor on the x-axis is limiting.
2. Where the curve is flat, something else is limiting.
3. To find what, compare two curves at the same x-value that differ in ONE condition.
4. A big gap between them means that condition is the limiting factor there.
5. Quote the values from the graph.
method_templates.watch_out: A small gap between two curves means that condition is NOT limiting there, even though it was changed.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describe how to prepare a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble solid
method_templates.method:
1. Warm the acid.
2. Add the solid a little at a time, stirring, until some is left undissolved.
3. Filter off the excess solid.
4. Heat the filtrate until it is saturated.
5. Leave it to cool so crystals form.
6. Filter, rinse with a little cold distilled water, dry between filter paper.
method_templates.watch_out: To check for saturation, dip a glass rod in and take it out: crystals form on the rod as it cools.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Using a test cross to find an unknown genotype
method_templates.method:
1. Cross the organism that shows the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive one.
2. Look at many offspring.
3. All show the dominant trait: the unknown is homozygous dominant.
4. About half show the recessive trait (1 : 1): the unknown is heterozygous.
method_templates.watch_out: Even one recessive offspring proves the unknown parent is heterozygous.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Deciding exothermic or endothermic from an experiment
method_templates.method:
1. Compare the starting and final temperature of the mixture.
2. Temperature rises: energy was given out to the surroundings, exothermic.
3. Temperature falls: energy was taken in from the surroundings, endothermic.
4. Quote both temperatures as your evidence.
method_templates.watch_out: The solution and the thermometer are part of the surroundings.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Structuring the answer to any planning question
method_templates.method:
1. Name the apparatus and the amounts you measure.
2. State what you change and what you keep constant.
3. Give the steps in order.
4. State what you observe or measure.
5. Say how you process the readings.
6. End with a conclusion that answers the aim.
method_templates.watch_out: The last mark is usually the conclusion: say which result means what.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Relative formula mass (including hydrates)
method_templates.method:
1. Write the formula.
2. Count each kind of atom. A number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it.
3. For a hydrate, add the number of waters × 18.
4. Multiply each count by its Ar and add.
method_templates.watch_out: The dot in CuSO₄.5H₂O means add, not multiply: 160 + 5 × 18 = 250.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Finding the rate at one time, or the average rate, from a graph
method_templates.method:
1. Rate at one time: draw a tangent to the curve at that time.
2. Find the gradient of the tangent, with units such as cm³/s.
3. Average rate: read the total change in volume or mass.
4. Divide it by the time taken for that change.
method_templates.watch_out: For average rate over the whole reaction, use the time at which the curve first becomes flat.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.topic: Impact of Humans on the Environment
method_templates.question_type: Describing how fertiliser or sewage in a lake kills fish
method_templates.method:
1. Nitrates and phosphates make algae grow fast on the surface.
2. Light is blocked from the plants below.
3. These plants cannot photosynthesise and die.
4. Bacteria decompose the dead plants and multiply.
5. The bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen in respiration.
6. Fish and other organisms die for lack of oxygen.
method_templates.watch_out: The oxygen is used up by the bacteria, not by the algae.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Plan how to remove an unwanted gas and get a dry sample of the wanted gas
method_templates.method:
1. Decide if the unwanted gas is acidic or alkaline.
2. Acidic gas (carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide): bubble the mixture through aqueous sodium hydroxide.
3. Ammonia: bubble through a dilute acid.
4. Dry the gas LAST, with concentrated sulfuric acid, calcium oxide or fused calcium chloride.
5. Collect by the method that suits the gas.
method_templates.watch_out: The drying agent must not react with the gas: concentrated sulfuric acid cannot dry ammonia, and calcium oxide cannot dry an acidic gas.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining what each part does in simple distillation
method_templates.method:
1. Flask: the mixture is heated and the liquid with the lower boiling point turns to vapour.
2. Thermometer: shows the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, which is the boiling point of the distillate.
3. Condenser: cools the vapour back into liquid.
4. Boiling chips: make the boiling smooth.
5. The liquid collected is the distillate.
method_templates.watch_out: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, the reading stays at 78 °C while ethanol distils.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why a reaction is exothermic in terms of bonds
method_templates.method:
1. Name the bonds broken in the reactants and say breaking them takes in energy.
2. Name the bonds formed in the products and say forming them gives out energy.
3. Compare the totals: more energy is given out in forming bonds than is taken in breaking bonds.
4. So the reaction is exothermic overall.
method_templates.watch_out: Compare total energy, not the number of bonds.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining why one chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules
method_templates.method:
1. Point to the step where the atom reacts with ozone.
2. Point to the later step where the same atom is formed again.
3. Say the regenerated atom reacts with another ozone molecule.
4. Conclude: the cycle repeats, so one atom destroys thousands.
method_templates.watch_out: Refer to the given equations by step number. The same chain works for nitrogen monoxide.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Finding relative atomic mass from isotope abundances
method_templates.method:
1. Turn each percentage into a fraction (divide by 100).
2. Multiply each isotope's mass number by its fraction.
3. Add the results.
4. Check the answer lies between the two mass numbers, nearer the more common isotope.
method_templates.watch_out: Do not just average the mass numbers. The abundances are the weights.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing the pathway of a reflex action
method_templates.method:
1. Name the stimulus and the receptor that detects it.
2. The receptor produces nerve impulses.
3. A sensory neurone carries them to the spinal cord (or brain).
4. They cross a synapse to a relay neurone, then another synapse to a motor neurone.
5. The motor neurone carries them to the effector.
6. Name the effector and what it does (the muscle contracts).
method_templates.watch_out: Use the names from the question: which receptor, which muscle. Write "nerve impulses", not "messages".

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Draw the addition polymer (repeat unit) from a given alkene monomer
method_templates.method:
1. Redraw the monomer with the C=C in the middle and the other groups above and below.
2. Change the double bond to a single bond.
3. Draw one bond out from each of the two carbons, left and right.
4. Put brackets round this one unit, with the two outer bonds crossing the brackets.
5. Write n at the bottom right.
method_templates.watch_out: Only the two C=C carbons go in the chain. Any other carbon, such as CH3 in propene, hangs off as a side group.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: Finding the gradient of a best-fit line
method_templates.method:
1. Pick two points ON the line, far apart (more than half the line).
2. Draw a dotted triangle between them.
3. Write both coordinates on the graph, read to half a small square.
4. Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x, with working shown.
5. Give 3 s.f. and the unit (y unit per x unit).
method_templates.watch_out: The numbers in the working must be the coordinates marked on the graph.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how to test a leaf for starch
method_templates.method:
1. Put the leaf in boiling water for a few minutes.
2. Turn off the flame.
3. Put the leaf in a tube of ethanol and stand the tube in the hot water until the leaf is pale.
4. Dip the leaf in warm water to soften it.
5. Spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution.
6. Blue-black = starch present; brown = no starch.
method_templates.watch_out: Give the reason for each step if asked: ethanol removes chlorophyll; warm water softens the brittle leaf.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Explaining in terms of bonds why a reaction is exothermic
method_templates.method:
1. Name the bonds broken in the reactants.
2. Name the bonds formed in the products.
3. Breaking bonds takes in energy; forming bonds gives out energy.
4. Exothermic: energy given out forming bonds is MORE than energy taken in breaking bonds.
method_templates.watch_out: Name the actual bonds (C–H, O=O, C=O, O–H), not just "the bonds".

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Describing how carbon dioxide reaches the chloroplasts in a leaf
method_templates.method:
1. In the light, photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide, so its concentration inside the leaf is lower than in the air.
2. It diffuses in through the stomata.
3. It moves through the air spaces between the spongy mesophyll cells.
4. It dissolves in the thin film of moisture on the mesophyll cells.
5. It diffuses into the cells and their chloroplasts.
method_templates.watch_out: State the concentration gradient and name diffusion. The dissolving step is often left out.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Limiting reagent
method_templates.method:
1. Write the balanced equation.
2. Change both given amounts to moles.
3. Pick one reactant. Use the ratio to find the moles of the other needed to use it all up.
4. Compare with the moles you have. Not enough? The other is limiting. More than enough? The one you picked is limiting.
5. Use the limiting reactant's moles for every later step.
method_templates.watch_out: Amounts given for two reactants is the sign of a limiting reagent question. A quick check: the reactant that gives less product is the limiting one.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Reading a chromatogram
method_templates.method:
1. Count the spots from the mixture: that is how many substances it has.
2. Match each spot to a known sample at the same height.
3. The spot that moved furthest is the most soluble in the solvent.
4. One spot only means the sample is pure.
method_templates.watch_out: Compare heights from the start line, not from the bottom of the paper.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Telling aluminium ions from lead(II) ions
method_templates.method:
1. Note that both give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide and stays in excess ammonia.
2. Take a fresh sample of the solution.
3. Add aqueous potassium iodide.
4. Yellow precipitate: lead(II) ions. No precipitate: aluminium ions.
method_templates.watch_out: The two alkali tests cannot separate these two ions. A third test on a fresh sample is needed.

method_templates.subject: PHYS
method_templates.question_type: How resistance changes when a wire's length or thickness changes
method_templates.method:
1. Resistance is proportional to length: scale by the same factor.
2. Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area: divide by the area factor.
3. If the diameter is given, square the diameter factor to get the area factor.
4. Apply both changes one after the other.
method_templates.watch_out: Doubling the diameter makes the area four times, so the resistance is one quarter.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Predict the properties of an unfamiliar element from its group trend
method_templates.method:
1. Find the group and where the element sits in it.
2. Group I going down: softer, lower melting point, MORE reactive.
3. Group VII going down: darker colour, higher melting and boiling point, LESS reactive.
4. Place the unknown one step beyond its neighbour.
5. Give a value or word that fits the trend.
method_templates.watch_out: Example: astatine is a dark solid, less reactive than iodine; rubidium reacts with water faster than potassium.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Comparing diamond and graphite (hardness and conductivity)
method_templates.method:
1. Diamond: each carbon atom is bonded to four others, so there are no free electrons and the structure is rigid. Hard, does not conduct.
2. Graphite: each carbon atom is bonded to three others, leaving one electron per atom free to move. Conducts.
3. Graphite: layers are held by weak forces and slide over each other. Soft.
method_templates.watch_out: Give the number of bonds per carbon atom. "Graphite has free electrons" with no reason is not a full answer.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Preparing a soluble salt by titration (sodium, potassium or ammonium salts)
method_templates.method:
1. Pipette a fixed volume of one solution into a conical flask and add indicator.
2. Add the other solution from a burette until the colour just changes. Record the volume.
3. Repeat with the same volumes and no indicator.
4. Heat until saturated, cool to form crystals.
5. Filter, wash with a little cold water and dry.
method_templates.watch_out: The second run without indicator is what gives a pure salt.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining the result of a ringing experiment
method_templates.method:
1. Removing a ring of bark removes the phloem; the xylem is left.
2. Sucrose made in the leaves cannot pass the ring, so it collects above it: the stem swells there.
3. Parts below get no sucrose, so growth is reduced.
4. Leaves stay healthy because water still rises in the xylem.
method_templates.watch_out: The swelling is ABOVE the ring. It shows food moves down in the phloem, not water.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Explaining how meiosis and fertilisation give variation
method_templates.method:
1. Crossing over between homologous chromosomes gives new combinations of alleles.
2. Homologous pairs line up at random at the equator, so each gamete gets a different mix of chromosomes.
3. So the gametes are genetically different.
4. Fertilisation is random: any sperm can fuse with any egg.
method_templates.watch_out: Give both the meiosis points and the random fertilisation point when the question names both.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Preparing a soluble salt by titration
method_templates.method:
1. Pipette a fixed volume of the acid (or alkali) into a conical flask and add a few drops of indicator.
2. Add the other solution from a burette until the indicator just changes colour.
3. Record the volume used.
4. Repeat with the same volumes but no indicator.
5. Evaporate to saturation and cool if crystals are wanted.
method_templates.watch_out: The run with indicator only finds the volume. The salt comes from the repeat without indicator.

method_templates.subject: BIO
method_templates.question_type: Drawing cells seen under a microscope
method_templates.method:
1. Use a sharp pencil. Draw large: more than half the space.
2. Draw single, smooth, unbroken lines that join up.
3. No shading. Keep the proportions of the specimen.
4. Rule label lines to touch the part. No arrowheads, no crossing.
5. Label only what can be seen.
6. Add a title and the magnification.
method_templates.watch_out: A plant cell wall is drawn as a double line. Sketchy, feathered outlines lose the drawing mark.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Describing how rate changes from a volume–time or mass–time curve
method_templates.method:
1. Start: gradient is steepest, so the rate is fastest.
2. Middle: gradient becomes gentler, so the rate is slowing, because the reactant concentration is falling.
3. End: gradient is zero, so the reaction has stopped, because the limiting reactant is used up.
method_templates.watch_out: Quote the gradient each time. The rate is read from the gradient, not from the height.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Writing the formula of an ionic compound from its ions
method_templates.method:
1. Write the positive ion first, with its charge.
2. Write the negative ion with its charge.
3. Choose the smallest numbers of each so the total charge is zero.
4. Write those numbers as subscripts; leave out 1.
5. Put brackets round a polyatomic ion if there is more than one of it.
method_templates.watch_out: A polyatomic ion stays whole: Ca(OH)₂, not CaO₂H₂ or CaOH₂.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Following a reaction by loss of mass on a balance
method_templates.method:
1. Stand the flask of acid on a balance and plug the mouth with cotton wool.
2. Add the solid, note the reading and start a stopwatch.
3. Record the reading at regular times.
4. The mass falls because gas escapes.
5. A faster fall in mass means a faster rate; a flat line means the reaction has ended.
method_templates.watch_out: The cotton wool lets the gas out but keeps acid spray in. Compare LOSS in mass, not the readings themselves.

method_templates.subject: CHEM
method_templates.question_type: Showing from a table that the rate falls as a reaction goes on
method_templates.method:
