pitfalls.why_wrong: ½(a + b)h needs the two PARALLEL sides (arrow-marked); adding a slant side or dropping the ½ silently doubles or corrupts the area. With sides 5 and 9 and height 4 the area is 28, not 56.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Arrows pick the sides; don't lose the half.
source_files: S1 MATH 20B Mensuration 2 Area and Perimeter Parallelogram and Trapezium.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Drawing the full structural formula of an alcohol
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws the group as –OH with no line between O and H.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A full structural formula shows every bond. The O–H bond is one of them.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Alcohol? Draw C–O–H with both lines.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Tangent ⊥ radius
pitfalls.wrong_move: Marking the angle between a tangent and a CHORD as 90°
pitfalls.why_wrong: tan ⊥ rad holds only between the tangent and the radius/diameter at the point of contact. In Ex 2b the 90° is $\angle BAE$ (AB is the diameter); the chord angle $\angle RPT$ in Practice 2b is $90° - \angle OPR = 29°$, not $90°$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Trace from the tangent point to the CENTRE — that segment, and only that one, meets the tangent at 90°.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Representing a complex number on an Argand diagram in vector form
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the vector OP = z
pitfalls.why_wrong: A vector cannot be equal to a complex number; the point P merely represents z.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write P = z (P represents z), never equate the position vector to z.
source_files: 13891 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 7. Complex Numbers.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Data summarised as sum (x - a) about an assumed mean a
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting (sum (x - a))/n as the estimate of the population mean
pitfalls.why_wrong: Every value has had a subtracted from it, so the average of the coded values is a below the true mean. The estimate is out by exactly a.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Add the assumed mean back: xbar = (sum (x - a))/n + a. The variance, by contrast, needs no such correction.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Deciding whether a substance is an electrolyte
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treats any liquid that conducts as an electrolyte, or expects a solid ionic compound to conduct.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A liquid metal conducts by electrons and is not decomposed. A solid ionic compound has ions that cannot move.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Electrolyte = ions free to move (molten or aqueous) and it is decomposed.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Sketching application graphs such as $P = 5080(1.3)^n$ (Adrian's margin note: "there is no negative n")
pitfalls.wrong_move: Drawing the model curve for negative time as well, like a plain $y = e^x$ sketch
pitfalls.why_wrong: Years/minutes/hours cannot be negative — the model only exists for $t \geq 0$. Adrian's sketch deliberately starts at the vertical intercept (the initial value) and only draws the positive part.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Application sketches start ON the vertical axis at the initial value and run right — label that intercept.
source_files: AM 08 Indices and Logarithms Graphs and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Integrating a derivative over its own function to give a logarithm
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing ln f(x) with no modulus bars
pitfalls.why_wrong: f(x) can be negative on part of the interval, where ln f(x) is undefined, and the missing modulus costs marks.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write ln|f(x)| every time. Drop the bars only when you can say f(x) is positive throughout, such as x^2 + 4.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why dust or smoke specks in air are seen moving randomly
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying air currents carry them, or that the specks move by themselves.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A current would push them all one way. The jerky random path comes from uneven hits by fast air particles too small to see.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say: moving air particles hit the dust from all sides at random.
source_files: 12154 - ACSBR Kinetic Particle Theory - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Answers requested 'in terms of π'
pitfalls.wrong_move: Evaluating π and rounding
pitfalls.why_wrong: 93π cm³ is the answer; 292.2 cm³ scores nothing when the question says 'in terms of π'. The symbolic form is exact and the marker checks the coefficient — evaluate only when a numeric π (22/7 or 3.142) is explicitly given.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: See 'in terms of π' → π stays a letter to the last line.
source_files: S2 MATH 06 Area and Volume Pyramid Cone Sphere 2.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Items sold or used in fixed groups (packs of 5, boxes of 120)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving per item when the story only allows whole groups
pitfalls.why_wrong: Apples sell in packs of 5: the profit condition rounds up to 63 PACKS = 315 apples, not 313 individual apples. Tablets come in boxes of 120: a year needs 730 tablets → 7 whole boxes. Round at the group level.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Identify the indivisible unit before rounding.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: A reaction that gets faster soon after it starts
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the acid becomes more concentrated, or the acid acts as a catalyst.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The acid is being used up. The reaction is exothermic, so the mixture warms and the rate rises.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rate rising early on? Think heat given out by the reaction.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping the inequality sign unchanged
pitfalls.why_wrong: $-2x > 12$ gives $x < -6$, not $x > -6$ — dividing by $-2$ reverses the ordering. A substitution check exposes it instantly: $x = 0$ fails $-2x > 12$, so the answer region cannot contain $0$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Negative multiplier/divisor → flip the sign, every time. Then substitute one value from your range to confirm.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Energy changes in changes of state
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treats condensation or freezing as endothermic.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Melting, boiling and evaporation take in heat. Condensation and freezing give it out.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Particles moving closer together? Heat is given out.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Deciding the parabola's shape
pitfalls.wrong_move: Sketching a smiley face out of habit when a is negative
pitfalls.why_wrong: The sign of the $x^2$ coefficient fixes everything downstream: $-3x^2 - 5x + 2$ and $-2(x-4)(x+1)$ open DOWNWARD, so their turning points are maxima and the curve falls away steeply (to $-35$ by $x = 0$ for $-4(x+3)^2 + 1$). Wrong shape makes every labelled point sit on the wrong side.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: First mark: a > 0 smiley/minimum, a < 0 sad/maximum — before drawing anything.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Concluding that two non-parallel lines intersect
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving two of the three component equations and stopping
pitfalls.why_wrong: Two equations always fix lambda and mu, so a solution exists whether or not the lines actually meet. The third equation is the real test, and in three dimensions non-parallel lines usually miss each other.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Substitute lambda and mu into the equation you did not use. If the two sides agree the lines intersect; otherwise they are skew.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Projection questions naming two vectors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Giving the projection of b onto d when the question asked for d onto b
pitfalls.why_wrong: The two projections are different vectors of different lengths, because each one normalises the other vector. Reading the sentence backwards swaps which vector becomes the unit vector.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: The vector named after the word onto is the one you turn into a unit vector.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Water flow in a condenser
pitfalls.wrong_move: Sends water in at the top.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The jacket does not fill fully, so cooling is poor.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Water goes in at the bottom and out at the top.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Using lambda*a = mu*b to compare coefficients
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding lambda = mu = 0 without checking that a and b are non-zero and non-parallel
pitfalls.why_wrong: If a and b are parallel, say b = 2a, then lambda = 2 and mu = 1 also satisfy the equation and the conclusion collapses. That condition is the whole reason one vector equation may be split into two scalar ones.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Put the words non-zero and non-parallel on their own line before you compare coefficients.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Finishing a combine-into-one-fraction question
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stopping before cancelling a factor common to top and bottom
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Simplest form" includes the final cancel: (p−1)(1+3p) / [2(1−3p)(1+3p)] still shares (1+3p) — the answer is (p−1)/(2(1−3p)). Marks are lost even when every earlier step is right (a printed key in this set stops early too).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After combining, factorize the numerator and look for one last cancel.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Integrating a → v → s
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dropping the constant of integration (or reusing the first constant for the second integral)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Each integration has its OWN constant, fixed by its own condition: Ex 1c needed $c = 4$ from $v(2) = 16$ and separately $c' = 3$ from $s(2) = 19$. Omitting them silently sets initial values to zero — wrong whenever the particle doesn't start at rest at the origin.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: +c every integration; immediately substitute the given (t, v) or (t, s) pair to pin it.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Comparing local vs overseas prices
pitfalls.wrong_move: Comparing sticker prices without the fees, or converting in the wrong direction
pitfalls.why_wrong: Shipping, tax and courier charges are part of the overseas cost: the RMB TV looks cheaper until the 1026 shipping lifts it to 3509.80. And at 1 local = RMB 5.10 you DIVIDE the RMB total by 5.10 — multiplying inflates it 26-fold.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Total every charge first, convert once, and check the direction against the rate's units.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: What a catalyst does
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says a catalyst gives more product, raises the activation energy, or is an oxidising agent.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A catalyst only speeds the reaction up, by giving a pathway with lower activation energy. The yield is unchanged.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Catalyst: faster, not more.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Copying derivative constants down a 'show' argument
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting each printed line's constants without re-deriving
pitfalls.why_wrong: This source's Ex 1c prints $3 + \frac{43}{x^3}$ twice for $3 + \frac{54}{x^3}$ ($27 \times 2 = 54$), and Ex 2b's sign chain switches to $(x+3)^3$ for $(x+2)^3$ — the logic survives, but memorising the wrong constants poisons reuse.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Recompute the constant at each step ($an$ from $ax^n$) rather than copying the previous line.
source_files: AM 17 Differentiation 5 Increasing and Decreasing Functions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Translating subtraction sentences
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping the words' order for "subtract A from B"
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Subtract 5 from af" means START with af: $af - 5$. Writing $5 - af$ reverses the meaning — the word "from" points at what comes first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: From B → B goes in front.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Reading E(X) and Var(X) from 1-Var Stats on the graphing calculator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Quoting sigma-x as the variance of X
pitfalls.why_wrong: sigma-x on the 1-Var Stats screen is the standard deviation; the variance is its square, so quoting sigma-x directly gives the wrong value.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Square sigma-x for the variance. With probabilities in L2, sum x and sum x^2 give E(X) and E(X^2).
source_files: 13895 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S3 Discrete Random Variables.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: No precipitate after adding a test reagent
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves the observation blank or writes nothing about what it shows.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A negative result is evidence: no precipitate with acidified silver nitrate rules out chloride and iodide.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Nothing seen? Write "no visible change" and state which ions are absent.
source_files: 21961 - SASS Chem P3 Qualitative Analysis Revision.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reverse problems with a built-in minus in the target, e.g. x^2 + px - q < 0 vs x^2 - 5x - 14 < 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing q = -14 because the constant term is -14
pitfalls.why_wrong: The target carries -q, so -q = -14 gives q = +14. Copying the visible constant sign flips the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compare term by term including the built-in sign: -q matches -14, so q = 14.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Forming equations from two-draw probabilities
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping an invalid root (fractional/negative count) or not updating the second-draw counts
pitfalls.why_wrong: The class problem's quadratic $7x^2 - 167x + 880 = 0$ has roots 16 and $\frac{55}{7} \approx 7.86$ — a class can't have $7.86$ students, so $x = 16$; and the equation itself needs $\frac{x-10}{x}\cdot\frac{x-11}{x-1}$ (both counts drop), not $(\frac{x-10}{x})^2$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Second draw: numerator −1 AND denominator −1. Reject non-integer or impossible roots aloud.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Solving f(x) = f^-1(x)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Finding f^-1 explicitly and equating it to f
pitfalls.why_wrong: This creates messy surd equations and extraneous roots; for an increasing f the intersections of the two graphs lie on the line y = x.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solve f(x) = x instead, then reject any root outside the domain of f.
source_files: 13886 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 2.Functions + Graphing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Answering a word problem after solving the system
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting x and y instead of what was asked
pitfalls.why_wrong: The question asked for John's age NOW, the perimeter, or the cost of ONE apple — not the raw solution pair. After x = 9, y = 67 the answer to 'how many boxes' is 9, and quoting 67 loses the mark.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reread the question line; answer that, in a sentence.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5C Simultaneous Equations 3 Word Problems.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Composite regions (curve + line + axis boundaries)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forcing one integral over the whole region (or integrating the straight-edged piece)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Regions like Ex 4a split naturally at the intersection's x-value: integrate the curved piece, use $\frac{1}{2}bh$ for the triangle. One-integral setups double-count or use the wrong upper boundary; integrating a triangle wastes time and invites limit errors.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the vertical split at each corner point; geometry for straight edges, integration for curves.
source_files: AM 18 Integration 2 Area and Definite Integrals.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Stating long-run behaviour of a decaying model, e.g. $P = 30000e^{-0.025n}$ as $n \to \infty$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Giving the INITIAL value (30 000) as the long-run population
pitfalls.why_wrong: The long-run value is where the curve is heading, not where it started: $e^{-kn} \to 0$, so $P \to 0$. The printed notes themselves slipped here — Method 1 says "approach 30000" while Method 2 beside it correctly concludes $P \to 0$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Let $t \to \infty$ ALGEBRAICALLY: kill the $e^{-kt}$ term and read what survives.
source_files: AM 08 Indices and Logarithms Graphs and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Area formula ½ab sin C
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using an angle that is not between the two chosen sides
pitfalls.why_wrong: The formula needs the INCLUDED angle. Practice 3a(iii) gives sides $AB = 9$, $BC = 18$ but angles at $A$ and $C$ — you must compute $\angle B = 37°$ first ($48.7$ units²). Plugging $116°$ or $27°$ straight in gives $73$ or $36.8$, both wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the angle's vertex touches BOTH sides you're multiplying; otherwise find the included angle first.
source_files: EM 08 Trigonometry 2 Sine Rule and Cosine Rule.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Solving bx − a = 0 type factors, e.g. 3x − 2 = 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the root as the constant (x = 2)
pitfalls.why_wrong: 3x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2/3, not 2 — the coefficient divides. The notes print x = 2 for exactly this factor; substitute-back into the original equation exposes it immediately.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: From bx − a = 0 the root is a/b — divide, don't copy.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Test for sulfur dioxide
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses potassium dichromate(VI) without acid, or gives the colour change backwards.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reagent must be acidified. It turns from orange to green.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sulfur dioxide: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), orange to green.
source_files: 12648 - ACSBR 6 Identification of Ions and Gases - Assignment ANS.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Rounding a result you already rounded
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding in two stages
pitfalls.why_wrong: 8979.999 to the nearest whole number is 8980; rounding that again to the nearest 100 gives 9000 — which happens to work, but 2.449 to 1 dp via 2.45 gives 2.5 instead of the correct 2.4. Every rounding must read the ORIGINAL number.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One look, one cut — never round a rounded answer.
source_files: S1 MATH 05 Numbers 5 Approximation and Estimation.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Two percentage changes in a row
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding the percents
pitfalls.why_wrong: Length +10% with breadth −20% changes area by ×1.1 × 0.8 = ×0.88, a 12% DROP — not −10%. Three years of −10% is 0.9³ = 27.1% down, not 30%. Percents of different bases never add.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert each change to a multiplier and multiply.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining how paint, oil or grease prevents rusting
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes only that it "covers" or "protects" the iron.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mark is for saying what is kept away: the layer stops oxygen and water from reaching the iron.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Barrier method: name both oxygen (air) and water.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Volume/area formulas with two variables (cones especially)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Differentiating V = ⅓πr²h with both r and h still in it
pitfalls.why_wrong: AM rates problems need ONE variable. Similar triangles tie $r$ to $h$ ($r = \frac{3h}{8}$ for the 24-by-9 cone), collapsing $V$ to $\frac{3}{64}\pi h^3$. Skipping this leaves an expression you can't differentiate with AM tools.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cone question → draw the triangle, write r/R = h/H, substitute before differentiating.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Reading gradient and intercept from a non-standard form (3y + 2x = 6)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading m and c straight off without rearranging to y = mx + c
pitfalls.why_wrong: In 3y + 2x = 6 the '2' is NOT the gradient and '6' is NOT the intercept: solving for y gives y = −⅔x + 2, so m = −⅔ and c = 2. Only the y = mx + c form exposes them.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Make y the subject first; then read m and c.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5A Simultaneous Equations 1 Linear Functions (Recap).pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Testing a gas with litmus paper
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using dry litmus paper.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The gas must dissolve in water on the paper before it can act as an acid or alkali.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Always write 'moist' or 'damp' litmus paper.
source_files: 12208 - ACSBR Identification of Ions & Gases - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Finding the overlap
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting in the wrong order (or halving the excess)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $n(A \cap B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cup B)$: the excess $38 - 28 = 10$ IS the overlap — the double-counted people appear once in each set total. Halving it or subtracting from the total gives plausible-looking wrong counts.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sum of the two sets minus the union — nothing else.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Grouping like terms across the equals sign in surd equations, e.g. x√3 + 5 = 8x
pitfalls.wrong_move: Moving a term across = without flipping its sign: writing x√3 − 8x = 5 instead of −5
pitfalls.why_wrong: Every term that crosses the equals sign flips sign. The slip survives all the later (correct) algebra and lands on an answer with the wrong sign — which fails substitution back into the original equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Move a term, flip its sign — then sub the answer back to confirm.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Hemisphere surface area
pitfalls.wrong_move: Halving the sphere's 4πr² and stopping at 2πr²
pitfalls.why_wrong: A solid hemisphere has a flat circular face as well: total SA = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr². The notes' own key uses 3πr² (r = 7 gives 462, and 4158 = 3πr² gives r = 21); answering 2πr² loses a third of the surface.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cut solids grow a new face — count it.
source_files: S2 MATH 06 Area and Volume Pyramid Cone Sphere 1.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Volume of the solid formed by rotating the region between two curves about the x-axis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing pi times the integral of the square of (upper curve minus lower curve)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Each curve sweeps its own disc, so the volumes subtract as squares. The square of the difference is not the difference of the squares.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write pi times the integral of [f(x)]^2 minus [g(x)]^2, expanding each square separately before subtracting.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Reading activation energy from an energy profile diagram
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measures activation energy from the products, or from the bottom of the diagram, to the peak.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Activation energy is the energy the reactants need to reach the top of the hump.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the arrow from the reactants' level up to the peak.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Keying a normal distribution into normalcdf or invNorm on the GC
pitfalls.wrong_move: Entering the variance in the sigma field
pitfalls.why_wrong: The calculator expects the standard deviation; typing sigma^2 produces a wrong probability that still looks believable
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Square-root the variance first - if X ~ N(150, 22^2), the sigma field takes 22
source_files: 13898 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S5 Normal Distribution Lecture Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Solving an equation graphically on an existing sketch
pitfalls.wrong_move: Drawing the line straight from the given equation without first matching the sketched function exactly
pitfalls.why_wrong: If the sketch shows $f(x) = 1 + 2\cos 2x$ but the equation is $2 + 4\cos 2x = 10 - \frac{3x}{\pi}$, the RHS is not the line to draw — the LHS is $2f(x)$. Divide the whole equation by 2 first; the correct line is $5 - \frac{3x}{2\pi}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rearrange until one side IS the sketched f(x), then whatever remains is the line.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Completing the square when the x² coefficient is not 1
pitfalls.wrong_move: Halving the x-coefficient while the leading coefficient is still there
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$ only completes $x^2+bx$, not $2x^2-5x$. For $2x^2-5x+1 = 0$ you must divide through by 2 first ($x^2-\frac{5}{2}x+\frac{1}{2} = 0$), then use $\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^2$, giving $\left(x-\frac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{17}{16}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Make a = 1 before halving; and remember ± when you finally square-root.
source_files: EM 01 Quadratic Equations 1 Solving Quadratic Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Echo calculation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses distance = speed × full echo time.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The sound travels to the surface and back, so that answer is twice the real distance.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Echo: 2d = v × t.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Gradient of an equation like 3y = 2x − 12
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the x-coefficient (2) as the gradient
pitfalls.why_wrong: The gradient is read from y = mx + c AFTER dividing through: y = (2/3)x − 4, gradient 2/3. Skipping the division inflates the gradient by the y-coefficient.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Make y the subject first; gradient = coefficient of x then.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Measured gas volume lower than calculated
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives no reason, or says the reaction was incomplete when a reactant was in excess.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The usual cause is gas escaping: a leaking joint, or gas lost before the stopper was in place.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Low gas volume? Check for leaks; make the apparatus airtight and start the reaction only after it is sealed.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Splitting a power to prepare for factorising (e.g. 3^{n+1} in 3^{n+1} − 3^{n−2})
pitfalls.wrong_move: Split the power additively: 3^{n+1} = 3^n + 3.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Splitting a power is the reverse of the add-powers law, which is multiplicative: 3^{n+1} = 3^n × 3^1. An additive split changes the value.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Splitting a power always produces a PRODUCT: a^{x+k} = a^x · a^k.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reading the turning point from a(x + b)^2 + c
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading (x + 3)^2 as turning point at x = +3
pitfalls.why_wrong: Completed square form is a(x - h)^2 + k, so (x + 3)^2 means h = -3; the sign flips
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compare with (x - h): the bracket sign flips — (x + 3)^2 turns at x = -3

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Manipulating an expression that contains two vectors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing ab, a/b, or a.b.c
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only two products are defined for vectors: the scalar product a.b, which returns a number, and the vector product a x b, which returns a vector. There is no plain multiplication and no division by a vector, and since a.b is already a scalar there is nothing left to dot with c.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Decide which product you need before writing it: a.b for angles and perpendicularity, a x b for perpendicular directions and areas.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Concluding a test when the test statistic is outside the critical region
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing "accept H0" or "H0 is true"
pitfalls.why_wrong: Not rejecting H0 only means the sample gives insufficient evidence against it; the test can never prove H0 true.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write "do not reject H0: there is insufficient evidence, at the alpha% level, that [H1 in context]".
source_files: 13900 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S7 Hypothesis Testing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Events described with 'not'
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forgetting the complement and hunting for a direct count
pitfalls.why_wrong: P(not red) on the spinner is fastest as 1 − 60/360 = 5/6, and 'not Chinese' among 6+5+4 girls is (5+4)/15. Complements avoid re-listing everything — and P(not A) + P(A) must total exactly 1, a free check.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: See 'not' → 1 minus the easy probability.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Writing division in an expression
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving a ÷ sign or dividing by only part of a product
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Divide 2w by 3xy" is $\frac{2w}{3xy}$ — the WHOLE product sits underneath. Writing $2w \div 3 \times xy$ or $\frac{2w}{3}xy$ divides by 3 only and multiplies the rest.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One fraction bar; everything after "by" goes below it.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Copying coordinates through a multi-part solution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting printed coordinate pairs without re-evaluating y
pitfalls.why_wrong: This source slips repeatedly: Ex 1b's conclusion names $(2,-39)$ (from the previous example) instead of $(0,-7)$; Ex 3b evaluates $y(3)$ as "(2,1)" when it is $-1$ (point $(3,-1)$); Practice 1 Q5's key prints $(0,0)$ for $(0,1)$; the old condensed entry then 'fixed' Ex 3b to $(3,1)$ — still wrong. One substitution catches every case.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Recompute the y-coordinate from the curve for every final point you quote.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Steps or platforms inside a container
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the three steps as equal blocks
pitfalls.why_wrong: Stacked steps occupy columns of heights 0.3, 0.6, 0.9 (not 3 × 0.3): volume = (0.12 + 0.24 + 0.36) × 8 = 5.76 m³. Equal blocks undercount the lower steps' support.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Each step column reaches the floor — heights stack.
source_files: S1 MATH 20E Mensuration 5 Miscellaneous Area and Volume Questions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Tangents to a circle parallel to a coordinate axis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Confusing "parallel to the y-axis" (vertical, x = a ± r) with "parallel to the x-axis" (horizontal, y = b ± r)
pitfalls.why_wrong: A tangent parallel to the y-axis is a VERTICAL line one radius left/right of the centre. The source's Example 3b answers a "parallel to the y-axis" question with horizontal lines — the two directions are easy to swap under exam pressure.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Parallel to an axis = same direction as that axis: y-axis → vertical x = a ± r; x-axis → horizontal y = b ± r.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Choosing the term to add and subtract when completing the square
pitfalls.wrong_move: Squaring the whole coefficient of x (adding b^2) instead of half of it
pitfalls.why_wrong: The perfect square (x + b/2)^2 expands to x^2 + bx + (b/2)^2 — only halve-then-square reproduces the middle term
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Divide the coefficient of x by 2, THEN square it

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Choosing the acid to react fully with calcium carbonate
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses dilute sulfuric acid.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Insoluble calcium sulfate forms a layer on the solid and stops the acid reaching the rest of the carbonate.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Calcium carbonate to be fully reacted? Use hydrochloric or nitric acid.
source_files: 9424 - Chem Practical Planning Questions with Anskey.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Recalling the tan (and cos) derivative signs
pitfalls.wrong_move: Attaching a minus to tan's derivative (or forgetting cos's)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only $\cos$ differentiates with a minus: $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$, hence $\frac{d}{dx}\cos^n x = -n\cos^{n-1}x\sin x$. $\frac{d}{dx}\tan^n x = +n\tan^{n-1}x\sec^2x$ — the source's own formula box misprints a minus there.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One minus in the whole trio, and it belongs to cos.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Max/min application answers (heights, areas)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Answering with the wrong feature or wrong units
pitfalls.why_wrong: 'Maximum height' is $k$; 'when' is $h$ (the t-coordinate) — from $-4(t-2)^2 + 17$: 17 m AT 2 s, two different answers. Initial value means $t = 0$, not the vertex. And units matter: the fencing key prints '15625 cm²' for a 125 m × 125 m yard — it's m².
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Vertex gives a PAIR (when, how high) — pick the coordinate the question asks for, and carry the units through.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Word problems: finding the initial height/value
pitfalls.wrong_move: Setting h = 0 (or solving the equation) to find the initial value
pitfalls.why_wrong: Initial means at the beginning of time, t = 0; h = 0 is when the object is on the ground
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Initial means at the beginning — so sub t = 0

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Leaks, drains, and simultaneous fill+leak setups
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the raw inflow as dV/dt, or dropping the negative sign for a draining container
pitfalls.why_wrong: The chain rule wants the NET rate: pumped 15 in, leaks 3 out → $\frac{dV}{dt} = +12$; purely leaking 30 → $\frac{dV}{dt} = -30$, which makes $\frac{dh}{dt}$ negative — and the answer to "rate of DECREASE" is then the positive $\frac{40}{3\pi}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Signed bookkeeping first (in minus out), state the final answer in the direction the question asks.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Transforming every data value
pitfalls.wrong_move: Shifting the SD along with the mean (or forgetting to scale it)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Adding/subtracting a constant slides every point equally → mean moves, SD unchanged (faulty scale +2 kg: SD identical). Multiplying by $k$ (e.g. 'increased by 200%' = ×3, or taking 16.5%) scales BOTH: SD $6.7 \to 20.1$, $0.0683 \to 0.0113$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Shift → SD frozen. Scale → SD scales by |k|. '+200%' means ×3, not ×2.
source_files: EM 13 Statistics 1 Standard Deviation and Interquartile Range.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Time units inside a rate
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating 2 h 40 min as 240 minutes
pitfalls.why_wrong: 2 h 40 min is 160 minutes; the flow rate 480 ÷ 160 = 3 l/min becomes 2 l/min with the sloppy conversion. Mixed units are the most common rate error.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert hours-and-minutes to pure minutes before dividing.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Combining like terms after factoring out a power (fractions with halves)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding coefficients like $-3x + \frac{3}{2}x$ carelessly
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source's own Example 4b slips exactly here: $3-3x+\frac{3}{2}x-1$ is $2-\frac{3}{2}x$, but the print shows $2-\frac{1}{2}x$ and carries the error into the final answer $\frac{4-x}{2(1-x)^{3/2}}$ (correct: $\frac{4-3x}{2(1-x)^{3/2}}$). Its assignment key does it too: $4x(4x-3)-8x^2$ printed as $8x^2-24x$ instead of $8x^2-12x$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Combine fractional coefficients on paper ($-3+\frac{3}{2} = -\frac{3}{2}$), then spot-check the answer at one numeric $x$.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Large-sample test where the question gives a standard deviation computed from the sample
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the sample standard deviation directly as sigma in the test statistic
pitfalls.why_wrong: The sample variance underestimates the population variance; it is neither the population parameter nor the unbiased estimate.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert first: s^2 = n/(n-1) x sample variance, then use s in the test statistic.
source_files: 13900 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S7 Hypothesis Testing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Solving for a side when it sits in the denominator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying by the trig value instead of dividing
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\cos 52° = \frac{8}{x}$ gives $x = \frac{8}{\cos 52°} = 13.0$, NOT $8\cos 52° = 4.93$. The wrong version is shorter than the given side even though $x$ is the hypotenuse — a built-in sanity check that gets ignored.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: If $x$ is underneath, swap: $x = \frac{\text{top}}{\text{trig value}}$. Then check: hypotenuse must be the longest side.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Electrolysis with a copper or silver anode
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives oxygen at the anode, as with carbon electrodes.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A metal anode that is not inert takes part: its own atoms lose electrons and go into solution.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Look at the electrode material first. Copper anode in a copper salt: the anode dissolves, no gas.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Any related-rates question
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting the instantaneous values (r = 3, h = 4, ...) before differentiating
pitfalls.why_wrong: The instant's values hold only at that instant; the derivative needs the general relationship. Substitute into $\frac{dA}{dr}$ or $\frac{dV}{dh}$ only AFTER differentiating — e.g. keep $V = \frac{3}{64}\pi h^3$ general, get $\frac{dV}{dh} = \frac{9\pi h^2}{64}$, THEN put $h = 4$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Differentiate the formula with letters; numbers go in at the final evaluation step.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Solving a modulus inequality where the other side contains x, e.g. |x-3| < 4 - 2x
pitfalls.wrong_move: Applying "|x| < a is the same as -a < x < a" with a taken to be 4 - 2x
pitfalls.why_wrong: That property requires the right-hand side to be a positive constant. Here 4 - 2x changes sign with x, so the double inequality is not equivalent; sketching y = |x-3| and y = 4 - 2x gives x < 1.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Constant on the right, use the property. Variable on the right, sketch both graphs and read off where one lies below the other.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Choosing a congruency test
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using ASS (two sides + a non-included angle) to prove triangles congruent
pitfalls.why_wrong: ASS does not determine a triangle — two sides and a non-included angle can fit two different triangles. The valid tests are SSS, ASA, SAS, AAS, RHS only.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Adrian's rule, printed on the theorem sheet: "(No ASS please)". If the angle is not between the two sides, look for AAS or RHS instead.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Complements of unions and intersections (De Morgan)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating P′ ∪ Q′ and P′ ∩ Q′ as the same region
pitfalls.why_wrong: $P' \cup Q' = (P \cap Q)'$ (everything but the lens) while $P' \cap Q' = (P \cup Q)'$ (outside both). The file's own Assignment Q1(c) prints the $\cup$ version but keys the $\cap$ value (8 instead of 22) — the two differ by every 'only' region.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Prime swaps ∪ and ∩ when it moves through brackets; shade both if unsure.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Computing the monthly installment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing (cash price + interest) by the number of months
pitfalls.why_wrong: The deposit is paid up front — installments cover only the BALANCE plus its interest. The file's own Ex 1 divides $\frac{4500 + 490}{24} = 207.92$ and double-charges the 1000 deposit; the correct $\frac{3500 + 490}{24} = 166.25$ matches every practice answer's method.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Installment = (balance + interest) ÷ months. The deposit never comes back.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Finding unknown constants in a polynomial identity by substituting values
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting arbitrary values (e.g. x=5) that make nothing zero, producing tangled simultaneous equations in every unknown at once
pitfalls.why_wrong: Any value works — it is an identity — but values that zero a bracket eliminate everything except one unknown; arbitrary values mix all the unknowns into each equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: We can sub in any values we want, it will still work — but we usually sub in values so as to make things 0. Pick the roots of the brackets.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Similarity correspondence order
pitfalls.wrong_move: Pairing sides by position on the page instead of by equal angles
pitfalls.why_wrong: In $\triangle AED \sim \triangle ABC$ (from $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$) the correspondence CROSSES: $AD \leftrightarrow AC$ and $AE \leftrightarrow AB$, giving $\frac{8}{6+x} = \frac{6}{12}$ — pairing $AD$ with $AB$ gives a wrong (and plausible-looking) equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write the similarity statement vertex-by-vertex from the equal angles, then read side pairs strictly from it.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Metal with dilute acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes copper + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so they do not react with dilute acids.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the metal is above hydrogen before writing metal + acid.
source_files: 12862 - NYGH Acids, Bases and Salts Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Optimising a quantity that contains a square root
pitfalls.wrong_move: Differentiating the rooted expression directly
pitfalls.why_wrong: Distances $L = \sqrt{x^4 + (18-x)^2}$ and face areas $A = \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{x^2/4 + h^2}$ are painful to differentiate. $L$ and $L^2$ are extremal at the same $x$ (squaring is increasing for positives), so optimise the SQUARE and root the final value.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: See a root in the target → work with $A^2$/$L^2$/$V^2$; convert back only at the end.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Simplifying a sigma-notation sum whose general term is a product of two sequences
pitfalls.wrong_move: Splitting the sum of u_r x v_r into (sum of u_r) x (sum of v_r)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Sigma notation distributes over addition and subtraction only; the sum of products is not the product of the sums
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Only split a sigma across + and -. For a product, expand or simplify the general term first, then sum each piece separately.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Answering scale questions with converted units
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving with a different figure than the question printed
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes' Example 1b(c) asks for a 1.2 km perimeter but the solution answers 6.5 cm — the map length for 1.3 km. At 1 : 20000 the printed question's answer is 6 cm. Copying a worked structure without re-reading the given figure imports someone else's numbers.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Re-read the printed figure right before substituting it.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Transferring angles between points
pitfalls.wrong_move: Ignoring that all north arrows are parallel
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes' Useful Tip: any two norths are parallel, so interior/co-interior angles move bearings across the figure ($\angle ABN_2 = 180° - 116°$; $\angle QSN_1 = \angle PQS$ when $QP$ points due south). Without it, students re-derive angles with fragile ad-hoc geometry.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the north arrow at EVERY named point; hunt for Z- and C-shapes between them.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Differentiating e^f(x) and solving e^f = 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Turning $e^{f}$ into $f e^{f-1}$ (power-rule reflex), or hunting solutions of $e^{-x} = 0$
pitfalls.why_wrong: The exponential is not a power function: $\frac{d}{dx}e^{f} = f'e^{f}$, with $e^f$ copied unchanged. And $e^{-x} > 0$ always — in $e^{-x}(3\cos x - \sin x) = 0$ only the bracket can vanish.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Exponentials copy themselves; they never equal zero.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: 'Hence solve' questions with a repeated bracket, e.g. 4(y−1)² − 7(y−1) = 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expanding the brackets and solving from scratch
pitfalls.why_wrong: The bracket IS the variable of the quadratic you just solved: from $4x^2 = 7x$, $x = 0$ or $\frac{7}{4}$, so $y-1 = 0$ or $\frac{7}{4}$ directly. Expanding wastes time and invites algebra slips, and examiners award the 'hence' marks for reusing the earlier result.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match the bracket to the solved variable and transfer its roots; only ever expand as a last resort.
source_files: EM 01 Quadratic Equations 1 Solving Quadratic Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Solving a line-curve or curve-curve pair, after finding the x-values
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stopping at "x = -1 or x = 5/3" and presenting the x-values as the final answer
pitfalls.why_wrong: A solution to simultaneous equations is a pair (x, y) — an intersection point. Each x has a matching y, and the question expects the coordinates or both values.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: For simultaneous equations, remember to find y — sub each x back into the linear (easier) equation.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Observation when heating zinc carbonate or zinc oxide
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives one colour for the solid left behind.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Zinc oxide is yellow when hot and white when cold. Both colours are expected.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Zinc oxide: write "yellow when hot, white on cooling".

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Subtracting a negative number
pitfalls.wrong_move: Changing the number as well as the sign
pitfalls.why_wrong: $5 - (-2)$ becomes $5 + 2 = 7$: only the SIGN of the subtracted number flips, never its size. The notes themselves print "$5 + 7 = 12$" here — a cautionary typo that doubles the error.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flip the sign, keep the digits: minus-minus is plus-the-same-number.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Reading measurements off sphere and cone figures
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating a marked diameter as the radius
pitfalls.why_wrong: The '14' drawn across a sphere's centre and the '14 cm base' of the conical container are DIAMETERS: r = 7 in both. Substituting 14 as r multiplies volumes by 8 and areas by 4 — the largest single error available in this topic.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Does the marked line cross the whole circle? Then halve it.
source_files: S2 MATH 06 Area and Volume Pyramid Cone Sphere 1.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Intersections of two lines
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading intersection points off intercepts (or vice versa)
pitfalls.why_wrong: An intercept zeroes one variable; an intersection satisfies BOTH equations simultaneously — substitute one into the other ($16(-0.75x + 1.75) + 48 = 7x$ → $C(4, -1.25)$). They coincide only when the crossing happens to lie on an axis.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Two lines → simultaneous equations. One line + axis → set the other variable to zero.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Counting objects in melt-and-recast questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding the count to the nearest whole number
pitfalls.why_wrong: 843.75 balls means 843 complete balls — the 0.75 is scrap, not a ball. But 6.77 cups of smoothie needs 7 cups, because 6 cups overflow. The direction comes from the story (producing vs containing), never from 'nearest'.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Produce → round down; contain → round up.
source_files: S2 MATH 06 Area and Volume Pyramid Cone Sphere 2.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Total distance travelled over an interval
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing |s(end) − s(start)| without checking for turns
pitfalls.why_wrong: If the particle reverses ($v = 0$ inside the interval), displacement differences cancel the doubling-back: Ex 1a's $t=2..4$ gives $|s(4)-s(2)| = \frac{2}{3}$, but the true distance is 2 m (turn at $t=3$). Solve $v = 0$ FIRST, then add |leg| by |leg|.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rest times inside the window → split the journey at each turn; sum absolute leg lengths.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Currency exchange with a fee
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying when you should divide, or applying the fee to the wrong base
pitfalls.why_wrong: At S$1 = R5.58, converting R6700 needs DIVISION (÷5.58 = S$1200.72); multiplying gives a five-digit nonsense. And a 2.3% admin fee means paying 102.3% of the price — adding 2.3% of the wrong amount (or forgetting the base ticket) misses the key 1228.34.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Track the units through the rate; a k% fee means paying (100 + k)% of the price.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Choosing sine vs cosine (and the sign) for a model
pitfalls.wrong_move: Defaulting to +sine or +cosine without checking the starting position
pitfalls.why_wrong: The starting position dictates the function: highest point at t = 0 → $+a\cos$; lowest point → $-a\cos$; centre going up → $+a\sin$. The waterwheel (starts at top) is cosine; the Ferris chair (starts at bottom) needs $a = -8$; the fox population (max at a quarter period) is sine.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Evaluate your model at t = 0 and check it reproduces the stated starting value.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Describing what happens when a carbonate is heated strongly
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calling it burning or combustion, or writing oxygen as a reactant.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Thermal decomposition is one compound breaking down by heat alone. Nothing reacts with oxygen.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One reactant only: metal carbonate -> metal oxide + carbon dioxide.
source_files: 12208 - ACSBR Identification of Ions & Gases - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Equations with a common trig factor (4 sin x cos x = cos x; sin x = 4 tan x)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing both sides by the common factor
pitfalls.why_wrong: Dividing by $\cos x$ (or $\sin x$) discards every solution where that factor is zero — here $x = 90°, 270°$ vanish. The source solves these by bringing over and factorizing precisely to keep both branches.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bring to one side, factorize, solve every factor (including the one you were tempted to cancel).
source_files: AM 16 Trigonometry 03a Simple Trigo Identities and Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining what discontinuous variation means
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes only "distinct groups" for a three-mark question.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The marks are for several points: clear-cut phenotypes with no in-betweens, one or a few genes, not affected by the environment, plus an example.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Discontinuous: clear-cut, few genes, no effect of environment, e.g. blood group.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Adding a less reactive metal to a salt solution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes a displacement equation for copper in magnesium nitrate.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Less reactive metal added: no reaction, no visible change.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Calculating a gradient from a plotted graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws a small triangle near the middle of the line.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A small triangle makes reading errors a large fraction of the answer; the mark needs a triangle longer than half the line.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Triangle longer than half the drawn line, every time.
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Transfer problems (moving items between boxes)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adjusting only the box that receives (or only the one that gives)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Moving a apples from B to A changes BOTH: A becomes 225 + a and B becomes 260 − a. Percent conditions apply to the NEW totals (478 + a + r and 472 − a − r), not the original ones.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Every move has two entries: +to the receiver, −from the giver — totals included.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5C Simultaneous Equations 3 Word Problems.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Substituting the given pair to find k
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting the wrong given value into the variable slot
pitfalls.why_wrong: With p = 3 when m = 2, the slot (m+1)² takes m = 2, giving k = 27. The notes substitute (3+1)² — the value of p in m's place — and everything downstream inherits it (k = 48, m = 7 or −9, contradicting their own printed key m = 5 or −7). One mis-slotted digit corrupts every later part.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Label the pair 'when m = …, p = …' before substituting; each value has one slot.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Hidden heights in circle-trapezium composites
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the height as unknown when the circle fixes it
pitfalls.why_wrong: A semicircle on the top side tangent to the base makes height = radius (9); a circle of radius 4 between two parallel lines makes the gap 2r = 8; a 5-cm slant over a 4-cm offset hides a 3-4-5 height. Missing these leaves the problem 'unsolvable'.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Tangent circles measure the gap: r or 2r; slants hide Pythagoras.
source_files: S1 MATH 20B Mensuration 2 Area and Perimeter Parallelogram and Trapezium.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Pascal row sums
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing 2^n for the Row-n sum
pitfalls.why_wrong: Row 1 sums to $1 = 2^0$, so the exponent trails the row number: $S = 2^{n-1}$, and Row 20 gives $2^{19} = 524288$, not $2^{20}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Anchor with Row 1: the exponent is n − 1.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Triangle areas built on parabola features (△ABC with base on the x-axis)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using a coordinate as the height instead of a distance
pitfalls.why_wrong: Height is the DISTANCE from the third point to the base line: for C(0, −24) under the x-axis the height is 24, not −24; base AB is the root gap (6 − (−4) = 10). Signs belong to coordinates, not lengths.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Base = |root − root|; height = |y| of the third point.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6C Quadratic Graphs (Coordinate Geometry).pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Recording observations in a gas test or ion test
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the space blank when nothing seems to happen.
pitfalls.why_wrong: 'No change' is still an observation and carries the mark. A blank reads as a test not done.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write what you saw even if nothing changed: 'colourless, odourless gas', 'no effect on moist litmus', 'no precipitate'.
source_files: 12208 - ACSBR Identification of Ions & Gases - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Quoting ratio answers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the ratio in the reverse of the asked order
pitfalls.why_wrong: The assignment key prints '8 : 27' for the explicitly-asked LARGE-to-small tin volumes (correct 27 : 8), and lists the pond (1 : 9) and sphere (5 : 6, 125 : 216) ratios smaller-first against the question's order. The numbers are right; the order communicates which object is which.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Underline the asked order in the question and mirror it exactly in the answer.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Mass given in kilograms or milligrams
pitfalls.wrong_move: Divides a mass in kg (or mg) by Mr without changing it to grams.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Mr gives grams per mole. 0.030 kg of magnesium is 30 g, which is 1.25 mol, not 0.00125 mol.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Chemistry sums use grams and dm³. Change kg, mg and m³ first.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Crystallising a salt solution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Heats the solution until dry.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Strong heating can break the salt down, and a dry solid is not crystals.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Heat until saturated, then leave to cool.
source_files: 12862 - NYGH Acids, Bases and Salts Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Ages in n years or n years ago
pitfalls.wrong_move: Shifting only one person's age
pitfalls.why_wrong: In ten years Mary is $x + 10$ AND Peter is $2x + 10$ — both age. Leaving Peter at $2x$ makes the combined-age equation unbalanced by 10.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Add (or subtract) the same n to every single age.
source_files: S1 MATH 10B Algebra 5B Forming Linear Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Removing chlorophyll from a leaf with ethanol
pitfalls.wrong_move: Heats the tube of ethanol directly over a flame.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Ethanol is flammable and can catch fire.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flame off. Stand the ethanol tube in a beaker of hot water.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Why acid is added in the chloride and sulfate tests
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves out the dilute nitric acid, or cannot say what it is for.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Carbonate ions also give a white precipitate with silver or barium ions. The acid removes them first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: White precipitate that dissolves in acid is not chloride or sulfate.
source_files: 12648 - ACSBR 6 Identification of Ions and Gases - Assignment ANS.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Rates written as 1 local = x foreign
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying by x when converting foreign back to local
pitfalls.why_wrong: With 1 local = 0.5156 euro, euros are WORTH MORE than local dollars: 3000 euros is $\frac{3000}{0.5156} = 5818.46$ local. Multiplying gives 1546.80 — off by the square of the rate.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Put the currency you want on the "1" side of the equation before scaling; sanity-check which currency is stronger.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Units in journey problems (km distances, m heights)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Copying the wrong unit onto the answer line
pitfalls.why_wrong: This file's own keys print "$25.4$ m" and "$4.34$ m" for distances built from 20 km and 5.3 km legs — both are km. Speed×time also fixes units: 12 km/h × 2 h = 24 km. A correct number with the wrong unit still loses the mark.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Carry the unit through the arithmetic, don't re-guess it at the end.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining why a mean of several readings is used in an experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that taking a mean makes the readings more accurate, or removes extreme values.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A mean does not change any reading, and odd values are thrown out before the mean is worked out. The mark is for reliability.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Repeats and a mean? Write: more reliable, because the effect of chance differences between plants is reduced.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Quartile positions on a CF curve
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using (n+1)/2 positions as with raw sorted data
pitfalls.why_wrong: On a cumulative frequency CURVE the median is read at height $\frac{n}{2}$ (and quartiles at $\frac{n}{4}$, $\frac{3n}{4}$) — 65 teachers → read at 32.5, not 33. The $(n+1)$ convention belongs to raw listed data; mixing them shifts every read-off.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Curve → n/2, n/4, 3n/4. Sorted list → (n+1) positions.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Interpreting a zero product of two non-zero vectors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading a x b = 0 as perpendicular, or a.b = 0 as parallel
pitfalls.why_wrong: They are opposite tests. a.b = |a||b|cos(theta) vanishes at 90 degrees, so a zero dot product means perpendicular. a x b = |a||b|sin(theta) n-hat vanishes at 0 or 180 degrees, so a zero cross product means parallel.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Dot zero means perpendicular, cross zero means parallel. Write the cross-product result as the zero vector, not the number 0.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Effect of a catalyst on the amount of product
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws the catalysed curve finishing higher, or says more product forms.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The amount of product depends on the limiting reactant only. A catalyst changes how fast, not how much.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Catalyst curve: steeper start, same final height.
source_files: 21974 - SASS Chem Speed of Rxn AfL Ans.pdf
21967 - SASS Chem Rate of Rxn Summary.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Differentiating a term in y with respect to x
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing d/dx (y^2) = 2y
pitfalls.why_wrong: y is itself a function of x, so the chain rule applies and d/dx (y^2) = 2y (dy/dx). The notes set this beside d/dx (x^2) = 2x precisely because the two look alike and are not.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Attach dy/dx every time you differentiate a y term with respect to x. A mixed term such as xy also needs the product rule.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Evaluating a trigonometric integral on the graphic calculator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the calculator in degree mode
pitfalls.why_wrong: Every calculus result for trigonometric functions assumes radians, so a degree-mode value is wrong even when the written working is right.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Set the mode to radian before any calculus, and give exact answers in terms of pi where they are asked for.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Optimising a quantity that is still written in two other variables
pitfalls.wrong_move: Differentiating before using the constraint to eliminate one of them
pitfalls.why_wrong: Differentiating A = xy with respect to x is meaningless while y is an unknown function of x. The constraint has to reduce the problem to one variable first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Use the constraint to write one variable in terms of the other, substitute, and only then differentiate.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Naming control variables in a planning question
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives vague or irrelevant constants, such as "type of lens" or the room.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A control variable must be a quantity that would change the measured result if it varied.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name the exact quantity: "focal length of the lens", "mass of the bob".
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Polarity in a simple cell
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the more reactive metal is the positive electrode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The more reactive metal gives up electrons, so it is the negative electrode and the source of electron flow.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Simple cell: more reactive = negative = dissolves.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Empirical and molecular formula
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounds a ratio like 1 : 2.5 to 1 : 2 or 1 : 3.
pitfalls.why_wrong: 2.5 is not close to a whole number. Rounding it gives a different compound.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ratio ends in .5? Double everything: 1 : 2.5 becomes 2 : 5.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Checking a factorization
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting a tidy-looking answer without expanding it back
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own grouping example prints $(x+3)(y-5)$ for $xy + 3y - 2x - 6$ — expansion gives $xy + 3y - 5x - 15$, a different expression (the solution drifted to another question). Thirty seconds of expanding exposes it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Expand your answer — it must rebuild the exact question.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Using anhydrous copper(II) sulfate or cobalt(II) chloride paper on a liquid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding the liquid is pure water because the test is positive.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The colour change only shows water is present. Any aqueous solution gives the same result.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Presence of water: chemical test. Purity: check it boils at exactly 100 °C or freezes at 0 °C.
source_files: 12208 - ACSBR Identification of Ions & Gases - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing how easily different metal carbonates decompose
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the same mass of each carbonate.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The carbonates have different molar masses, so equal masses hold different numbers of moles and give different gas volumes anyway.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Fair test between different compounds: same number of moles.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Rate questions built on trigonometry (balloon rising)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the height gained by the clock interval in minutes
pitfalls.why_wrong: 300(tan 60° − tan 25°) ≈ 379.7 m gained between 10.00 and 10.02 am is 2 MINUTES = 120 s, so the speed is 3.16 m/s. Dividing by 2 gives 189.9 — nearly sixty times too large for an answer demanded in m/s.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match the time unit to the requested speed unit before dividing.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Tangent/normal problems on trig, e^x, or ln curves
pitfalls.wrong_move: Working in decimals when the question says 'exact form'
pitfalls.why_wrong: Points like $(e, e^2)$, gradients like $\frac{2+\pi}{4}$ or $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ must stay symbolic; rounding then reconstructing loses marks and precision. The whole point of these questions is fluency with $e$, $\pi$, and surds as CONSTANTS.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Treat $e$ and $\pi$ like numbers you never evaluate; only decimalise when the question asks.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Classifying self-pollination
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calls self-pollination asexual reproduction because only one plant is involved.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Gametes still fuse to form a zygote, so it is sexual reproduction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Pollen and ovule involved? It is sexual, whether self or cross.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Solving simultaneous equations in two unknown complex numbers z and w
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting z = a+bi and w = c+di at the outset
pitfalls.why_wrong: This turns the problem into four real unknowns and four equations — far more tedious than necessary.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Eliminate or substitute whole complex expressions first; only split into x+iy when one unknown remains with its conjugate.
source_files: 13891 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 7. Complex Numbers.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Reading the notation f^-1 and f^2
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating f^-1(x) as 1/f(x), or f^2(x) as [f(x)]^2
pitfalls.why_wrong: f^-1 denotes the inverse function and f^2 denotes ff — both are about composing the function, not algebraic powers of the output.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read an index on f as 'apply the function again or backwards', never as a power.
source_files: 13886 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 2.Functions + Graphing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Naming the reducing agent in the blast furnace
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives coke, carbon dioxide or limestone as the substance that reduces the iron oxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Coke burns to carbon dioxide, which reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide reduces the iron(III) oxide.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Blast furnace reducing agent = carbon monoxide. Limestone is only for removing silica.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Metal ribbon reacting with acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the ribbon straight from the bottle.
pitfalls.why_wrong: An oxide layer on the surface reacts with the acid first, so the timing is not for the metal alone.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Clean the metal with sandpaper before each run.
source_files: 11486 - Beatty 5. R3 Effect of Temp and QA_ Ans 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Where the fuse and switch are placed
pitfalls.wrong_move: Puts the fuse or the switch on the neutral wire.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The appliance would still be joined to the live wire at high voltage when switched off or after the fuse blows, so it can still give a shock.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Fuse and switch always on the live wire.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Reading stem-and-leaf diagrams
pitfalls.wrong_move: Ignoring the key (or the back-to-back reading direction)
pitfalls.why_wrong: '5 | 3 means 53' fixes the scale — the same picture with key '1 | 2 = 1.20 dollars' encodes prices, not marks. In back-to-back diagrams the LEFT side reads outward (right-to-left), so English '6 8' on stem 0 is 6 and 8, not 68.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read the key first; left leaves read away from the stem.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Making a simple cell brighter
pitfalls.wrong_move: Swaps in a more reactive metal without checking the other electrode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The voltage depends on the gap between the two metals. A swap can make the gap smaller.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compare the gap in the reactivity series before and after the change.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Simple vs compound growth
pitfalls.wrong_move: Growing simple interest on the accumulating balance (or flat-lining compound interest)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Simple interest is always on the ORIGINAL principal — 3.15% for two years is $2 \times 157.50$ on $5000$, full stop. Compound (and step-rate schemes like 2.75% then 3.55%) use the grown balance as the next principal. Mixing the two swaps the winners in comparison questions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Simple → same base every year. Compound/step → last year's total is the new base.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 1 Simple and Compound Interest.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Long multiplications in money chains
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting one calculator transcription without an estimate
pitfalls.why_wrong: $89999 \times 3.8 \times 3/100$ is about $90000 \times 0.114 = 10260$, yet the print carries $10249.87$ through three subsequent lines to a wrong final amount ($117457.59$ vs $117469.32$). Early digits corrupt everything downstream.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Estimate to 3 s.f. before accepting any big product; re-key if they disagree.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 1 Simple and Compound Interest.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Division and multiplication (or + and −) in one expression
pitfalls.wrong_move: Doing all multiplication before any division (or grouping right-to-left)
pitfalls.why_wrong: D and M share one rank and run LEFT TO RIGHT: $20 - 5 \div 5 \times 2 = 20 - 1 \times 2 = 18$, not $20 - 5 \div 10$. Same for A and S: $18 - 16 \div 2 + 6 = 18 - 8 + 6 = 16$, not $18 - 14$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: ÷ and × are equals — sweep left to right.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Identifying a, b, c before applying a discriminant condition
pitfalls.wrong_move: Read a, b, c off the equation while terms still sit on both sides (or out of order)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The discriminant belongs to ax² + bx + c = 0. Reading coefficients off an unarranged equation (e.g. (p+3)x² = 12x − 2p) gets b and c with wrong signs — Adrian's working always arranges x², then x, then constant first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Arrange first: everything on one side, in x², x, constant order — only then name a, b, c.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Asymptotes of an improper rational function y = (ax^2+bx+c)/(dx+e)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stating a horizontal asymptote without dividing first
pitfalls.why_wrong: When the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's, long division gives y = px + q + r/(dx+e), so the non-vertical asymptote is the oblique line y = px + q.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Long-divide first; the quotient line is the asymptote.
source_files: 13886 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 2.Functions + Graphing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Planning how to keep an enzyme mixture at a set temperature
pitfalls.wrong_move: Heats the test tube directly over a Bunsen flame.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The temperature cannot be held steady this way. The marker note accepts a water bath and rejects direct heating.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Set temperature? Write "water bath at … °C", checked with a thermometer.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Electricity rates quoted in cents
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying units by the cents figure as if it were dollars
pitfalls.why_wrong: 23.07 cents is 0.2307 dollars: 1156 units cost 266.69, not 26669. A hundredfold error survives sanity checks surprisingly often because the digits look right.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert cents to dollars before touching the multiplication.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 5 Personal and Household Finance.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Pyramid lengths from the apex
pitfalls.wrong_move: Interchanging the slant edge, the midpoint slant, and the height
pitfalls.why_wrong: Three distinct lengths hang off $VX$: the edge $VB = \sqrt{VX^2 + XB^2}$ with $XB$ = HALF THE DIAGONAL (10 in Practice 4), and the midpoint slant $VM = \sqrt{VX^2 + XM^2}$ with $XM$ = HALF THE PERPENDICULAR SIDE (8). Swapping $XB$ and $XM$ gives 20.6 vs 19.7 — close enough to look right and be wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch the base top-down: X to a corner = half diagonal; X to a side's midpoint = half the other side.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Reading 'more than' or 'at least' off a bar graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Including the boundary bar in a strict inequality
pitfalls.why_wrong: 'More than 2 passengers' means the 3-passenger bar only (5 taxis → 12.5%), not the 2-passenger bar's 15 taxis. Including the boundary triples the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: 'More than 2' starts at 3; 'at least 2' starts at 2.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Order of petroleum fractions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Places diesel before kerosene, or bitumen near the top.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Boiling point and molecule size increase down the column.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Top to bottom: petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, bitumen.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Counting word problems with two groups
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forgetting the 'neither' region (or treating it as an element)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The union is the TOTAL minus the outsiders: $n(P \cup C) = 40 - 12 = 28$ in Q1 — adding $23 + 15$ and comparing against 40 instead of 28 gives the wrong overlap. The 12 outside the circles counts people, not an element.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: First move, always: union = total − neither. Then place the overlap.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Frustums and partially filled cones
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the frustum (or the wet wall) as similar to the whole cone
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the apex-side small cone is similar to the whole. Frustum quantities are DIFFERENCES: $[C] : [D] = 16 : (81 - 16) = 16 : 65$; the wet wall is whole wall − dry apex cone $= 81 - 9 = 72$ (then + base). Direct scaling of the frustum fails.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name the two similar cones (top and whole), scale those, subtract for the frustum piece.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Testing a mean with a large sample from a population of unknown distribution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assuming X itself is normally distributed, or omitting any justification for normality
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the sample mean is approximately normal, and only because n is large by the Central Limit Theorem; X need not be normal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: State "since n is large, by the Central Limit Theorem, X-bar is approximately normal" — no assumption on X is needed.
source_files: 13900 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S7 Hypothesis Testing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Complements of compound sets
pitfalls.wrong_move: Distributing the prime over ∩ or ∪ unchanged
pitfalls.why_wrong: $(A \cap B)'$ is everything EXCEPT the lens — not $A' \cap B'$, which is the region outside BOTH circles ($= (A \cup B)'$). Shading questions plant exactly this trap; the two regions differ by both crescents.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Prime flips ∩ and ∪ when it moves inside (De Morgan); when unsure, shade step by step.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Counting stacked figures
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the base count instead of the running total
pitfalls.why_wrong: Figure n has n circles at its base but $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ in total — Figure 100 holds 5050, not 100. The total column grows as a sum, not a step.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask: is this column a count-per-figure or a cumulative total?

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Question asks for the TOTAL of n observations, not the average
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using Xbar ~ N(mu, sigma^2/n) and comparing the total against it
pitfalls.why_wrong: A total is the sum, which has mean n mu and variance n sigma^2. Dividing the variance by n instead of multiplying makes the spread wrong by a factor of n^2.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Underline the key words "total" or "average" before starting. Total: N(n mu, n sigma^2). Average: N(mu, sigma^2/n).
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Finding an unknown mean or standard deviation from a given probability
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reaching for invNorm with mu or sigma still unknown
pitfalls.why_wrong: invNorm needs numeric values for both parameters; with an unknown it cannot run
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Standardise first: Z = (X - mu)/sigma ~ N(0,1), apply invNorm to Z, then solve the equation(s) for the unknown
source_files: 13898 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S5 Normal Distribution Lecture Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Isosceles triangles with an altitude drawn
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating a given slant side or half-base as if it were the full base
pitfalls.why_wrong: The altitude from the apex bisects the base: with AB = AC = 12 and AK = 7, each half-base is √(144 − 49) = √95, so BC = 2√95 — not √95, and not 12. Forgetting to double (or halving the wrong thing) corrupts every later step.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Altitude of an isosceles triangle halves the base — compute half, then double.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Stating the source of sulfur dioxide as an air pollutant
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "burning fuels" or "factories".
pitfalls.why_wrong: The gas forms only when the fuel contains sulfur. The mark is for the sulfur in the fossil fuel.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write "combustion of fossil fuels that contain sulfur". Natural source: volcanoes.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining the set-up without leaves in a water-uptake experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Cannot say what the second set-up is for.
pitfalls.why_wrong: It is the control. It shows that the larger fall in water level in the other set-up is caused by the leaves.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same set-up minus one thing = control. Say what it proves.
source_files: 22001 - SASS Bio Transport in Flowering Plants Handout.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Evaluating trig/exp derivatives numerically (0.8 rad, x = 0.2, ...)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calculator in degree mode
pitfalls.why_wrong: All AM calculus is radian-based: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ is FALSE in degrees. The 0.207 and 0.948 answers here only come out in radian mode.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Derivative + trig + a number → radian mode before anything else.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Commission when the customer is buying
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting the commission from the cost (and skipping the minimum charge)
pitfalls.why_wrong: A fee moves AGAINST the customer. The file's own key prices Bank B at $625.50 \times 0.998 = 624.249$ for a buyer and picks B — but the buyer PAYS the commission, and 0.2% (1.251) sits below the stated 5-dollar minimum, so B really costs 630.50 and Bank A (627.75) wins.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Buying: add max(percentage, minimum). Selling: subtract it.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Washing the crystals of a soluble salt
pitfalls.wrong_move: Washes with warm water, or with a lot of water.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The salt is soluble, so the crystals dissolve and yield is lost.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Soluble salt: a little cold distilled water only.

pitfalls.subject: S2
