pitfalls.context: Journeys with a lunch break or waiting time
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the stop out of the total time
pitfalls.why_wrong: The tour bus that stops an hour for lunch still takes 08 50 → 15 00 for the whole journey — 6 h 10 min — so its average is 325 ÷ (37/6) = 53 km/h. Only questions that say "while in motion" exclude the stop (Hassan: 68 116/413 km/h).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Elapsed clock time counts unless the question says 'in motion'.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Volume left when air is passed over hot copper
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives the volume of oxygen removed as the answer.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The question asks for the gas remaining, which is mostly nitrogen, about four-fifths of the air.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read the last line of the question: "used up" or "remained"?

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Describing the knee-jerk reflex
pitfalls.wrong_move: Includes a relay neurone in the pathway.
pitfalls.why_wrong: In the knee jerk the sensory neurone passes the impulse straight to the motor neurone in the spinal cord.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Knee jerk: sensory → motor, one synapse. Hand off a hot object: sensory → relay → motor.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Stating the range of a function on a restricted domain
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the range from the two endpoint values only
pitfalls.why_wrong: A turning point inside the domain can give a minimum or maximum beyond the endpoint values, so the true range is wider than the endpoints suggest.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch the curve on its domain and check for turning points before stating the range.
source_files: 13886 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 2.Functions + Graphing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Finding the angle between two lines
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the obtuse angle when the acute one was asked for
pitfalls.why_wrong: A pair of lines makes two supplementary angles. The formula uses |d1.d2|, and it is that modulus which forces the acute answer; dropping it returns the obtuse partner instead.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Keep the modulus bars. If the obtuse angle is wanted, find the acute one and subtract it from 180 degrees.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Splitting a fraction whose denominator has a repeated linear factor like (x-1)²
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing only A/(x+2) + C/(x-1)² and dropping the middle B/(x-1) term
pitfalls.why_wrong: The decomposition is incomplete — comparing numerators then gives contradictory equations (e.g. the x² coefficients cannot match).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Repeated linear factor → one denominator without square & one with square.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Writing bearings
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measuring anticlockwise, from the wrong reference, or dropping the leading zero
pitfalls.why_wrong: A bearing is clockwise from NORTH at the observation point, three digits always. Ex 1(c)'s answer is $074°$ — writing "74°" or measuring from south/east gives a different-looking (and mark-losing) answer for the same direction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: North arrow at the FROM point, sweep clockwise, pad to three digits.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Comparing two distributions (means/SDs given)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Declaring the 'expected' data set more consistent without checking the SDs
pitfalls.why_wrong: Town A's SD is 0.924, town B's is 1 — A is more consistent, yet the printed key says B (and similar keys often assume the summary-table data wins). Consistency claims must quote the SMALLER SD, whichever side it is on.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write both SDs down and point at the smaller one; never argue consistency from the mean.
source_files: EM 13 Statistics 1 Standard Deviation and Interquartile Range.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Stating a source of error in a practical
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "parallax error", "zero error" or "human error".
pitfalls.why_wrong: These can be avoided with care, so they are not accepted as a source of error in the result.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name something you could NOT control, the reading it changed, and whether it made the reading too big or too small.
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Chained equations like 2p + 3q = 5p − 6q = 9
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading it as one equation instead of two
pitfalls.why_wrong: A double equals means BOTH expressions equal 9: 2p + 3q = 9 and 5p − 6q = 9 — a normal simultaneous pair (p = 3, q = 1). Treating it as a single equation loses one condition and gives a family of wrong answers.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Split a = b = c into a = c and b = c.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5B Simultaneous Equations 2 Simultaneous Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Acid plus insoluble solid method
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stops adding the solid while acid is still left.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Leftover acid stays in the filtrate and contaminates the crystals.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Add solid until some is left undissolved, then filter.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Describing corrosion of metals other than iron
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying aluminium or copper 'rusts'.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. The word is used for iron and steel only.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Iron and steel rust. Other metals corrode.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Claiming a line is tangent to a circle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Asserting tangency without checking that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius
pitfalls.why_wrong: A vertical line $x = k$ is tangent iff $|k - a| = r$ exactly. The source's printed question "explain why $x = -13$ is tangent" fails this check (distance 10 ≠ √10) — a 5-second verification catches it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Tangent ⟺ distance from centre to line = radius. Check the number before writing 'tangent'.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Questions asking for a ratio like 2b/3a
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trying to find a and b individually
pitfalls.why_wrong: One equation cannot pin down two unknowns — only their ratio. Find $\frac{b}{a}$ first, then scale: $\frac{b}{a} = \frac{5}{8} \to \frac{2b}{3a} = \frac{5 \times 2}{8 \times 3}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solve for the simple ratio first, then scale numerator and denominator.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Splitting a length in a ratio
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing by the wrong number of parts
pitfalls.why_wrong: A 4 : 7 split has 11 parts: shorter = 4/11 × 220 = 80 cm. The key's 44 = 220 ÷ 5, a 1 : 4 split — one misread digit halves the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Total parts = sum of the ratio numbers; each share = fraction of the whole.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Prism surface area
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counting only one end face (or none)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own key does it: the trapezoidal prism's 546 cm² adds one 34 cm² end instead of two (correct 580). SA = perimeter × length + 2 × cross-section, always two ends for a closed prism.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Wrap plus TWO ends — count them off explicitly.
source_files: S1 MATH 20C Mensuration 3 Volume and Surface Area Cylinder and Prism.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Wanting dx/dV (or dr/dV) when the formula gives V in terms of x
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using dV/dx in the chain rule where dx/dV belongs
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dV}\times\frac{dV}{dt}$ needs the RECIPROCAL of the natural derivative: $\frac{dx}{dV} = \frac{1}{3x^2}$ when $\frac{dV}{dx} = 3x^2$. Forgetting to flip multiplies instead of divides and inflates the answer by $(3x^2)^2$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the chain rule 'cancels' like fractions: the dV's must be adjacent — flip if they aren't.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Converting ratios to equations
pitfalls.wrong_move: Inverting a ratio at the substitution step
pitfalls.why_wrong: $AD : DY = 2 : 1$ means $DY = \frac{1}{2}AD$ — the source's Ex 3 concludes "$\therefore DY = 2AD$" from that very line and gets $2\mathbf{q}$ where the key (and coordinates) give $\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{q}$. Ratio flips survive because both versions look plausible.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rewrite $P : Q = m : n$ as $nP = mQ$ immediately, then solve for the one you need.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Finding the y-intercept of a log graph, e.g. $y = \lg(x-2)$ at $x = 0$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Evaluating $\lg(-2)$ on the calculator or marking a y-intercept regardless
pitfalls.why_wrong: A logarithm is only defined for positive arguments. When the expression inside the log is negative at $x = 0$ there is NO y-intercept — the curve lives entirely on one side of its vertical asymptote.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Before writing a y-intercept, check the sign inside the log at $x = 0$; negative → "no solution".
source_files: AM 08 Indices and Logarithms Graphs and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Choosing the axes for a graph of results
pitfalls.wrong_move: Puts the measured quantity on the x-axis and the concentration on the y-axis.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mark scheme rejects the axes mark if they are the wrong way round.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: What you changed goes across (x). What you measured goes up (y).

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: One quantity as a percentage of another
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing mismatched units
pitfalls.why_wrong: 30 g against 0.8 kg read as 30/0.8 gives 3750%. Converting first (30/800) gives the true 3.75%. The ratio underneath a percentage needs like-for-like units.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert to the same unit, then divide.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Rounding whole numbers to significant figures
pitfalls.wrong_move: Discarding the place-value zeros (or slipping a digit)
pitfalls.why_wrong: 39078 to 3 sf keeps its size: 39100 — not 391, and not the print's 38100 (a digit slip). The zeros after the kept figures are placeholders, and the kept figures themselves must come from the original number.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same number of digits before the decimal point as the original.
source_files: S1 MATH 05 Numbers 5 Approximation and Estimation.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Flat-rate time in PRT
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting months for T (or mismatching the installment count)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $T$ is in years while installments are monthly: 18 installments → $T = 1.5$ but 18 divisions; 30 payments over $2\frac{1}{2}$ years → $T = 2.5$. Mixing 18 with $T = 18$ makes rates 12× too small.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: T = months ÷ 12 for the interest; keep the raw month count for the division.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Computing a gradient from two points
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mismatching the subtraction order between numerator and denominator
pitfalls.why_wrong: (y1 − y2)/(x2 − x1) flips the sign: a clearly rising line comes out negative. Both subtractions must lead with the SAME point.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sign-check against the picture: up-rightwards must be positive.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Questions asking for a squared quantity (area of a square on a side)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Square-rooting and then re-squaring, or rounding the root midway
pitfalls.why_wrong: The overlapping-squares area is QP² = 17² + 19² = 650 cm² directly — taking QP = √650 ≈ 25.5 and squaring back introduces rounding error for no reason. Same in chained figures: AE² accumulates 50 → 75 → 100 without ever rooting until the end.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Stay in squares as long as the question lets you.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Kite diagonal properties
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assuming both diagonals of a kite bisect each other
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the axis of symmetry bisects the OTHER diagonal; the print's own bullet overstates it. Mutual bisection at 90° is the rhombus/square property. Claiming a midpoint that isn't there produces phantom equal segments.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Kite: perpendicular diagonals, ONE bisected. Rhombus: both, at 90°.
source_files: S1 MATH 17B Polygons and Angles 2 Quadrilaterals and Polygons.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Finishing a simultaneous-equations question
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stopping after finding one variable
pitfalls.why_wrong: The solution is a PAIR. After x = 1/3, the y = 7/3 step still carries a mark — and substituting back into BOTH original equations is the free self-check that catches sign errors.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Two letters, two values, one check in both equations.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5B Simultaneous Equations 2 Simultaneous Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Exterior angle of a triangle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Equating the exterior angle to the sum including the ADJACENT interior angle
pitfalls.why_wrong: The exterior angle equals the two interior OPPOSITE angles: x + (x+10) = 230 − 2x gives 55. Including the adjacent angle instead double-counts the straight line and the equation contradicts itself.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Exterior = the two angles far from it.
source_files: S1 MATH 17A Polygons and Angles 1 Angles Recap.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Writing a negative test result
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves the observation blank or writes "nothing".
pitfalls.why_wrong: An observation is still required.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write "no visible change" (or "solution remains colourless").
source_files: 11486 - Beatty 5. R3 Effect of Temp and QA_ Ans 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Right angle in a semicircle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Claiming a 90° at the circumference from a chord that is not a diameter
pitfalls.why_wrong: The property needs the subtending side to pass through the CENTRE. In these figures the diameter is often disguised in prose — 'AC passes through E and O' (Assignment Q3), 'COD is a straight line' (Misc Q6) — and conversely, prominent chords like $BD$ carry no right angle at all.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Before writing 'rt ∠ in semicircle', point at the centre and check the chord runs through it.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Rationalizing any fraction (single surd or conjugate)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying only the denominator by the surd/conjugate and leaving the numerator alone
pitfalls.why_wrong: Multiplying top AND bottom by the same thing is multiplying by 1 — the value is unchanged. Touching only the bottom changes the value of the fraction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Multiply the TOP and the bottom — you are only multiplying by 1.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reading the centre from the expanded form x² + y² − 2ax − 2by + c = 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the x and y coefficients by 2 instead of −2 (or forgetting the sign flip)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Expanding $(x-a)^2$ produces $-2ax$, so the printed coefficient already carries a minus. Adrian's margin note asks "Why?" and derives it: centre $= \left(\frac{\text{coeff of }x}{-2}, \frac{\text{coeff of }y}{-2}\right)$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Divide by MINUS 2 — for $x^2+y^2-6x+2y-15=0$ the centre is $(3, -1)$, not $(-3, 1)$.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Reversing a bearing (bearing of A from B given B from A)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting one long chain of angle arithmetic with no check
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reverse bearing is exactly ±180°. The source's own Ex 1(b) computes $360° - 64°$ and prints $294°$ — a subtraction slip; the check $116° + 180° = 296°$ exposes it in one line. Unchecked chains let single-digit slips survive to the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Every from-to reversal: add or subtract 180° and compare with your chained answer.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Writing the equation for photosynthesis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adds energy on the right-hand side as a product.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Light energy is taken in and stored in glucose. Only respiration releases energy.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Photosynthesis: products are glucose and oxygen only. Light and chlorophyll go on the arrow.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Area ratios of non-similar triangles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Squaring a base ratio (or using base ratio on similar triangles' slant sides)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Squaring applies ONLY to similar triangles. Same-height triangles ($\triangle BCX$, $\triangle ABX$ on bases $CX$, $AB$) use the plain base ratio $\frac{2}{3}$ — squaring gives $\frac{4}{9}$ and marks vanish. The notes flag $\triangle AXY$/$\triangle BAX$ as 'not similar' for exactly this reason.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask first: similar (AA)? → square. Same height? → bases, unsquared.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Writing side ratios from similar triangles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Pairing sides that do not correspond, e.g. writing RY/RQ = RX/RP instead of RY/RX = RP/RQ after proving triangle PYR similar to triangle QXR
pitfalls.why_wrong: Ratios must follow the vertex correspondence of the similarity statement; mispaired sides give a false equation that can still look plausible and even lead to a "proof" of the wrong identity.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Adrian's margin arrow: "need to identify the correct sides to form the ratio: try highlighting them in the diagram" — read the vertex order position by position before writing any ratio.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Counting recast items
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding the quotient to the nearest whole number
pitfalls.why_wrong: 131.8 sheets means 131 complete sheets — the 0.8 of a sheet cannot be made. Rounding up claims metal that isn't there; 45.8 rods → 45, 545.5 cubes → 545.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Whole items round DOWN, always.
source_files: S1 MATH 20D Mensuration 4 Volume and Surface Area Composite Figures.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Planning a fair comparison
pitfalls.wrong_move: Changes the catalyst but does not say what is kept the same.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Volume and concentration of the solution, mass of catalyst and temperature all change the rate. Without fixing them the comparison is not fair.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name the one thing changed, the thing measured, and at least two things kept the same.
source_files: 13288 - S4 Pure Chemistry Extra Planning Revision 2024 Prelim.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Regions between touching circles and tangent lines
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the centre-line angle as equal on both circles (or guessing the tangent length)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The two angles are CO-INTERIOR: $\angle XQB = \pi - \angle APX$ (1.792 vs 1.349 in Ex 3b). The tangent segment needs the constructed right triangle: legs $R + r$ (hypotenuse $PQ$) and $R - r$, giving $AB = \sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = 40$ — not $\sqrt{41^2}$ or a copied angle.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the parallel from the small centre; read off legs $R−r$ and hypotenuse $R+r$; angles are supplementary, not equal.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 2 Cones and Miscellaneous (With Volume of Prism).pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Recording observations in qualitative analysis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes a conclusion as the observation, such as "a gas is evolved" or "carbon dioxide is given off".
pitfalls.why_wrong: An observation is what is seen. The gas is only named after its test.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write: effervescence; gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. Then, separately: the gas is carbon dioxide.
source_files: 21952 - SASS Chem Data of Ionic Cmpds Summary.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Real-world increasing/decreasing intervals (time, workers, lengths)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the raw algebraic interval
pitfalls.why_wrong: The algebra for the drug-absorption model gives $-2 < x < 2$, but $x$ is TIME: the answer is $0 \leq x < 2$. The workers question needs $x > 2.25$ hundreds converted to the least integer NUMBER of workers, 226.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Intersect with the physical domain, then convert to the units the question asks for.
source_files: AM 17 Differentiation 5 Increasing and Decreasing Functions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: 'Is the gradient increasing or decreasing?'
pitfalls.wrong_move: Checking the sign of dy/dx instead of d²y/dx²
pitfalls.why_wrong: The gradient is itself a function; its monotonicity is governed by ITS derivative, $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ — one level up. Example 2b: $f' = \frac{9}{(x+2)^2} > 0$ says $f$ increases, but $f^{(2)} < 0$ says the GRADIENT decreases.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Underline what must increase/decrease; differentiate THAT once.
source_files: AM 17 Differentiation 5 Increasing and Decreasing Functions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Quantities with metric prefixes (tera, mega, micro, pico…)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Polishing into standard form before converting to the base unit
pitfalls.why_wrong: The prefix IS a power of ten: $0.1294$ megabytes must become $0.1294 \times 10^6$ bytes first, THEN $1.294 \times 10^5$ bytes. Skipping the unit step invites the source's Ex 1(f) fate — its final line is a copy-paste from the previous part ('$5.062 \times 10^{13}$ metres', wrong value AND unit).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Prefix → power of ten → base unit, then tidy A. Re-read the final line's UNITS against the question.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Squaring and powering matrices
pitfalls.wrong_move: Squaring each entry (or grinding out high powers term by term)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\mathbf{B}^2$ means $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 15 \\ -5 & 13 \end{pmatrix}$, nothing like the entry-squares. High powers are pattern problems: $\mathbf{A}^2 = \mathbf{A}$ collapses $\mathbf{A}^{23}$ to $\mathbf{A}$ in one line.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Powers = repeated full multiplications; compute two or three, then look for a repeating pattern.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Money equations
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing cents with dollars in one equation
pitfalls.why_wrong: Pens at 60 cents with a total of 10 DOLLARS needs $0.6x$, not $60x$ — or convert the total to 1000 cents. Half-converted equations are off by a factor of 100.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Pick one unit, convert everything to it before the equals sign.
source_files: S1 MATH 10B Algebra 5B Forming Linear Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Expected gain of a game stall
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the full prize as the owner's loss (or forgetting the charge on losses)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The owner keeps the 2-token charge either way, so a player win costs him only $5 - 2 = 3$ net. Using 5 gives $180 - 90 = 90$ instead of the correct $180 - 54 = 126$; the same slip wrecks the break-even prize ($x = 12$ comes from $180 = 18(x-2)$).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Owner's net per player-win = prize − charge. He always pockets the charge.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Denominator contains a quadratic factor that CAN be factorized, e.g. x²+4x+3
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating it like a non-factorizable quadratic and writing (Bx+C) over the whole quadratic
pitfalls.why_wrong: x²+4x+3 = (x+3)(x+1) — the intended split is separate constants over each linear factor; the Bx+C form hides the simpler structure Adrian's method expects.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Factorize first — always try to factorize the quadratic before choosing the split.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Percentage-of-space answers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing by the wrong whole (or inverting occupied/unoccupied)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The pencil box is 21.45% EMPTY: (409.5 − 321.7)/409.5. Dividing the gap by the pencils' volume, or reporting the occupied 78.55%, answers a different question.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Percent OF the container: gap ÷ container volume.
source_files: S1 MATH 20E Mensuration 5 Miscellaneous Area and Volume Questions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Substituting into D = S × T
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing units (minutes into an hours formula, km/h with seconds)
pitfalls.why_wrong: 42 km/h × 15 gives 630 of nothing useful; converting first (42 km/h = 11.67 m/s) gives the true 175 m. Similarly 30 minutes must enter a km/h formula as 0.5 h, not 30.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Make speed, distance and time speak the same units before multiplying.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Giving the value of a gradient
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves the gradient without a unit.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A gradient is one quantity divided by another, so it carries a unit unless the two units cancel.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Unit of gradient = unit on the y-axis ÷ unit on the x-axis.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Reporting how acidic or alkaline a solution is
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives a pH number from litmus paper, or reports Universal Indicator only as "acidic".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Litmus shows only acidic or alkaline. Universal Indicator gives a colour that matches a pH number.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Litmus: state the colour change. Universal Indicator: state the colour and the pH number.
source_files: 21952 - SASS Chem Data of Ionic Cmpds Summary.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Using printed answer keys
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reconciling your work to a key that contradicts the question's numbers
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice 3 Q8 states 5% but its key (796.37, 3.19%) only follows from 3% — chasing the key would 'fix' correct work into wrong work. Keys can lag question edits.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: If your value disagrees, re-derive with the printed data; a key matching different inputs is the key's problem.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 1 Simple and Compound Interest.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Chained products and 'arrange the matrices' tasks
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying left-to-right without checking every neighbouring pair chains
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice 1a Q3(k) dead-ends: after $(1\ 2)\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ the shapes are $(1\times2)(3\times2)$ — undefined, and deliberately left keyless. Q4/Q6 require REORDERING ($\mathbf{BAC}$; $(2\times3)(3\times1)(1\times4)$) before any arithmetic.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Chain the dimensions first: inner numbers must match at EVERY junction; reorder until they do.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Computing a maximum/minimum point
pitfalls.wrong_move: Botching the sign product and accepting an impossible vertex
pitfalls.why_wrong: $-2(5)(-5) = +50$, but the print writes $-50$ and boxes 'maximum $(-3, -50)$' — impossible: a downward parabola that crosses the $x$-axis must peak ABOVE it. (The file's own key and its reused assignment figure both say $(-3, 50)$.)
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count negatives in the product, then check the vertex is on the correct side of the axis for the curve's shape.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Planning a comparison of fuels
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measures the temperature of the burning fuel.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The energy given out is shown by the temperature rise of the water that the fuel heats.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Thermometer goes in the water. Record it before and after burning.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Coefficients when simplifying (16 ÷ 8, 6/36, powers of 2 in (2ab)³)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Letting plain numbers vanish or survive unreduced
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own keys slip here: Practice 1(j) prints $a^4$ for $16a^{-5} \div 8a^{-9}$ — the correct answer is $2a^4$ ($\frac{16}{8} = 2$ must stay); Practice 2(a) prints $27a^{13}b^{12}$ for the correct $27a^{13}b^{21}$ (digits transposed). Cube the 2 in $(2ab)^3 = 8a^3b^3$ every time.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Track the numeric coefficient as its own 'base' through every step, and re-derive keys that look off.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Generating solutions after applying the R-formula
pitfalls.wrong_move: Generating θ-values directly instead of values of the shifted angle (θ + α)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The equation is in $(\theta + \alpha)$, whose range is the θ-range shifted by α (and scaled, if the angle is 2x). Generating for θ misses solutions and produces out-of-range artefacts — the worked example's first branch gives $\theta = -29.6°$, which must be caught and rejected.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write the shifted (and scaled) range first, generate every value inside it, then unshift/unscale.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Recording a precipitate in qualitative analysis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "the solution turns white" or "turns cloudy".
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mark is for a precipitate and its colour, then what happens in excess reagent.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write "white precipitate, insoluble in excess" or "soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution".
source_files: 18856 - 2025 Montfort Sec 6092 Revision Guide for Practical.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Direction of current in a circuit
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws conventional current from the negative terminal, the way electrons move.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Conventional current goes from the positive terminal round to the negative terminal. Electrons go the other way.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Current arrow: + to −. Electron arrow: − to +.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Conductor or electrolyte
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calls a metal or mercury an electrolyte because it conducts.
pitfalls.why_wrong: An electrolyte conducts by moving ions and is decomposed. A metal conducts by electrons and is not changed.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Conducts and decomposes: electrolyte. Conducts unchanged: metal or graphite.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Calcium carbonate with dilute sulfuric acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expects the reaction to carry on until all the carbonate is used up.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Insoluble calcium sulfate forms a coat on the solid and keeps the acid away, so the reaction stops early.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solid + acid giving an insoluble salt? The coat stops the reaction.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Mixed numbers in substitutions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating 2½ as 2.1 or splitting it
pitfalls.why_wrong: $a = 2\frac{1}{2}$ enters as $\frac{5}{2}$ (or 2.5): $34 = 12(2.5 + l)$. Mangling the mixed number derails an otherwise easy solve for $l = \frac{1}{3}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before substituting.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining the layer of oil on the water in a transpiration set-up
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives no reason, or says the oil stops the plant losing water.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The oil stops water evaporating from the water surface, so any fall in level is due to the plant alone.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Oil layer: prevents evaporation from the water surface.
source_files: 22001 - SASS Bio Transport in Flowering Plants Handout.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why an alloy is harder
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes only that the alloy has stronger bonds, or that the atoms are packed more tightly.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The marks are for atoms of different sizes disrupting the orderly layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Different size, orderly arrangement disrupted, layers cannot slide.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Drawing without replacement
pitfalls.wrong_move: Updating only the denominator (or neither) on the second draw
pitfalls.why_wrong: After a ball leaves, the total drops by 1 AND the count of that colour drops by 1: both-white is $\frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9}$, not $\frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{6}{9}$ or $(\frac{6}{10})^2$. One stale number silently shifts every later branch.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: No replacement → numerator AND denominator both shrink for the colour just drawn.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Using "the term independent of x" of a product like (x−1)(x−2)(ax²+bx+c)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Setting c equal to the given constant directly (e.g. c = −2)
pitfalls.why_wrong: c is only the constant of the last bracket; every bracket contributes — the constant term of the product is (−1)(−2)(c) = 2c.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Constant term of a product = product of the constant terms of all the brackets.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Solving x² = c or (m+1)² = c inside proportion questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking only the positive square root
pitfalls.why_wrong: (m+1)² = 36 gives m + 1 = ±6, so m = 5 or −7; y = 7x² with y = 28 gives x = ±2 (the notes' key lists only 2). Drop the negative root only when the context forbids it — like time, where s = −3.5 is rejected explicitly.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Un-square with ±, then let the context reject a root — not habit.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Recording a copper(II) ion test
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes only "blue precipitate" for aqueous ammonia.
pitfalls.why_wrong: There are two stages: a light blue precipitate, then it dissolves in excess to give a dark blue solution.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Always record a few drops and excess as two separate observations.
source_files: 12648 - ACSBR 6 Identification of Ions and Gases - Assignment ANS.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Relative formula mass and % by mass
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves out part of the formula: the water in a hydrate, or a subscript when finding the percentage of an element.
pitfalls.why_wrong: CuSO₄.5H₂O is 250, not 160. The oxygen in NaNO₃ is 3 × 16, not 16.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: List every atom with its count before adding. The water after the dot counts too.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Scaling a temperature (or any level) along a gradient
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying by the level itself instead of the CHANGE
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own working does this: for "where is it 7.5°C", it scales by 7.5 and prints 1096.875 m — the height of a 7.5-degree DROP. The change from the foot is 23 − 7.5 = 15.5°C, giving 2266⅞ m (the key's answer).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Turn the asked value into a difference from the reference point first.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Gas volumes collected being lower than expected
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expects the collected volumes to match the equation ratio exactly.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Chlorine dissolves in the solution, and oxygen dissolves slightly, so less of that gas is collected.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Less gas than the ratio predicts? Say it is soluble in water.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Doing qualitative analysis in the practical paper
pitfalls.wrong_move: Carries out gas tests or extra tests that the instructions did not ask for.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Extra tests waste time and reagents. A gas test is needed only when a gas is actually seen.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bubbles or fumes seen? Then test the gas. Otherwise follow the instructions only.
source_files: 18856 - 2025 Montfort Sec 6092 Revision Guide for Practical.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Simplifying a quotient of two logarithms, e.g. $\frac{\log_4 27}{\log_4 81}$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Cancelling into a single log: $\frac{\log_a x}{\log_a y} = \log_a\frac{x}{y}$
pitfalls.why_wrong: Dividing logs is the change-of-base pattern ($\frac{\log_a x}{\log_a y} = \log_y x$), not the Minus Power law. $\log_a x - \log_a y = \log_a\frac{x}{y}$ needs a subtraction, not a fraction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: A fraction of logs is a change of base in disguise — express both as powers and cancel instead.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Ordering negative decimals
pitfalls.wrong_move: Ranking negatives by digit size as if they were positive
pitfalls.why_wrong: $-0.66 < -0.6$ even though $0.66 > 0.6$ — the bigger magnitude sits further left of zero. In the close quartet, $-0.\dot{7}1\dot{4} = -0.714714\ldots$ is the SMALLEST because its expansion is largest in size.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: For negatives: bigger size = smaller number.
source_files: S1 MATH 04 Numbers 4 The Real Number System.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Dividing a polynomial by a quadratic divisor
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the remainder as a single constant r instead of ax+b
pitfalls.why_wrong: Degree of remainder = degree of divisor − 1, so a quadratic divisor can leave a linear remainder. Assuming a constant silently discards the ax part and the equations come out wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Degree of remainder = degree of divisor − 1: linear divisor → constant; quadratic divisor → write ax+b.
source_files: notes_inbox/AM/AM 06 Polynomials 1 Remainder and Factor Theorem.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: A bisector that must cut a specific segment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stopping the bisector short of the target line
pitfalls.why_wrong: Questions say 'produce it to cut AC at X' — the raw bisector segment often ends before reaching. If it is not extended, X does not exist on the diagram and the follow-up measurement cannot be taken.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Extend (produce) constructed lines until they actually cross the target.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Strict vs inclusive bounds when picking integers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Including the boundary of a strict inequality
pitfalls.why_wrong: x > −20 excludes −20: the smallest integer is −19. Likewise x < 13 excludes 13, so the largest prime is 11. Only ≥ and ≤ admit the boundary itself.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: > and < shut the boundary out; ≥ and ≤ let it in.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reading off the calculator after solving an exponential equation, e.g. $x = \frac{\lg 7 - 3\lg 5}{\lg 7 - \lg 5}$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dropping the minus sign when rounding a negative display ($-8.56654 \to$ "8.57")
pitfalls.why_wrong: Log-equation answers are often negative (whenever the smaller-base side needs a bigger exponent). The magnitude rounds correctly but the sign is part of the answer — the source notes themselves slipped here, printing 8.57.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Before rounding, sanity-check the SIGN: should x be positive or negative for the two sides to balance?

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Deciding whether a given point lies on a line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Finding lambda from one component and stopping there
pitfalls.why_wrong: Every component must be satisfied by the same lambda. A point can match one or two rows by coincidence: one row may give lambda = 1 while another gives lambda = 3/4, and that inconsistency is what proves the point is off the line.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solve lambda from one row, substitute into the other two, and state explicitly whether the system is consistent.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Defining isomers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says isomers have the same structural formula or the same general formula.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Definition needs both parts: same molecular formula, different structural formula.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Answer keys and printed working in this chapter
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting every printed line
pitfalls.why_wrong: Three slips found: a stray 'A(0,16)' fragment beside the correct $A(0,15)$; the 5.75/5/11.875 area box (key says 9.5); and the assignment key $p = \frac{5}{4}$ for a question whose printed point $(-p, 1+p)$ actually gives $p = 2$. All catchable by one substitution back into the original equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Substitute your answer into the ORIGINAL equation; if a key disagrees, re-derive before believing either.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Recording a negative food test
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "no change" or "nothing happened".
pitfalls.why_wrong: An observation must state the colour seen.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Negative result: "iodine remained brown", "Benedict's remained blue", "biuret remained blue".

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Stating the line of symmetry
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing a bare number instead of an equation
pitfalls.why_wrong: The line of symmetry is a vertical LINE: for $y = x(2x-5)$ it is $x = \frac{5}{4}$. Writing just "$\frac{5}{4}$" names a number and drops the mark; the midpoint-of-roots shortcut $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$ gives the value, but the answer needs the '$x =$'.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Answer the symmetry question with 'x = …' every time.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Solving for an unknown that makes three algebraic expressions a GP
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping every root of the resulting quadratic
pitfalls.why_wrong: A GP needs non-zero terms and a common ratio that is not 1. In the notes m = 7 or m = -1/2, but m = -1/2 makes the middle term 2m + 1 equal to zero, so it is rejected and only m = 7 survives.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Substitute each root back: does any term become 0, or does r come out as 1? If so, reject that root and say why.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Proving proportionality from a table
pitfalls.wrong_move: Checking a single column and declaring proportionality
pitfalls.why_wrong: m/x for the plastic-cube table matches nothing consistent (1.6 then 6.4), yet m/x³ = 0.4 in every column. One matching pair can be coincidence; the claim is about ALL pairs, and examiners award the marks for showing every column (the notes underline 'we must show all values of k are the same').
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Test every column; state the common k, then conclude.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Questions asking for the most likely number
pitfalls.wrong_move: Quoting the expected value np as the most likely value, or using mode and expectation interchangeably
pitfalls.why_wrong: They are different concepts with different values: the mode is the x with the largest probability, the expectation is the long-run average — e.g. mode 10 while np = 9.6.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Asked for the most likely number: compare probabilities near np and pick the largest; never quote np itself.
source_files: 13896 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S4 Binomial Distribution.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Breaking a big surd that carries a minus sign, e.g. −√40 in a numerator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dropping the sign during the breakdown: −√40 becomes +2√10
pitfalls.why_wrong: Breaking 40 = 4 × 10 changes the surd, never its sign — the minus belongs to the whole term. The printed sheet's (2+√5)/(3+√8) example makes exactly this slip.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: The minus stays glued to its surd through the breakdown.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Drawing a dot-and-cross diagram of a molecule
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws only the shared pairs and leaves out the other outer electrons, or ends with an atom short of a full shell.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The diagram must show every outer electron of each atom, and each atom must end with a full outer shell.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After drawing, count round each atom: 8 (hydrogen 2), and the total equals the electrons the atoms started with.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Making an insoluble salt
pitfalls.wrong_move: Starts from an insoluble base or insoluble carbonate.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The new solid forms on the old one. Two insoluble solids cannot be separated by filtering.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Insoluble salt: start with two solutions.
source_files: 12862 - NYGH Acids, Bases and Salts Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Recasting with mixed units
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing a cm³ volume by a mm-dimension product
pitfalls.why_wrong: The gold sheets are 297 × 210 × 2 mm; dividing 16 436.875 cm³ by mm³ inflates the count 1000-fold. Convert to 29.7 × 21 × 0.2 cm first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One unit system before any division.
source_files: S1 MATH 20D Mensuration 4 Volume and Surface Area Composite Figures.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing mass-loss experiments that start at different balance readings
pitfalls.wrong_move: Picks the faster experiment from the lower final balance reading.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The flasks started at different masses. Rate is shown by the loss in mass in the same time.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Subtract: initial reading − final reading for each experiment, then compare.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Position vectors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating any vector ending at a point as its position vector
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only origin-anchored vectors give coordinates: $\overrightarrow{OA}$ yes, $\overrightarrow{BO}$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}$ no. Reading $\overrightarrow{PQ}$'s components as Q's coordinates ignores where P sits — Q is $\overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PQ}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Coordinates come only from O-to-point vectors. Build OQ before reading off Q.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Sketching the curve when the solid is powdered but its mass is unchanged
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws the new curve finishing higher.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Powder only makes the reaction faster. The same mass gives the same total amount of gas.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same moles of limiting reactant: steeper curve, same final height.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Subtract A from B with multi-term A
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting only A's first term
pitfalls.why_wrong: Subtracting $2x^3 + x - 3$ from $x^2 - x + 4$ without brackets gives $x^2 - x + 4 - 2x^3 + x - 3$ — the $+x$ and $-3$ kept their old signs. Bracketing forces $-2x^3 - x + 3$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: B − (all of A), then expand the minus.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Comparing potato pieces in different solutions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Compares the change in mass in grams.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The pieces did not start with the same mass, so a bigger piece shows a bigger change. The mark scheme asks for percentage change to allow for this.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Pieces start at different masses? Use percentage change.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Describing where a function is strictly decreasing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying that y = 1/x is strictly decreasing for all x because its gradient is negative everywhere
pitfalls.why_wrong: The domain is in two separate pieces. Taking x1 = -1 and x2 = 1 gives f(x1) = -1 less than f(x2) = 1 with x1 less than x2, so the definition fails across the gap.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Give the intervals separately: strictly decreasing for x < 0 and for x > 0. Test the definition across the whole interval you are claiming.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Finding a rate from a graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives a gradient with no triangle shown on the graph and no unit.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The scheme needs the triangle drawn, and takes a mark off for a missing or wrong unit.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw a big triangle on the line; unit = y-unit per x-unit.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: A point R described as lying on AB produced
pitfalls.wrong_move: Applying the Ratio Theorem to R as though it lay between A and B
pitfalls.why_wrong: Produced means R is beyond B and outside the segment, so the three points are still collinear but B is now the middle one. The internal-division formula applied to R returns a point inside AB instead.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the three points in order first, then apply the Ratio Theorem to whichever point lies between the other two.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Evaluating big squares via (a ± b)², e.g. 701²
pitfalls.wrong_move: Letting a or b drift mid-working
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes' own example mixes 701 and 702 — (700+2)² with 2(700)(1) — and lands on 491404, which is neither 701² (491401) nor 702² (492804). Once you write a = 700, b = 1, every line must use exactly those.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Declare a and b once; check the last digit at the end.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Charging interest
pitfalls.wrong_move: Applying the rate to the full cash price instead of the balance
pitfalls.why_wrong: Hire-purchase interest is simple interest on what is BORROWED: the TV's 6% applies to $3380$ (after the 500 deposit), not 3880 — using the full price inflates the interest from 507 to 582 and every figure after it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: First line of working: balance = price − deposit. Interest lives on that.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Writing angle working for marks
pitfalls.wrong_move: Giving values without reason tags
pitfalls.why_wrong: Sec 1 marking awards the reason as well as the number: (∠s on a str line), (vert opp ∠s), (corr ∠s), (alt ∠s), (int ∠s), (∠ sum of △), (ext ∠ of △). Correct values with no tags lose the reasoning marks the question explicitly requests.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Every line of angle working ends with its bracketed reason.
source_files: S1 MATH 17A Polygons and Angles 1 Angles Recap.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why plastics cause pollution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that plastics pollute because they are 'durable' or 'strong'.
pitfalls.why_wrong: That does not say why the waste stays in the environment.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say plastics are non-biodegradable: bacteria cannot break them down.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Substituting values into a formula
pitfalls.wrong_move: Putting a value into the wrong letter's slot
pitfalls.why_wrong: In $s = 3t + \frac{1}{2}av$ the 3 belongs to t while $a = 3$ is a different quantity — swapping them changes the equation. Write the substitution line with every value in brackets before simplifying.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Copy the formula, replace one letter at a time, in brackets.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Stopwatch timing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says "human reaction time" without the direction.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A late start makes the time too short; a late stop makes it too long.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: State which delay and whether the time is too long or too short; improve by repeating and averaging.
source_files: 11486 - Beatty 5. R3 Effect of Temp and QA_ Ans 2023.pdf
11485 - Beatty 6. R1 6092 Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide_Answers.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Tree diagrams with two draws
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating RG and GR as the same path (or forgetting one of them)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $RG$ (red first) and $GR$ (green first) are DIFFERENT sequences, each with its own path probability — 'one of each colour' needs both added. Counting one path halves the answer (Assignment Q2: one gum one mint $= \frac{7}{30} + \frac{7}{30} = \frac{7}{15}$, not $\frac{7}{30}$).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: 'One of each' → list BOTH orders, add across.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Working with f(x) = divisor × Q(x) + remainder
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading Q(x) as "Q times x" — treating Q as a number and trying to divide or expand it away
pitfalls.why_wrong: Q(x) is like f(x): Q stands for quotient, a whole polynomial written in function notation. It is just a way of writing a polynomial.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Q(x) does not mean Q × x — it names the quotient polynomial, which vanishes when you sub a root of the divisor.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Copying a fraction from the question into the working
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving a neighbouring or misread value
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own Example 1(b) prints 3/5 : 8/9 but its solution works 18/45 : 40/45 — that is 2/5 : 8/9 — and answers 9 : 20 instead of the correct 27 : 40. One misread numerator and every later line is consistent but wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Re-read the printed numbers after your first line of working.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing two acid samples with different volume and concentration, solid in excess
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the more concentrated acid gives more gas.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Gas depends on moles of acid = concentration × volume. 400 cm³ of 1.5 mol/dm³ has more moles than 100 cm³ of 3 mol/dm³.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Concentration sets the gradient. Moles set the final height. Calculate the moles.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Classifying numbers written with root signs or powers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calling anything with a root sign irrational (or classifying before evaluating)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\sqrt{9} = 3$, $\sqrt{169} = 13$, $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$ and $\frac{-4}{-2} = 2$ are all rational — some are even prime. Only roots of non-perfect powers ($\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{7}, \sqrt{12}$) are irrational. Evaluate every expression first, then classify the VALUE.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Simplify first — classify the value, not the costume.
source_files: S1 MATH 04 Numbers 4 The Real Number System.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Comparing rates of photosynthesis per unit area and per unit mass of leaf
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treats the two measures as the same thing.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Two leaves with the same area can have different thickness, so different mass. The two rates need not agree.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Per area or per mass? Think of a thin leaf and a thick leaf of the same size.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Two-particle questions (meet, overtake, catch up)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Equating velocities to find overtaking
pitfalls.why_wrong: Equal velocity means neither is gaining — overtaking happens when DISPLACEMENTS are equal. Ex 3c: $v_x = v_y$ at $t = 2, 4$, yet $s_x = s_y$ has no positive root, so no overtaking ever occurs.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Meet/overtake/collide → set $s_1 = s_2$ (with both constants from their own initial data); equal-v is only about relative speed.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Diagonal statements about a parallelogram
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading |b + a| = |b − a| as 'rhombus' (or |a| = |b| as 'rectangle')
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ are the DIAGONALS — equal diagonals make a rectangle. Equal SIDES ($|\mathbf{a}| = |\mathbf{b}|$) make a rhombus. Swapping the two conclusions is the classic trade.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sum/difference = diagonals → rectangle test. Plain |a|, |b| = sides → rhombus test.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Ladder slides down the wall (or any re-configured right triangle)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reusing the original angle after the configuration changes
pitfalls.why_wrong: After sliding 4 m down, the ladder's LENGTH (11.547 m) is what survives — the 60° does not. New horizontal $= \sqrt{11.547^2 - 6^2} = 9.87$ m; keeping 60° gives $11.547\cos 60° = 5.77$, silently wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask what physically stays fixed (the ladder), carry THAT to the new triangle, and rebuild.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining the flat part of a heating curve
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying no heat is taken in because the temperature is not rising.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Heat is still being absorbed. It is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to make them move faster.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flat = heat going into separating particles. Two states are present until the change is complete.
source_files: 12154 - ACSBR Kinetic Particle Theory - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Trends down the alkane series
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says flammability increases as the molecules get bigger.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Bigger molecules have higher boiling points and are harder to turn to vapour, so they catch fire less easily.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Down the series: boiling point up, viscosity up, flammability DOWN.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Comparing transport in xylem and phloem
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says phloem carries glucose, or that phloem only carries food downwards.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids, both up and down the plant. Xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards only.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Phloem: sucrose and amino acids, both directions. Xylem: water and mineral salts, up only.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Magnitude equations
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking only the positive square root
pitfalls.why_wrong: $|expr|$ conditions square to $(\ldots)^2 = c$, which has TWO roots: $(2+h)^2 = 1$ → $h = -1$ AND $-3$; $(u-1)^2 = 64$ → $u = 9$ AND $-7$. Dropping the negative branch loses half the marks on 'find the possible values' questions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After squaring, write ± before unsquaring. 'Possible valueS' = expect two.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Reading ratios off a labelled triangle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing a numerator or denominator that is not an actual side of the triangle
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source's own Ex 1 prints $\sin\angle ACB = \frac{7}{13}$ — but the sides are 5, 12, 13 and part (a) computes $AB = 12$ one line earlier; the 7 matches nothing. Plausible-looking fractions can be pure phantoms.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Point at both sides of the fraction on the diagram before writing it down.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Recording a decrease in length or mass in a results table
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes the decrease as a plain number with no sign.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A gain and a loss then look the same. The sign carries its own mark.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Change column: + for a gain, − for a loss, every row.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Dividing small decimals in area-scale steps
pitfalls.wrong_move: Slipping a decimal place in quotients like 0.1024 ÷ 0.0025
pitfalls.why_wrong: 0.1024 ÷ 0.0025 = 40.96, but the notes' working prints 4.096 — one lost power of ten. Scaling both numbers by 10⁴ first (1024 ÷ 25) makes the division safe, and the direction check (must exceed 16 cm²) catches the slip instantly.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Clear the decimals before dividing; then sanity-check the size.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Describing what happens when DNA replicates before mitosis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the number of chromosomes doubles.
pitfalls.why_wrong: After replication each chromosome is two joined chromatids. The amount of DNA doubles; the number of chromosomes stays the same until the chromatids separate.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Replication doubles the DNA, not the chromosome count.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Solving an interior-angle equation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Fumbling the final division and not substituting back
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own key turns 11x = 440 into x = 44; the substitute-back test (11·44 + 100 = 584 ≠ 540) exposes it instantly. The correct 40 checks: 40 + 80 + 120 + 200 + 100 = 540.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After solving, feed x back into the angle list — the sum must close.
source_files: S1 MATH 17B Polygons and Angles 2 Quadrilaterals and Polygons.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Saying whether bond breaking or bond forming releases energy
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that energy is given out when bonds are broken.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Breaking bonds always takes in energy. Energy is given out only when bonds form.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Break = take in. Make = give out.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Gas volume ↔ moles (24 dm³)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Divides by 24 whenever a gas is named, even when the amount given is a mass. Or uses 24 for a solid or a solution.
pitfalls.why_wrong: 24 dm³ goes with a volume of gas only. 48 dm³ of ozone is 2 mol, but 48 g of ozone is 1 mol.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Look at the unit, not the substance: dm³ of gas → ÷ 24; grams → ÷ Mr.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Simplifying a discriminant inequality whose x² coefficient is negative (e.g. −8p² − 24p + 144 < 0)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Divide through by the negative number and keep the inequality sign
pitfalls.why_wrong: Dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses it; keeping the sign silently swaps the answer ranges (inside vs outside the roots).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Divide by the negative to make x² positive — and flip the inequality sign in the same breath.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: "Greatest angle of elevation from the path"
pitfalls.wrong_move: Evaluating the elevation at an endpoint of the path (or at a random labelled point)
pitfalls.why_wrong: With fixed height, $\tan\theta = \frac{h}{d}$ is largest where $d$ is SMALLEST — the perpendicular foot on the path, not an endpoint. Ex 2(b), Practice 1(e)/2(b) and both Assignment (c) parts all hinge on first computing the shortest distance.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: "Greatest elevation" is code for: perpendicular distance first, then tan⁻¹(h/d).
source_files: EM 08 Trigonometry 4 Angles of Elevation and Depression.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Applying the Ratio Theorem when P divides AB in the ratio lambda:mu
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing OP = (lambda*a + mu*b)/(lambda + mu)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The weights sit opposite their segments. AP:PB = lambda:mu gives OP = (mu*a + lambda*b)/(lambda + mu), so the coefficient of a is mu, the part of the ratio that does not touch A. Swapping them puts P on the wrong side of the midpoint.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch the segment and label both parts. The end nearer P must finish with the larger share.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Choosing add vs subtract in a² + b² = c²
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding the two given squares regardless of which side is unknown
pitfalls.why_wrong: With hypotenuse 15 and leg 9, adding gives √306 ≈ 17.5 — longer than the hypotenuse, which is impossible. The hypotenuse is the side OPPOSITE the right angle; if it's already given, the unknown leg comes from subtracting.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Mark the right angle, name c first; unknown c → add, unknown leg → subtract.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Naming the reducing agent in the blast furnace
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says coke reduces the iron(III) oxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The ore is reduced mainly by carbon monoxide, which is made when carbon dioxide reacts with more coke.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Coke makes CO; CO reduces Fe₂O₃.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Adding labels to a drawing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws label lines freehand, with arrowheads, or crossing each other.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Label lines must be ruled, end exactly on the part, and never cross.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ruler for every label line. No arrowheads. No crossings.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Perimeter of a sector
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forgetting to add the two radii (or adding only one)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Perimeter = arc + $2r$. The file's own Practice 1 key prints "$(8\pi + 2)$ cm" where the answer is $8\pi + 12$ — the two 6 cm radii contribute 12. Wire-bending equations fail the same way: $2r + r\theta = 80$, not $r\theta = 80$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: A sector's outline is one arc and TWO straight radii — three pieces, three terms.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 2 Cones and Miscellaneous (With Volume of Prism).pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Dividing an equation by x (or √x) during transformation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forgetting that the division assumed x ≠ 0, and losing (or inventing) the x = 0 solution
pitfalls.why_wrong: In Example 1a(c), solving $y = 2x$ via $\frac{y}{x} = 2$ silently drops $x = 0$ (which satisfies $y = 2x$ trivially on the original curve). Usually harmless for the intended answer, but on "find ALL values" questions it can matter.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Whenever you divide by a variable, note the excluded value and test it separately at the end.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Building the fraction in fraction problems
pitfalls.wrong_move: Letting x be the fraction itself (or the denominator when the relation names the numerator)
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Numerator is 5 less than denominator" wants $\frac{x}{x+5}$ with x the NUMERATOR. A vague let-statement produces an equation you cannot write down.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Let x be one concrete part (the numerator), build the rest from it.
source_files: S1 MATH 10B Algebra 5B Forming Linear Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Measuring an accurate volume of solution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses a measuring cylinder for a volume that needs to be accurate.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A measuring cylinder is less precise than a pipette or burette.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Fixed accurate volume: pipette. Varying accurate volume: burette. Rough volume: measuring cylinder.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Naming a source of error in an osmosis experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives parallax error, a careless reading or poor technique.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A source of error is a limit of the method or apparatus, not a mistake by the student.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask: what could change even if I did everything right? (evaporation, different potatoes, uneven pieces)

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Describing a reversible reaction such as the Haber process
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the reactants are all turned into product.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The forward and backward reactions happen at the same time, so the mixture always contains nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reversible arrow? The reaction never goes to completion. Unreacted gases are recycled.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Weighing or measuring tissue after soaking
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measures the piece straight out of the solution.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Liquid on the surface adds to the mass, so the reading is too high.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Blot dry with filter paper before every final reading, and say why.
source_files: 11483 - Beatty Answering Planning Questions for Practicals (ans) (edited).pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Justifying or assuming a binomial model
pitfalls.wrong_move: Copying the four generic binomial conditions without tying them to the question
pitfalls.why_wrong: Examiners want the model justified in context — the notes warn 'do not just copy the generic characteristics'; generic statements show no understanding of the actual trials.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name the actual trial, the two outcomes and the success probability from the question in every condition you write.
source_files: 13896 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S4 Binomial Distribution.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Choosing the two parts for integration by parts
pitfalls.wrong_move: Following LIATE even when the remaining part cannot be integrated
pitfalls.why_wrong: LIATE is only a guideline. If the part left as dv/dx has no antiderivative you can write down, the method stalls at the first line.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check you can integrate the dv/dx part before starting, and look back at an earlier part of the question that may already have given you that integral.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: How magnesium blocks protect a steel hull
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says magnesium forms a coating or keeps oxygen away from the iron.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The blocks cover only a small part. Magnesium is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sacrificial protection: "more reactive, corrodes in preference to iron".

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Preparing the conical flask for a titration
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rinses the conical flask with the solution that will go into it.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Drops left behind add extra moles to the measured 25.0 cm³, so the titre is too large.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flask: distilled water only. Burette and pipette: rinse with their own solution.
source_files: 21965 - SASS Chem P3 Volumetric Analysis Revision.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing fats using bromine or iodine
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the oil that reacts with more iodine contains more fat.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Iodine and bromine react only with C=C bonds, so they measure unsaturated fat, not total fat.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: More iodine reacted = more unsaturated, nothing else.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Describing how air particles move in a sound wave
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the air particles travel along with the wave from the source to the ear.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Particles only vibrate back and forth about fixed positions, along the direction of the wave. The wave carries energy, not matter.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Particles vibrate to and fro; energy moves on.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Obtaining a reactive metal such as sodium by electrolysis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Chooses electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride or aqueous sodium hydroxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: In water, H⁺ is discharged at the cathode before Na⁺, so hydrogen forms and no sodium.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reactive metal wanted? The compound must be MOLTEN, with no water.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Choosing the sign of a square root while deriving an inverse trigonometric derivative
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the answer with a plus or minus in front of the root
pitfalls.why_wrong: In general cos y is plus or minus sqrt(1 - sin^2 y), but the principal range -pi/2 to pi/2 forces cos y to be non-negative, so only the positive root survives.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Use the principal range to settle the sign, then check it against whether the inverse function is increasing or decreasing.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Starting readings in a photosynthesis experiment after moving the lamp
pitfalls.wrong_move: Takes the reading immediately.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The plant needs a few minutes to adjust to the new light intensity before its rate is steady.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After each change, wait about 5 minutes, then measure.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Area between a curve and a line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using axis-intercepts as limits instead of the intersection points
pitfalls.why_wrong: The bounded region starts and ends where the graphs MEET — solve the equations simultaneously (Ex 3a: $x = -1, 3$; Ex 3b: $x = -2, 1$). Axis intercepts are usually irrelevant to a curve-vs-line region.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Intersections first, then top-minus-bottom between them.
source_files: AM 18 Integration 2 Area and Definite Integrals.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Distinguishing between gene and allele
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the two words as if they mean the same, or gives a definition with no example.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A gene is a length of DNA for one characteristic; alleles are the different forms of that one gene. The question also asks for an example.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Gene = height of pea plant. Alleles = tall and short.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Finding the basic angle when the ratio is negative
pitfalls.wrong_move: Feeding the negative value into the inverse function
pitfalls.why_wrong: The basic angle is ALWAYS positive — take $\alpha$ from the absolute value, and let the SIGN choose the quadrants instead. $\cos^{-1}(-0.15)$ on a calculator returns $98.6°$, which silently mixes the two steps and breaks the generation formulas.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: α from |value|; sign → quadrants; then generate with 180°±α / 360°−α.
source_files: AM 16 Trigonometry 03a Simple Trigo Identities and Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Marking an angle of depression
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measuring the angle from the cliff face or wall instead of the horizontal
pitfalls.why_wrong: Depression is defined from the observer's HORIZONTAL line of sight. Measuring 26° from the vertical cliff face puts the complement (64°) into the working and every length that follows is wrong. The horizontal also gives the free alternate-angle transfer to the other end.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the horizontal dashed line at the eye before marking any angle.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: "Average monthly rainfall over five years" and similar phrasing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking n = 5 because the phrase says five years
pitfalls.why_wrong: n counts the observations being averaged, and the variable is monthly rainfall, so five years supplies 60 of them. Using n = 5 inflates Var(Xbar) twelvefold.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask "what is one observation?", then count how many of THOSE the question averages over.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Units inside scaling problems (litres, m², tonnes)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Scaling first and stamping the requested unit on the result
pitfalls.why_wrong: 9.6 litres must become 9600 cm³ BEFORE the ratio is applied (the print labels a litre-based 5.4 as cm³); 7.04 m² must become 70400 cm² before comparing with 800 cm²; kg → tonnes at the end (35 084 kg ≈ 35.1 t).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert every quantity to the target units first, then scale.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Adding slaked lime to soil that holds an ammonium fertiliser
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the lime just neutralises the soil and the fertiliser is unaffected.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Calcium hydroxide reacts with the ammonium salt and releases ammonia gas. Nitrogen is lost from the soil, and the lime is used up.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Base plus ammonium fertiliser: ammonia escapes, nitrogen lost.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: A factored product equal to a non-zero number, e.g. (2x+3)(2x−1) = 5
pitfalls.wrong_move: Setting each bracket equal to 5 (or splitting while the RHS isn't 0)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The zero-product rule ONLY works for zero: ab = 5 does not force a = 5 or b = 5. Expand, bring the 5 over, re-factorize: x² + x − 2 = 0 → x = 1 or −2. Substituting the candidate roots back into the ORIGINAL equation is the free check — the notes' wrong x = 2 gives (7)(3) = 21 ≠ 5.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Split only when = 0; substitute back to confirm.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Two travellers moving toward each other
pitfalls.wrong_move: Setting one traveller's distance equal to the whole gap
pitfalls.why_wrong: When the lorry and van close a 210 km gap in 1.5 h, NEITHER covers 210 km — their distances sum: 1.5x + 112.5 = 210, giving 65 km/h. Assigning the whole gap to one vehicle doubles its speed.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Opposite directions: distance A + distance B = starting gap.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Reporting a length of projection
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the answer negative because b.d-hat came out negative
pitfalls.why_wrong: A negative scalar product only says the angle between the two vectors is obtuse. A length can never be negative, which is exactly why the formula carries modulus bars: length of projection = |b.d-hat|.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Take the modulus for the length, then comment separately that the negative sign means an obtuse angle.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Question says the equation 'has equal roots'
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treat 'equal roots' as a two-root case and use b²−4ac > 0 or ≥ 0
pitfalls.why_wrong: Equal roots means the two roots coincide — there is really only 1 root, the same scenario as a tangent.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: 'Equal roots' = 1 root = b²−4ac = 0.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Finding n from a ratio of coefficients
pitfalls.wrong_move: Cancelling the constants' powers wrongly (or ignoring them), and keeping invalid roots of the resulting equation
pitfalls.why_wrong: The powers of the constants rarely cancel to 1: in Example 4b, $\frac{(1/2)^{n-3}}{(1/2)^{n-2}} = 2$ and $\frac{2^3}{2^2} = 2$ contribute a factor 4 that changes $n$ entirely. And the final quadratic usually has a spurious root ($n = 0$, negative, or fractional) that must be rejected since $n$ is a positive integer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Handle the constant's power with laws of indices before touching the nCr ratio, and end every finding-n question by rejecting non-positive-integer roots.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why a solid ionic compound does not conduct
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that the solid has no ions.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The ions are there in the solid. They are held in fixed positions and cannot move to carry the current.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solid ionic: "ions are in fixed positions, not free to move".

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Empty sets in statements and counts
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing 0 for ∅ (or reading n(A ∩ D) = 0 as A ∩ D = 0)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $A \cap D = \varnothing$ is a statement about a SET; $n(A \cap D) = 0$ about a NUMBER. Q13's print even types "$B \cap C \ne 0$" where it means $\ne \varnothing$. Mixing them muddles 'no common elements' with arithmetic.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sets equal ∅; counts equal 0. Match the symbol to the object.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Setting up axes on graph paper
pitfalls.wrong_move: Ignoring the stated scale or domain
pitfalls.why_wrong: "2 cm to 1 unit" drawn as 1 cm to 1 unit halves every reading; a domain of −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 drawn short clips the line the later parts need. Scale and domain are printed because they are marked.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Circle the scale and domain before drawing anything.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Deciding whether to round up
pitfalls.wrong_move: Consulting a digit that is not the one immediately after the cut
pitfalls.why_wrong: The file's own box does this: rounding 7239.53 to 2 sf it checks "8" — a digit belonging to the 5187 example above it — and prints 7300. The digit after the 2nd significant figure is 3, so the answer is 7200.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Point at the n-th figure, read the ONE digit to its right, from THIS number.
source_files: S1 MATH 05 Numbers 5 Approximation and Estimation.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Choosing the most concentrated acid from masses dissolved in different volumes
pitfalls.wrong_move: Picks the solution with the largest mass of solute.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Rate depends on concentration. 20 g in 100 cm³ is more concentrated than 80 g in 1000 cm³.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert every option to grams per dm³ before comparing.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Integrating (ax+b)ⁿ forms
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing by the new power but not the inner coefficient (or vice versa)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\int(ax+b)^n dx = \frac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$ — BOTH divisions. Skipping the $a$ differentiates back wrong by a factor of $a$: $\int\sqrt{7-3x}$ needs ÷$\frac32$ AND ÷$(-3)$ → $-\frac29(7-3x)^{3/2}$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Differentiate your answer mentally; the chain rule must regenerate the integrand exactly.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Predicting the Benedict's test result for sucrose
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says every sugar gives a positive Benedict's test.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Sucrose is not a reducing sugar, so the solution stays blue.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose: positive. Sucrose: stays blue.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Constructing from a stated reflex angle
