pitfalls.context: Making an insoluble salt from a solid and an acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adds the insoluble carbonate, hydroxide or metal straight to the acid.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The insoluble salt forms a coat on the solid and stops the reaction, so the yield is poor and the product is impure.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Insoluble product? Both starting substances must be solutions.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: "Comment on the validity if the population were not normally distributed"
pitfalls.wrong_move: Answering that the calculations would no longer be valid
pitfalls.why_wrong: With a large sample the Central Limit Theorem still makes Xbar approximately normal, so the earlier working survives. The comment is a chance to quote CLT, not to withdraw the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check n first. If n is large, say that by CLT Xbar is still approximately normal and the calculations remain valid, quoting the value of n.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Distance between parallel chords
pitfalls.wrong_move: Always adding the two centre-to-chord distances
pitfalls.why_wrong: Adding is only right when the chords straddle the centre (Ex 1: $13.23 + 14.83 \approx 28.1$). On the SAME side the gap is the DIFFERENCE — Practice 2b Q2 needs $OE - OF = 13$, giving $r = 25$; adding sets up an unsolvable equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch the centre first: chords on opposite sides → add; same side → subtract.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Reverse tax problems
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the whole tax by the marginal rate
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the tax ABOVE the bracket floor comes from the marginal rate: 6857.50 divided by 11.5% gives a nonsense 59630, while subtracting the cumulative 3350 first gives the true excess 30500 and income 137500.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Subtract the floor's cumulative tax before dividing by the rate.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Question text conflicting with the diagram
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting the typed figure when the diagram and answer disagree with it
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes' Misc Q2 text says ∠BED = 50° while the diagram marks 59° — and the printed answer 31° only follows from 59°. Exam-style sources do carry typos; the internally consistent pair (diagram + key) identifies which number is wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: When text and figure clash, test which one the answer key agrees with.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Combining the two halves of a compound inequality
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking the looser bound (union) instead of the overlap
pitfalls.why_wrong: Both legs must hold simultaneously, so the answer is the INTERSECTION: $x < \frac{2}{3}$ and $x < \frac{8}{13}$ combine to $x < \frac{8}{13}$ (the tighter bound), not $x < \frac{2}{3}$. Opposite-side bounds make a two-sided range instead.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw both solution sets on one number line and keep only where the shadings overlap.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Taking logarithms of r^n < k when 0 < r < 1
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing by ln r and keeping the inequality sign unchanged
pitfalls.why_wrong: ln r is negative whenever r < 1, so the sign must reverse. In the notes, (2/49)^n < 0.0001 becomes n > ln(0.0001)/ln(2/49) = 2.88, giving least n = 3 — keeping the sign would give the opposite region.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the sign of the log you are dividing by. Negative divisor means flip the inequality, then round to the integer that satisfies it.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Saying what happens at each electrode
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that positive ions gain electrons at the anode, or that negative ions lose electrons at the cathode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Positive ions go to the cathode and gain electrons there. Negative ions go to the anode and lose electrons there.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cathode: cations, gain, reduction. Anode: anions, lose, oxidation. Check all three words agree.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Vector vs length statements
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing arrows on a length relation (or lengths on a vector one)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\overrightarrow{OP} = 2\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is a vector fact (direction included); $OP = 2PQ$ or $|\overrightarrow{OP}| = 2|\overrightarrow{PQ}|$ states lengths only. Mixing them costs the mark for the 'two facts' questions, which want one of each.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Two facts = one arrowed multiple + one plain-letter length equation.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: A bare minus before a bracket
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dropping the bracket without flipping anything
pitfalls.why_wrong: $-(p - q)$ is $-1 \times (p - q) = -p + q$. Copying $-p - q$ keeps the old sign on q and changes the value of the whole expression.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Treat the minus as −1 and expand it like any multiplier.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Labelling quartile answers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing 'IQR =' next to a quartile value (or vice versa)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The key prints "IQR = 26" where 26 is the LOWER QUARTILE (the IQR was the given 16) — one mislabel then corrupts $Q_3 = Q_1 + \text{IQR}$ downstream if taken literally. Values and labels must travel together.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Q₁, Q₃ are marks; IQR is their difference. Re-read the label before boxing the answer.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why a simple molecular substance melts or boils at a low temperature
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that the covalent bonds are weak, or that they break on melting.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Covalent bonds are strong and are not broken when the substance melts or boils. Only the weak forces between the molecules are overcome.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Melting a molecular substance? Write "weak forces between molecules", never "weak bonds".

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Property used to separate petroleum
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the fractions separate because of different densities.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Fractional distillation separates by boiling point.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Distillation of any kind: write "different boiling points".

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Concentrated aqueous salt of a reactive metal
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the reactive metal is deposited at the negative electrode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Hydrogen ions from water are discharged more easily, so hydrogen gas forms.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Aqueous + metal above hydrogen → bubbles of hydrogen at the negative electrode.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Two lines whose direction vectors are parallel
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding immediately that they are two distinct parallel lines
pitfalls.why_wrong: Parallel directions leave two possibilities: distinct parallel lines, or the same line written twice. Only a point test separates them.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Take a point from one line and see whether it satisfies the other. An inconsistent parameter means parallel and distinct.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Length of projection of a vector onto a plane
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using |b.n-hat| for the projection onto the plane
pitfalls.why_wrong: Dotting with the unit normal gives the component of b ALONG the normal — the perpendicular height off the plane, not the shadow on it. The two are complementary legs of a right triangle.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Project onto a plane with the cross product: |b x n-hat|. Keep |b.n-hat| for the along-normal component.
source_files: 13888 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 4. Vectors II.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing melting points of two simple molecular elements
pitfalls.wrong_move: Explains a higher melting point by stronger covalent bonds inside the molecule.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Melting does not break the bonds inside molecules. The larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Both simple molecular? Compare the intermolecular forces only.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Eliminating by subtraction when coefficients match with the SAME sign
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting only the matched terms and mis-signing the rest
pitfalls.why_wrong: (10x − 6y) − (10x + 35y) subtracts EVERY term of the second equation: −6y − 35y = −41y and the right side is 6 − (−35) = 41. Sign slips here flip the answer; even the notes' own example mislabels the surviving variable.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bracket both equations and subtract term by term — then name the survivor correctly.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5B Simultaneous Equations 2 Simultaneous Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Shifted curves with asymptotes (2 + 1/x², 2ˣ + 3, 4 − 2ˣ)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the horizontal asymptote at y = 0
pitfalls.why_wrong: The shift carries the asymptote with it: $y = 2 + \frac{1}{x^2}$ flattens toward $y = 2$; $y = 2^x + 3$ toward $y = 3$; $y = 4 - 2^x$ toward $y = 4$. An exponential drawn crossing its own asymptote is self-contradictory.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the dashed asymptote line FIRST at y = k, then hang the curve on it.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Formulas given as one fraction equal to another (2/(x+p) = 3/q)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Moving terms across while the fractions are still there
pitfalls.why_wrong: Terms can only move cleanly in a fraction-free equation. Cross-multiply first — 3(x+p) = 2q — then move terms. Mixing the two steps breeds sign and denominator errors.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Kill the fractions first; rearrange second.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 4 Subject of Formula.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Telling y = x⁻² and y = x⁻¹ apart
pitfalls.wrong_move: Drawing 1/x² with a branch below the axis
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\frac{1}{x^2}$ is a square — ALWAYS positive, so both branches spike upward either side of the $y$-axis. $\frac{1}{x}$ keeps the sign of $x$, giving opposite-quadrant branches. Mixing them up loses the shape mark instantly.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Even power → both branches up. Odd power → opposite corners.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Graph-read answers vs calculated answers
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rejecting your graph reading because it isn't the exact algebraic value
pitfalls.why_wrong: Graph questions carry a tolerance (±0.1 typically): x ≈ 4.3 for y = 2 is full marks even though the exact root is 1+√11. Conversely, quoting the exact surd when asked to 'use your graph' can lose the method mark.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Use the graph when asked; answer to half a small square.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6B Quadratic Equations Drawing Graph on Graph Paper.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: 'Exactly one' of three events
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing one product instead of all three single-success cases
pitfalls.why_wrong: Exactly one = A-only + B-only + C-only, each success multiplied by BOTH failures: the marksmen give $\frac{9 + 6 + 12}{60} = \frac{9}{20}$; any single term (e.g. $\frac{9}{60}$) badly undercounts.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Three events → three 'only-X' products, then add.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Gradient computation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing the order (y₁−y₂ over x₂−x₁), or writing y = mx + c for a vertical line
pitfalls.why_wrong: Swapped order negates the gradient. And vertical lines have UNDEFINED gradient — their equation is $x = a$; horizontal lines are $y = a$ with $m = 0$. Forcing $y = mx + c$ onto a vertical line is meaningless (the source stresses $y = mx + c$ is for slanted lines).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same point first in both numerator and denominator; flat → y = a, upright → x = a.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Passing a gas from a heated tube into limewater
pitfalls.wrong_move: Turns off the burner while the delivery tube is still in the limewater.
pitfalls.why_wrong: As the tube cools, the gas inside contracts and limewater is sucked back into the hot tube, which can crack it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Take the delivery tube out of the limewater first, then stop heating.
source_files: 18856 - 2025 Montfort Sec 6092 Revision Guide for Practical.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Using ΔH with an equation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the ΔH value as the energy for 1 mol of the substance asked about.
pitfalls.why_wrong: ΔH goes with the amounts in the equation as written. If 2 mol of the product appear, 1 mol gives half.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the number in front of the substance before scaling.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reading conclusions off congruent or similar triangles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading off a side pair that is not corresponding, e.g. taking QS = QU instead of QS = US after triangle STU ≡ triangle SRQ
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only corresponding sides (matching vertex positions in the triangle names) are equal (congruence) or in ratio (similarity); a mismatched pair states something false.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match letters position-by-position in the two triangle names before writing any side equation — S↔S, T↔R, U↔Q means US pairs with QS.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Electrode signs and electron flow in an electrolytic cell
pitfalls.wrong_move: Labels the cathode positive, or shows electrons leaving the positive terminal of the battery.
pitfalls.why_wrong: In electrolysis the cathode is joined to the negative terminal. Electrons flow from the negative terminal to the cathode, and from the anode back to the positive terminal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Electrolysis: cathode negative, anode positive. Electrons leave the battery's negative end.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Reading estimates off 1-Var Stats on the graphing calculator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking sigma-x as the standard deviation and squaring it for s^2
pitfalls.why_wrong: sigma-x divides by n, so sigma-x^2 is the sample variance, not the unbiased estimate. The calculator already reports the unbiased one as Sx.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Take Sx from the 1-Var Stats screen and use s^2 = Sx^2. Ignore sigma-x for estimation questions.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Rates with mixed units (dollars and cents)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing 6 dollars and 60 cents in one equation without converting
pitfalls.why_wrong: 6x + 60y = 153 (cents-as-dollars) is wrong: 60 cents is 0.6 dollars, so 6x + 0.6y = 153. A units slip scales one variable by 100 and the 'solution' is absurd (checking magnitude exposes it).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One currency unit per equation — convert before writing.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5C Simultaneous Equations 3 Word Problems.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Catalyst and energy profile
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says a catalyst changes the enthalpy change.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A catalyst lowers the activation energy only. Reactants and products have the same energy levels as before.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Catalyst: Ea down, ΔH unchanged.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Stating how elements are arranged in the Periodic Table
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying they are in order of relative atomic mass.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The order is by proton (atomic) number. A few pairs would be the wrong way round by mass.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Order = proton number. Period = number of shells. Group = number of outer electrons.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: How-many-fit capacity problems (files, photos, documents)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding to the nearest whole number
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\frac{0.34 \times 10^{12}}{45 \times 10^6} = 7555\frac{5}{9}$ (the print's $\frac{5}{6}$ is a slip, harmless here) — but the count must round DOWN to 7555: the 7556th file doesn't fit. Similarly $350.9 \to 350$ documents, never 351.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Storage counts are floors: chop the fraction, no matter how close to 1 it is.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Shortest distance from a point to a line using the cross product
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing |BP x d| with the raw direction vector
pitfalls.why_wrong: The formula is |BP x d-hat| and needs a unit direction. Using d instead multiplies the distance by |d|, so a direction vector of length 5 makes the answer five times too large.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Divide d by its magnitude before crossing, or divide the final magnitude by |d|.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Writing a formula with a hydroxide, nitrate, sulfate or carbonate ion
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes MgOH₂ for magnesium hydroxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Without brackets the 2 applies only to the hydrogen. Two whole hydroxide ions are needed.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: More than one of a many-atom ion? Bracket it first, then write the number: Mg(OH)₂.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Trusting printed answer keys
pitfalls.wrong_move: Copying a key value that contradicts your own exact working
pitfalls.why_wrong: This file's keys carry four confirmed slips: $8\pi + 2$ (for $8\pi + 12$), $r = 7.05$ (for the exact $\sqrt{49} = 7$), "50.8 m" (for cm) and "5.67 cm²" (for cm). When numbers are engineered to cancel ($154$ with $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$), a non-integer key is the red flag.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Exact-friendly givens → expect exact answers; re-derive before believing a strange key.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 2 Cones and Miscellaneous (With Volume of Prism).pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Concluding a relationship from a straight-line graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says y is directly proportional to x for any straight line.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Direct proportion needs a straight line that passes through the origin. Otherwise the relation is only linear.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Through the origin? Proportional. Not through the origin? Linear.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Combining A : B with B : C
pitfalls.wrong_move: Joining the ratios without matching the shared member
pitfalls.why_wrong: From A : B = 4 : 9 and B : C = 21 : 16, writing A : B : C = 4 : 9 : 16 ignores that 9 and 21 are the SAME quantity on different scales. Scaling B to its LCM 63 gives the true 28 : 63 : 48.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: The shared letter must show the same number in both ratios before joining.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Total volume of gas left after a reaction
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives only the volume of gas made, and leaves out the excess gas that did not react. Or counts the water formed as a gas.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The unreacted gas is still in the container. Water is a liquid at room temperature, so it takes up almost no volume.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Gas remaining = gas products + leftover gas reactant. Cross out the water.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Telling cations apart with aqueous ammonia
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says every white hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia, or that calcium ions give a precipitate with it.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonia. Aluminium and lead(II) hydroxides do not. Calcium ions give no precipitate with ammonia.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Learn the sodium hydroxide column and the ammonia column separately.
source_files: 12648 - ACSBR 6 Identification of Ions and Gases - Assignment ANS.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Perimeter equations
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counting the length and width once each
pitfalls.why_wrong: A rectangle's perimeter is $2(\text{length} + \text{width})$ — all four sides. Using $x + (x-4) = 72$ instead of $2x + 2(x-4) = 72$ doubles the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Walk the whole boundary: four sides for a rectangle.
source_files: S1 MATH 10B Algebra 5B Forming Linear Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Calculating electrical energy in kWh
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplies watts by minutes, or kilowatts by seconds.
pitfalls.why_wrong: kWh needs power in kW and time in hours. Joules need watts and seconds.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cost question: kW × h. Energy in J: W × s.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Grouping four terms
pitfalls.wrong_move: Pairing terms that share nothing
pitfalls.why_wrong: In $ax + 4by + ay + 4bx$ the given order pairs $ax$ with $4by$ — no common factor. Rearranged as $ax + ay + 4bx + 4by$ it splits into $a(x+y) + 4b(x+y)$. The terms are yours to reorder.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: If a pair shares nothing, swap the middle terms and try again.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Finding the second height of a parallelogram
pitfalls.wrong_move: Pairing the found area with the wrong base
pitfalls.why_wrong: Area 51.6 came from 6 × 8.6 (base AB with height AY); the height AX belongs to base BC = 10, so AX = 51.6 ÷ 10 = 5.16, not 51.6 ÷ 6. Each height divides by ITS base.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match each height to the base it lands on.
source_files: S1 MATH 20B Mensuration 2 Area and Perimeter Parallelogram and Trapezium.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Naming angle-pair reasons (alternate vs corresponding vs vertically opposite)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Attaching a parallel-lines reason to a vertical pair, or vice versa
pitfalls.why_wrong: Vertically opposite angles need NO parallel lines (they live at one crossing); alternate/corresponding pairs need the parallel lines cited. Ex 2c prints '∠DST = ∠BCT (Vertically Opposite ∠s, SD // BC)' — that pair is ALTERNATE (Z-shape across SC); the vertical pair at T is $\angle STD = \angle CTB$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Trace the two angles: same crossing point → vertical; Z-shape → alternate; F-shape → corresponding. The reason must match the shape.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Rounding after solving a word problem
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding to the nearest integer
pitfalls.why_wrong: x ≤ 7.5 files on a budget means 7 (round DOWN — 8 exceeds the money); x ≥ 8⅓ boxes on a requirement means 9 (round UP — 8 falls short). Nearest-integer rounding picks the wrong side half the time.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Budget floors, requirement ceilings — never 'nearest'.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Angle between a line and a plane
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using cos(theta) = |n.d|/(|n||d|) for the angle with the plane
pitfalls.why_wrong: That cosine gives the angle between the line and the NORMAL, not the plane. The plane angle is its complement, so the answer comes out as 90 degrees minus the true angle.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Use sin(theta) = |n.d|/(|n||d|) for line-plane angles; cosine belongs to line-line and plane-plane angles.
source_files: 13888 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 4. Vectors II.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Simple or fractional distillation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Chooses simple distillation for two liquids that mix.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Simple distillation works when the boiling points are far apart, as for a dissolved solid and its solvent. Miscible liquids with close boiling points need a fractionating column.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Two miscible liquids → fractional distillation.
source_files: 12656 - ACSBR 9 Methods of Separation - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Where the gas forms in a simple cell with an acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says hydrogen bubbles form on the more reactive metal.
pitfalls.why_wrong: In the cell, the electrons travel through the wire, so hydrogen ions pick them up at the less reactive metal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Simple cell: reactive metal dissolves, bubbles appear on the other electrode.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Identifying which axis a minus sign flips, e.g. $y = \lg(2-x)$ vs $y = -\lg x$ (Adrian: "learn when it is flipped in which axis")
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the minus in $\lg(2-x)$ as a flip in the x-axis (or ignoring it entirely)
pitfalls.why_wrong: A minus in front of $x$ (inside the function) reflects in the y-axis; a minus in front of the whole graph reflects in the x-axis. Mixing these up draws the curve on the wrong side of the asymptote or upside down.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Minus on the GRAPH → x-axis flip. Minus on $x$ → y-axis flip. Both → flipped twice.
source_files: AM 08 Indices and Logarithms Graphs and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Age problems with a time shift ('in 5 years...')
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding the years to only one person's age
pitfalls.why_wrong: Time passes for everyone: John x + 5 AND Mark y + 5. Writing x + 5 = 2y (instead of 2(y+5)) silently freezes Mark and gives ages that fail the original story.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Shift every age by the same n — brackets around (y + n).
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5C Simultaneous Equations 3 Word Problems.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Purpose of a polystyrene cup
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives a vague purpose such as "to hold the solution" or "to keep it safe".
pitfalls.why_wrong: The cup is an insulator. The mark is for reducing heat exchange with the surroundings.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write: it is an insulator, so less heat is lost to or gained from the surroundings.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Dividing by an algebraic fraction
pitfalls.wrong_move: Cancelling factors across the ÷ sign before flipping
pitfalls.why_wrong: Cancellation is only valid in a product. Flip the second fraction first (÷ becomes ×), then cancel: (2p−8)/6 ÷ (3p−12)/12 = 2(p−4)/6 × 12/(3(p−4)) = 4/3. Cancelling the (p−4)s across the ÷ first gives a wrong reciprocal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flip first, cancel second.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining codominance and multiple alleles using blood groups
pitfalls.wrong_move: Defines the two terms but never mentions the blood group alleles.
pitfalls.why_wrong: One mark is kept for the reference to blood groups.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Codominance: A and B alleles together give group AB. Multiple alleles: three alleles (A, B, O) for one gene.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Printed keys and annotated diagrams in this file
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting a key or sketch that was copy-pasted from a neighbouring question
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice 2 Q2(b)'s key repeats Q1's answer (the true line of symmetry is $x = -1$, confirmed by the key's own part (c) minimum $(-1,-8)$); Ex 2a's annotated sketch shows intercepts $-6, 5$ and midpoint $-\frac{1}{2}$ from a different question; Ex 3b's conclusion labels a point $R$ that is actually $T$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check that a key's numbers are consistent with the question's OWN other parts; if they contradict, re-derive.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Counting bonding electrons
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counts one electron for each bond, so three single bonds are "3 bonded electrons".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Each covalent bond is a shared pair, so it has two electrons. A triple bond has six.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bonding electrons = number of bonds × 2.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Commenting on a strong correlation between two variables, e.g. r = 0.8
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding that one variable causes the other because r is close to 1
pitfalls.why_wrong: The PMCC measures only the strength of the linear relationship; both variables may be driven by a third factor, so a causal link is never established by r alone
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say the variables have a strong linear correlation and stop there. Never claim causation from r, however close to 1 it is.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Unit conversions inside a solution (m ↔ mm, cm ↔ m)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Sliding the exponent by the wrong amount (or contradicting your own annotation)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\times 1000$ adds exactly 3 to the exponent: $4.52285 \times 10^{-8}$ m $= 4.52285 \times 10^{-5}$ mm. The print derives $10^{-8+3} = 10^{-5}$ in its margin and then writes $10^{-3}$ in the final line — the answer must copy the arithmetic, not a remembered digit.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write the exponent sum explicitly ($-8 + 3 = -5$) and transfer THAT number to the answer line.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Squares or cubes starting mid-list
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing n² for a shifted square sequence
pitfalls.why_wrong: $9, 16, 25$ is $3^2, 4^2, 5^2$ — the formula is $(n+2)^2$, not $n^2$. The notes flag this: sometimes you must adjust the general formula.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Identify WHICH square the first term is; that offset joins n.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Using a powdered solid in a mass-loss experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Suggests powder to get a better result.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Powder reacts so fast that the reaction may be over before the readings can be taken.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: A method only works if the change is slow enough to measure.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: A question asking for the sum of the first n even-numbered or odd-numbered terms
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing S(n) for that sum
pitfalls.why_wrong: S(n) means the sum of the first n terms of the ORIGINAL sequence. The terms u1, u3, u5, ... are a progression in their own right — for a GP the common ratio becomes r^2 — so the two sums differ. Odd-numbered terms are also not the odd numbers.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: List a few of the wanted terms, identify their own first term and common difference or ratio, and sum that new progression.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Answers asked as a product of prime factors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying the answer out (or stopping at index form when a value is asked)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes stress it: when the question says "leave your answer as a product of prime factors", $2^3 \times 3$ IS the final answer — computing 24 loses the mark; when a plain value is asked, index form is unfinished.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read the last line of the question before writing the last line of the answer.
source_files: S1 MATH 01 Numbers 1 Prime Numbers Square and Cube Roots.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Pressure as a factor
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says raising the pressure speeds up a reaction between a solid and a solution.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Pressure only pushes gas particles closer together. It does nothing to solids or solutions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Before naming pressure, check that a reactant is a gas.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: What carries the current
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says electrons move through the electrolyte.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Electrons move only in the wires and electrodes. In the electrolyte the charge is carried by ions moving to the electrodes.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Wire: electrons. Liquid: ions.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Time differences given in minutes ("60 minutes lesser", "30 minutes less")
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the minutes directly into an hours-based equation
pitfalls.why_wrong: Speeds are in km/h, so times are in hours: 60 min must enter as 1 and 30 min as ½. Writing 400/x − 400/(x+20) = 60 scales the whole equation by 60 and gives an impossible speed.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match units first: minutes ÷ 60 before the equation.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications (Supplementary Worksheet).pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: 'Find the interest earned' questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the final amount A instead of A − P
pitfalls.why_wrong: The formula outputs the TOTAL amount; the file's own Ex 2c prints $8494.10$ where the asked interest is $894.10$. One missing subtraction turns a right calculation into a wrong answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Last line of every interest question: subtract the principal, then re-read what was asked.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 1 Simple and Compound Interest.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Recovering constants from a log-plot's gradient and intercept
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting a = c and b = m directly from a lg y (or ln y) plot
pitfalls.why_wrong: For $y = ab^x$, the plot gives $\lg y = (\lg b)x + \lg a$: the graph's $m$ and $c$ are the LOGS of the constants. $a = 10^c$ and $b = 10^m$ (or $e^c$, $e^m$ for $\ln$). Skipping the un-log gives answers off by orders of magnitude.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: From a log plot: constants $= 10^{(\text{reading})}$ — un-log both the gradient and the intercept.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Choosing a polygon formula
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using (n−2)×180 for exterior angles or 360 for interior sums
pitfalls.why_wrong: Exterior angles of ANY polygon total 360° regardless of n; interior angles total (n−2)×180. Swapping them gives n values that aren't even integers — a decagon's exterior sum is not 1440°.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Inside grows with n; outside is always 360.
source_files: S1 MATH 17B Polygons and Angles 2 Quadrilaterals and Polygons.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Three-and-one grouping (x² + 4xy + 4y² − 1 type)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trying to group 2-by-2 when three terms form a perfect square
pitfalls.why_wrong: x² + 4xy + 4y² − 1 groups as (x+2y)² − 1² — a perfect square minus a square. 2-by-2 pairs like (x² + 4xy) + (4y² − 1) share no bracket and dead-end. Count the square-shaped terms before pairing.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Three terms square + one lonely square → (…)² − b².

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Temperature readings in distillation of an impure liquid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the liquid in the flask is at exactly 100 °C when water is distilled from a solution.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The liquid in the flask has dissolved solid in it, so it does not boil at 100 °C. Only the vapour at the thermometer bulb by the side arm is pure water.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: 100 °C is at the top by the condenser, not in the flask.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: An optimisation problem where setting the derivative to zero gives only one value
pitfalls.wrong_move: Declaring it the maximum or the minimum without any test
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes call the nature test mandatory even when only one stationary value is obtained. One root does not tell you which kind of stationary point it is.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Add a first or second derivative test and finish with a sentence such as hence A is a minimum, unless the question explicitly waives it.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: A charge given as a percentage of the whole bill
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying by the percentage instead of dividing
pitfalls.why_wrong: If 9.06 IS 12% of the bill, the bill is $\frac{9.06}{0.12} = 75.50$; multiplying gives 1.09 — nonsense. The known amount sits on the percentage side of the proportion, not the whole.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Known part ÷ its percentage = the whole.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 5 Personal and Household Finance.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Rotating a region about a line such as y = 2 or x = 2
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the usual axis formula with the original equation of the curve
pitfalls.why_wrong: The formula measures the radius from the axis, so every distance is measured from the wrong line and the volume comes out wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Translate the picture so that the line becomes the axis, shifting the equation of the curve by the same amount, then integrate as usual.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Volume of pyramids and cones
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forgetting the one-third factor
pitfalls.why_wrong: A pyramid or cone fills exactly a third of the prism or cylinder on the same base: 1/3 × 256 × 27 = 2304, not 6912. Dropping the 1/3 triples every volume; sanity-check that the answer is smaller than the box the solid sits in.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Pointy solids take a third; flat-topped solids take the whole.
source_files: S2 MATH 06 Area and Volume Pyramid Cone Sphere 1.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Explaining why two lines do not intersect
pitfalls.wrong_move: Saying "they are far apart" or "they point the same way" without citing gradients
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mark is for the property: both lines have the SAME gradient (here m = 2) and different intercepts, so they are parallel and never meet. The examiner wants the word 'gradient' (or 'parallel'), not a picture description.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same m, different c → parallel → no intersection.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5A Simultaneous Equations 1 Linear Functions (Recap).pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Recording the starch test on a variegated leaf
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "the leaf turned blue-black".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the parts that were green have starch. The white parts stay brown.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Describe each region: green parts stained blue-black; white parts remained brown.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Squaring both sides when the subject appears on both, e.g. √(m²−b) = m+b
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing (m+b)² as m² + b²
pitfalls.why_wrong: (m+b)² = m² + 2mb + b² — the cross term 2mb is exactly what makes the question solvable (the m² cancels and 2mb carries the subject). Dropping it strands the working.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Squaring a sum: three terms, always.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 4 Subject of Formula.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Measuring rate by loss in mass
pitfalls.wrong_move: Suggests following loss in mass for a reaction that gives off no gas.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mass on the balance only falls when a gas escapes from the flask.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Loss in mass or gas syringe? First check the equation has a gas product.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Spotting corresponding or alternate angles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using F/Z rules on lines that merely look parallel
pitfalls.why_wrong: The rules hold only for marked parallels (matching arrowheads). Two unmarked lines at slightly different slopes give near-equal angles that are NOT equal, and 'alt ∠s' as a reason earns no marks.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the arrows before writing corr/alt/int as a reason.
source_files: S1 MATH 17A Polygons and Angles 1 Angles Recap.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Entering a sample-mean probability into normalcdf or invNorm
pitfalls.wrong_move: Typing the variance sigma^2/n into the sigma field
pitfalls.why_wrong: That field expects a standard deviation. Supplying the variance silently rescales the distribution and returns a plausible-looking but wrong probability.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Key in sqrt(sigma^2/n). Writing the distribution as N(mu, sigma^2/n) first, then square-rooting the second slot, makes the step automatic.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Average speed over several legs
pitfalls.wrong_move: Averaging the leg speeds
pitfalls.why_wrong: Mr Tan's 20 km at 70 km/h plus 12 km at 60 km/h averages 32 ÷ (2/7 + 1/5) = 65.9 km/h, not (70 + 60)/2 = 65. The legs last different times, so the faster leg counts for less. The naive average only coincides when the durations are equal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, always.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Counting significant figures in decimals
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counting the leading zeros
pitfalls.why_wrong: Zeros BEFORE the first non-zero digit only mark place value: 0.0005182 has significant figures 5, 1, 8, 2 — so 3 sf gives 0.000518, not 0.001 or 0.0005. Zeros AFTER the first significant figure do count.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Start counting at the first non-zero digit.
source_files: S1 MATH 05 Numbers 5 Approximation and Estimation.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Solving the inequality for increasing/decreasing ranges
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping the inequality sign when dividing by a negative coefficient
pitfalls.why_wrong: $-2x^2 + 6x + 8 < 0$ becomes $x^2 - 3x - 4 > 0$ — the sign FLIPS on division by $-2$. Forgetting the flip selects the complement interval (the answer between the roots instead of outside them).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Every multiply/divide by a negative flips the inequality; count your flips.
source_files: AM 17 Differentiation 5 Increasing and Decreasing Functions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining a property of an ionic compound
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "particles" or "charged particles" without naming the ions.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mark is for the specific ions and the electrostatic attraction between them.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Name them: e.g. "between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions".
source_files: 13424 - Secondary 3 Chemical Bonding Notes - Pure Chemistry.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Answers that come out as a negative fraction, e.g. b = −ac/(a−6)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating an equivalent form as a wrong answer (or forcing a false extra minus)
pitfalls.why_wrong: −ac/(a−6) = ac/(6−a): flipping the denominator's sign and the leading sign together is legal, so printed keys often show two or three equivalent forms. Check equivalence before 'correcting' your answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Minus can live on top, on the bottom, or in front — same value.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 4 Subject of Formula.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing zinc coating and tin coating on iron
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says both stop protecting the iron once scratched.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes in its place even when scratched. Tin is less reactive, so exposed iron under tin rusts.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Scratched coating? Ask which metal is more reactive than iron.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Path-walking with reversed segments
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping the sign when travelling against an arrow
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\overrightarrow{BP}$ runs opposite to $\overrightarrow{AP}$'s direction along $AB$: the file's own Ex 4 working writes $+\frac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{RQ}$ for it and lands on $2\mathbf{n} + 2\mathbf{m}$, while the key's correct answer is $2\mathbf{m} - 2\mathbf{n}$. One dropped minus flips a component.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reverse letters → negate: $\overrightarrow{BP} = -\overrightarrow{PB}$. Check each leg's arrow before adding.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Describing the intercostal muscles during breathing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "the intercostal muscles contract" without saying which set.
pitfalls.why_wrong: There are two sets that work against each other. External contract to breathe in; internal contract to breathe out.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Always name the set: external in, internal out; the other set relaxes.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Asked for the unbiased estimate of the population variance
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing the sample variance, dividing the squared deviations by n
pitfalls.why_wrong: The sample variance systematically UNDERESTIMATES the population variance, so it is not an unbiased estimator. The unbiased estimate scales it up: s^2 = n/(n-1) x sample variance.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Divide by n - 1, not n. If a question hands you the sample variance, multiply by n/(n-1) before using it.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Predicting a value outside the sampled data range
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting an out-of-range value into the regression line and reporting the estimate as trustworthy
pitfalls.why_wrong: There is no way to check that the linear relationship still holds beyond the data range, so the estimate cannot be relied on.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Call it out as extrapolation and state the estimate is unreliable; only interpolate within the data range.
source_files: 13901 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S8 Correlation Regression.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Simplifying sqrt(x^2) inside a derivative
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing sqrt(x^2) = x
pitfalls.why_wrong: sqrt(x^2) = |x|. For a negative value such as x = -3 the root is 3, which is -x, so dropping the modulus gives the wrong sign over half the domain.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: When the sign of x has not been stated, keep the modulus in the answer.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: First-success games (first yellow wins, etc.)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing events that require the game to continue after it has ended
pitfalls.why_wrong: Once the first yellow is drawn the game STOPS — 'yellow drawn two consecutive times' has probability 0, and 'game ends at draw 5' forces draws 1–4 to be non-yellow. Ignoring the stopping rule invents impossible sequences.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Re-read the ending condition; anything after the end has probability 0.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Using a truncated expansion to estimate a number to a stated precision
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting the kept terms without checking the size of the first omitted term
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice 5b Q2's three-term estimate of $(1.96)^8$ gives 217.907, but the true value is 217.795… — the omitted term is about $-0.115$, far bigger than 3-dp precision. The method is only sound when the substituted value is small enough (Example 5d's $x = 0.02$) that omitted terms sit below the rounding threshold.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Before rounding, estimate the first omitted term; if it is not well below the required precision, keep more terms (and know that the exam still expects the instructed truncation).

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Simple cell with two different metals
pitfalls.wrong_move: Makes the less reactive metal the negative electrode, or the source of electrons.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily. It is the negative electrode, and electrons flow from it through the wire.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: More reactive metal: negative, gives electrons, dissolves.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Probability about the difference of two independent sample means
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing Var(Xbar - Ybar) = Var(Xbar) - Var(Ybar)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Variances of independent variables add whether you sum or subtract them. Subtracting can even produce a negative "variance", which is impossible.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Take the difference of the MEANS but the sum of the VARIANCES: Var(Xbar - Ybar) = sigma_x^2/n + sigma_y^2/m.
source_files: 13899 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S6 Sampling Estimation Theory.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Recording raw readings
pitfalls.wrong_move: Drops the last zero (12 cm for a metre-rule reading) or mixes decimal places in one column.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The number of decimal places shows the precision of the instrument.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Metre rule in cm: 1 d.p. always. Same d.p. down the whole column.
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Equations containing $(\log_a x)^2$, e.g. $(\log_5 x)^2 - 3\log_5 x + 2 = 0$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Bringing the square down: $(\log_a x)^2 = 2\log_a x$
pitfalls.why_wrong: The power law $\log_a x^n = n\log_a x$ only applies when the power is on the ARGUMENT. Here the square is on the whole logarithm — the equation is a quadratic in $\log_a x$, and 'bringing down' destroys one of the two roots.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Power on the argument → bring down. Power on the log → substitute $a = \log_5 x$ and solve the quadratic.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Max/min of a sin bx + c
pitfalls.wrong_move: Quoting ±a as the max/min and ignoring the vertical shift
pitfalls.why_wrong: The wave rides on the centre line $y = c$: max $= c + a$, min $= c - a$. For $3\sin x + 2$ the range is $[-1, 5]$, not $[-3, 3]$. Reading a and c from a graph reverses this: $c$ = average of max and min FIRST, then $a$ = max $-$ $c$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Centre line first, in both directions: drawing (c then peaks) and reading (average then amplitude).

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Radian formulas
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using ½r²θ or rθ with a degree angle (or dividing by 360° after converting)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ and $r\theta$ are the DEGREE formulas with $\frac{\theta}{360°} \cdot 2\pi$ already absorbed — feeding 70 (degrees) into them multiplies the answer by ~57. Mixing the two systems double-counts the conversion.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One system per line: degrees → fraction of 360; radians → the collapsed formulas.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 1 Arc Length and Sector Area.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Integrating sin², cos², tan² (and spotting tan or ln under an integral)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Integrating the square directly, or hunting for ∫tan x / ∫ln x
pitfalls.why_wrong: Squared trig has no direct AM antiderivative — convert first ($\sin^2x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}$, $\tan^2x = \sec^2x-1$). And neither $\tan x$ nor $\ln x$ is integrable in the AM syllabus; questions route around them (sec² forms, y-axis workaround).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: ∫ + squared trig → identity first; ∫tan/∫ln → you've mis-read the question.
source_files: AM 19 Differentiation and Integration Techniques Summary.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Squaring a binomial
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing (x + 7y)² = x² + 49y²
pitfalls.why_wrong: The square of a sum has THREE terms — the middle one, 2ab, is the whole point of the identity: (x + 7y)² = x² + 14xy + 49y². Dropping it is the single most common expansion error.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Square, TWICE the product, square.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Recovering a curve from dy/dx or d²y/dx²
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dropping +C, or reusing the same constant across two integrations
pitfalls.why_wrong: The constant is where the given point/gradient information enters: Ex 1c needs $c = 3$ (from the gradient) then a FRESH $c' = 0$ (from the point). One shared constant can't satisfy both conditions, and no constant at all silently forces the curve through the origin.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One +constant per integration; fix each immediately with its matching condition (gradient → first, point → second).

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Opposite vs adjacent when the reference angle changes
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeping the same opp/adj labels for a different angle in the same triangle
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\sin\angle ACB = \frac{12}{13}$ but $\sin\angle CAB = \frac{5}{13}$ — the labels swap when the angle moves to the other vertex. Practice 1 Q1 tests all six ratios precisely on this swap.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Re-label opp/adj from scratch for every new angle; only the hypotenuse never moves.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Squaring both sides of a > b
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding that a^2 > b^2 without checking the signs
pitfalls.why_wrong: That step needs a > b > 0. Counterexamples: -3 > -4 but 9 < 16; and 2 > -3 but 4 < 9. Squaring destroys sign information, so the ordering can reverse.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Square only when both sides are known to be positive — or when both sides are moduli, which are never negative.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Substitution method for indices equations (e.g. 4^x − 3(2^x) + 2 = 0)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stop after solving the quadratic and report the u-values (u = 1 or 2) as the answers for x.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The question asks for x; u = 2^x was only a temporary tool. Each u-value still needs the small indices equation 2^x = u solved.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Adrian: 'Recall you are solving for x, not a. You need to bring back x.'

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Deciding what scales like area vs volume
pitfalls.wrong_move: Scaling mass or cost with the wrong power
pitfalls.why_wrong: Mass at equal density is proportional to VOLUME ($k^3$): the smaller statue is $400 \times \frac{8}{125} = 25.6$ g. Cost of PAINTING covers a surface ($k^2$): $15.50 \times \frac{4}{25} = \$2.48$. Mixing these up gives plausible-looking wrong answers.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask what the quantity physically fills: space → k³; surface → k²; a line (circumference) → k.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Products of an alkane reacting with chlorine
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes hydrogen gas as the second product.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The hydrogen atom that leaves joins a chlorine atom, so hydrogen chloride forms.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Substitution with chlorine: chloroalkane + HCl.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
pitfalls.wrong_move: Halving the marked (non-reflex) centre angle when the rim point sits on the minor arc
pitfalls.why_wrong: The rim angle doubles to the centre angle on the SAME arc — Practice 2a Q3 gives obtuse $\angle AOC = 162°$ but $B$ is on the minor arc, so $\angle ABC = \frac{360° - 162°}{2} = 99°$, not $81°$. Halving the printed angle silently answers a different question.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check which arc the rim point is on; minor arc → use the REFLEX angle at the centre.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Meaning of endothermic
pitfalls.wrong_move: Defines an endothermic reaction as one that needs heating to start.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Many exothermic reactions also need heat to start; that is activation energy. Endothermic means energy is taken in overall, so the products have more energy than the reactants.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Define by overall energy taken in, not by how the reaction is started.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Computing area under a speed-time graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using a phase's END time instead of its DURATION for a piece's width
pitfalls.why_wrong: The 20 m/s constant phase lasting 20 s contributes $(20)(20) = 400$ m — the print writes $(20)(40)$ (the end-time), which would give 900 m against its own correct total of 500 m. Piece widths are durations.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Label each piece with its start and end times and use (end − start) as the width.
source_files: EM 04 Graphs 3 Applications Distance and Speed Time Graphs.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why an alloy is harder than the pure metal
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the added atoms form covalent bonds with the metal, or stop the electrons moving.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The bonding is still metallic. Hardness comes from atoms of a different size stopping the layers from sliding.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Alloy question: different-sized atoms, layers disrupted, cannot slide easily.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: A string plucked harder or a note played louder
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the pitch or the speed of the sound also increases.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A harder pluck only makes the amplitude bigger, so only the loudness changes. Frequency and speed stay the same.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Harder = bigger amplitude = louder. Nothing else changes.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Fractional powers and nested surds
pitfalls.wrong_move: Swapping the root and the power, or working outside-in
pitfalls.why_wrong: In $a^{\frac{n}{m}}$ the DENOMINATOR is the root: $16^{-\frac{3}{4}} = \frac{1}{(\sqrt[4]{16})^3} = \frac{1}{8}$. Nested surds must be collapsed inside-out — $\sqrt{x\sqrt{x\sqrt{x\sqrt{x}}}}$ builds $\frac{1}{2} \to \frac{3}{4} \to \frac{7}{8} \to \frac{15}{16}$ (the key's $\frac{1}{16}$ lost the 5).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bottom of the fraction = root, top = power. Start at the innermost root and work outward, one layer at a time.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Empty sets and edge conventions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing {0} for ∅ (or mis-handling 0 in rules like 'perfect square')
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\varnothing = \{\,\}$ has NO elements — $\{0\}$ has one. And conventions matter at the edges: Assignment Q7's key treats the perfect squares under 11 as $\{1,4,9\}$ (excluding 0), which is what makes its answer '$x = 0, 7$ or $8$' work; counting $0 \in T$ would drop the 0.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: ∅ means nothing inside. At boundaries (0, 1, the number itself), state the convention you're using.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Sources of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives lightning as a source of sulfur dioxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Lightning makes nitrogen and oxygen in the air react. Sulfur dioxide comes from volcanoes and from burning fossil fuels.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Lightning and car engines: nitrogen oxides. Volcanoes and fossil fuels: sulfur dioxide.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Shortest distance from a vertex to a line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Improvising a ratio instead of equating two area expressions
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reliable route is area two ways: $\frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(d) = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, giving $d = \frac{2 \times \text{area}}{\text{base}}$ (Ex 1: $\frac{2(8156.77)}{147.26} = 111$). Ad-hoc sines of non-included angles give near-miss values that are hard to spot.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write the area twice — once with sin, once with the unknown height — and divide.
source_files: EM 08 Trigonometry 4 Angles of Elevation and Depression.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Heating a reactive metal oxide in hydrogen or with carbon
pitfalls.wrong_move: Predicts that magnesium oxide is reduced to magnesium.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen and carbon, so its oxide is not reduced by them. Copper(II) oxide is: black turns reddish-brown.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the metal's position against carbon and hydrogen before predicting any change.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Deriving models before plotting (fenced plantation)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assigning the fence to the wrong sides
pitfalls.why_wrong: With the river covering one long side, the 180 m covers one length $x$ plus two widths: width $= \frac{180 - x}{2}$, so $y = 90x - \frac{1}{2}x^2$. Fencing all four sides (or two lengths) gives a different quadratic and every subsequent answer shifts.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch the rectangle, label which sides consume fence, and write the constraint before any algebra.
source_files: EM 04 Graphs 2 Graphs on Graph Paper (Newest).pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Evaluating expressions with different bases, e.g. $\log_3 2 - \log_9 36$
pitfalls.wrong_move: Combining logs of different bases directly with the add/minus laws
pitfalls.why_wrong: The laws only hold for a COMMON base. Adrian's working always changes base first ($\log_9 36 \to \frac{\log_3 36}{\log_3 9}$) precisely because $\log_3 2 - \log_9 36 \neq \log$ of anything until the bases match.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Different bases? Change of base first — usually to the smaller base.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: "Hence find the prime factors" after a factorization trick
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the two bracket values as prime factors without checking primality
pitfalls.why_wrong: 31605 = 301 × 105 gives FACTORS, but 301 = 7 × 43 and 105 = 3 × 5 × 7 — neither is prime (the true prime factorisation is 3 × 5 × 7² × 43). In 3403 = 83 × 41 both happen to be prime — the check, not the trick, is what earns the word 'prime'.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bracket values are factors; test primality before calling them prime.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Subtracting a multiplied bracket
pitfalls.wrong_move: Detaching the minus from its multiplier
pitfalls.why_wrong: In $7(a - 2b) - 4(6a + 11b)$, the second bracket's multiplier is $-4$, giving $-24a - 44b$. Expanding with $+4$ and subtracting only the first term produces $-24a + 44b$ — one sign wrong, whole answer wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read the multiplier WITH the sign in front of it.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Quotient rule numerator
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the two products in the wrong order (or with + instead of −)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The quotient rule is antisymmetric: $\frac{v u' - u v'}{v^2}$. Swapping gives the negative of the answer. The product rule is symmetric so no order issue exists there — which is exactly why students mix them up.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say it: diff TOP keep bottom, MINUS diff bottom keep top, over bottom squared.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Copying structure between the largest-case and smallest-case parts
pitfalls.wrong_move: Carrying the previous part's final number into the new conclusion
pitfalls.why_wrong: The notes' own Q11(b)(ii) derives x = 61 in the working and then concludes 'smallest possible value of x = 111' — pasted from part (i). Q1(a) similarly prints 39 × 5 = 109 while part (b) uses the true 195. The conclusion line must restate the number computed directly above it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Read your last line of algebra before writing the therefore-line.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Test for purity
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says a substance is pure because it is colourless, leaves no residue or looks uniform.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A solution can also look clear. Only a fixed, exact melting or boiling point shows purity.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Pure → melts and boils at one exact temperature. A mixture melts over a range.
source_files: 12656 - ACSBR 9 Methods of Separation - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Empirical formula of an oxide from heating data
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the mass of the oxide (or of crucible plus contents) as the mass of oxygen or of the metal.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The oxide holds both elements, and the crucible is neither. The masses needed come from subtraction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Subtract first: metal = (crucible + metal) − crucible; oxygen = oxide − metal.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Integrating composite powers like (5x+1)^6 or 1/(2x+3)^2
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding one to the power but forgetting to divide by the inner coefficient (or dividing by the OLD power)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reverse chain rule demands BOTH divisions: $\int(5x+1)^6dx = \frac{(5x+1)^7}{7\times 5}+c$. Dividing by 6 (old power) or skipping the 5 differentiates back to the wrong thing — always check by differentiating your answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Up one, over the NEW power, over the inside's derivative, +c; verify by differentiating.
source_files: AM 19 Differentiation and Integration Techniques Summary.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Listing what leaves a capillary into tissue fluid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Includes red blood cells or plasma proteins.
pitfalls.why_wrong: These are too large to pass through the capillary wall and stay in the blood. Small molecules and some white blood cells pass out.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Stay in: red cells, platelets, plasma proteins. Go out: glucose, oxygen, amino acids, water.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Simplifying after factorizing out the common bracket
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaving the second bracket unsimplified (or mis-adding its like terms)
pitfalls.why_wrong: (2a+b)(3p−5q) − (3a−4b)(3p−5q) = (3p−5q)[(2a+b) − (3a−4b)] — the second bracket still needs 2a + b − 3a + 4b = −a + 5b. Stopping early loses the mark; rushing the signs gives −a − 3b.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After factoring the bracket, simplify what's left — carefully.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives sodium at the cathode, or oxygen at the anode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Sodium is far above hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged instead. In a concentrated chloride solution, chloride ions are discharged instead of hydroxide ions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Brine gives hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, sodium hydroxide left in solution.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Finishing a word problem
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting x when the question asked for something else
pitfalls.why_wrong: For the evens summing to 78, x = 24 but the LARGEST is 28; Matthew's equation finds 12 pens but the question wants 14 pencils; Peter is 2x = 20, not x = 10. The last line of the question decides the last line of the answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reread the question after solving — x is usually one step short.
source_files: S1 MATH 10B Algebra 5B Forming Linear Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Checking a printed answer key or your own roots
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting the final line without a substitute-back
pitfalls.why_wrong: This chapter's notes contain three wrong worked roots (x = 3 for 0; x = 2, −1 for 1, −2; x = 2 for 2/3) — each detectable in five seconds by substituting into the original equation. The check is not optional busywork; it is the error detector.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Every root goes back into the original equation once.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Judging slope sign from a sketch
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calling any line through the top of the page 'positive gradient'
pitfalls.why_wrong: Sign comes from the direction of travel left-to-right: climbing = positive, falling = negative — regardless of where the line sits on the page. A high-up falling line still has m < 0.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Walk the line left to right: uphill +, downhill −.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5A Simultaneous Equations 1 Linear Functions (Recap).pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Finding an intersection the question asks you to draw
pitfalls.wrong_move: Computing or guessing instead of drawing the second line
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Draw x = 7 and state the intersection" awards the mark to the drawn line and the read-off point (7, 0.7). An unsupported coordinate — even a correct one — loses the drawing mark.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw, label, then read the crossing off the grid.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Any circle question (Adrian's double-starred rule)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Working purely algebraically without sketching the circle, its centre, and the given lines/points
pitfalls.why_wrong: Adrian: "For circles questions, it is helpful to draw a diagram to visualize the problem. (Like really, draw a diagram.)" Rejection decisions (which of two centres/radii), tangent positions and reflection directions are all read off the sketch.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Like really, draw a diagram — before any algebra.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reverse problems: comparing an expanded inequality with a target like 3x^2 + cx > d
pitfalls.wrong_move: Comparing x^2 + 2x - 8 > 0 directly against 3x^2 + cx > d without scaling
pitfalls.why_wrong: The x^2 coefficients differ, so term-by-term comparison is meaningless — it yields c = 2, d = 8 instead of c = 6, d = 24. The inequality must be scaled (by a positive constant) until the x^2 terms match.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Match the x^2 coefficient first, then compare the rest.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Rusting experiment with boiled water
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says iron rusts in boiled water because water is there.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Boiling drives out the dissolved air. Rusting needs both oxygen and water.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check for both oxygen and water. One missing means no rust.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Thiosulfate cross experiment at low concentration
pitfalls.wrong_move: Thinks the cross must always disappear in the end.
pitfalls.why_wrong: With too little reactant there is not enough sulfur to hide the cross, however long you wait.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cross never disappears: say the precipitate formed is insufficient (limiting reactant).

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Testing for chloride or sulfate ions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding silver nitrate or barium nitrate without adding dilute nitric acid first.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Carbonate ions also give a white precipitate with silver and barium ions, so the result could be a false positive.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Acid first, to remove carbonate. Then the silver or barium nitrate.
source_files: 12208 - ACSBR Identification of Ions & Gases - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Following a reaction by loss in mass
pitfalls.wrong_move: Chooses the balance method for a reaction that gives off no gas.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mass of the flask falls only when a gas escapes. Neutralisation or precipitation shows no change in mass.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Mass falls only if a gas leaves. Look for a carbonate with acid.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: GST inside a GST-inclusive price
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking 9% of the inclusive price
pitfalls.why_wrong: An inclusive price is 109%, so its GST component is 9/109 of it, not 9/100. Brian's 426.93 tablet carries 9/109 × 426.93 = 35.25 of GST; the printed key's 38.42 = 9% × 426.93 commits exactly this error — and contradicts the file's own worked method.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Inclusive → the GST is 9/109 (or k/(100+k)) of the price.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Changing money there and back
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expecting to break even on an unspent round trip
pitfalls.why_wrong: The changer sells RMB at 21.10 but buys back at 20.70 per 100: Tom's 1266 became 6000 RMB and returned as only 1242. The 24 lost IS the buy/sell spread — no spending required.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Round trip multiplies by buy ÷ sell, which is always below 1.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Recovering the length ratio from areas or volumes
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the exponent instead of taking the root
pitfalls.why_wrong: From areas $45 : 80$ the length ratio is $\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{4}$, not $\frac{45/2}{80/2}$; from volumes $135 : 40$ it is $\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{8}} = \frac{3}{2}$. All cross-quantity hops (area → volume) must pass through the length ratio.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: √ for areas, ∛ for volumes — then re-raise to the power the next part needs.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon electrodes
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the solution stays the same blue, or puts the pink-brown solid at the positive electrode.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Copper(II) ions are taken out at the cathode and not replaced, so the blue fades. Copper coats the negative electrode; oxygen bubbles off at the positive one.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Inert electrodes: blue fades, copper on the cathode, oxygen at the anode.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Substituting a point like (3, n) into a line equation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Swapping the coordinates (using 3 as y)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The first coordinate is always x, the second always y: (3, n) means x = 3, y = n, so n = 5(3) + 2 = 17. Swapped, you would solve 3 = 5n + 2 and get a wrong fraction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: (x, y) in that order — always.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 5A Simultaneous Equations 1 Linear Functions (Recap).pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Using the shoelace formula for the area of a polygon
pitfalls.wrong_move: Listing the vertices in clockwise order, or forgetting to repeat the first point at the end
pitfalls.why_wrong: Adrian's notes flag both explicitly: the first point IS repeated, and vertices must run anti-clockwise — clockwise ordering makes the bracket negative (the modulus rescues the area, but mixed-up orderings that jump around the polygon give garbage, not just a sign change).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sketch, pick a starting vertex, walk anti-clockwise, and write the first column again at the end.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Recording a stopwatch reading
pitfalls.wrong_move: Copies the display as it looks, e.g. 1:35.39 or 13539, or rounds to a whole second.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The time must be one number in seconds, to 2 decimal places.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Change minutes to seconds: 1 min 35.39 s = 95.39 s.
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Salt made by titration
pitfalls.wrong_move: Crystallises the mixture that still contains the indicator.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The indicator would contaminate the salt.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: First titration finds the volumes; repeat WITHOUT indicator to make the salt.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Doubling the range when the variable doubles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving sin 2x = k over the original x-range worth of angles
pitfalls.why_wrong: $0 < x < 2\pi$ means $2x \in (0, 4\pi)$ — TWO full cycles, so four solutions for sine/cosine (and four for tangent). Ex 2d and 2f both harvest their third and fourth answers from the added $2\pi$ copies.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Scale the range with the angle, list all base solutions plus their +2π copies, then divide back.
source_files: AM 16 Trigonometry 03b Further Trigo Identities and Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Deciding if a point is inside, on or outside a circle by a subtended angle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Concluding 'bigger angle → outside the circle'
pitfalls.why_wrong: The angle a chord subtends GROWS as you move closer to it: on the circle it is the same-segment value ($40°$ in Misc Q5), inside it is bigger, outside smaller. $\angle BPD = 50° > 40°$ means $P$ is INSIDE — reversing the comparison flips the answer with full confidence.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bigger view → closer → inside. Compare against the on-circle angle and say the comparison aloud.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Piecewise / two-part motion (different rule after time T)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using one formula across the switch, or forgetting the interface condition
pitfalls.why_wrong: The second phase has its own expression; its constant comes from matching $v$ at the changeover (Ex 3b: $v_1(1) = \frac{13}{2}$ seeds phase 2). Constant-deceleration tails need no integration — they're straight lines/triangles on the $v$–$t$ graph (Ex 3a: $\frac{1}{2}(9)(6)$).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One expression per phase; match v at the boundary; use geometry for the constant-rate part.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Improving the reliability of an enzyme experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes "be more careful" or "measure more accurately".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Reliability comes from repeating and averaging. Care is not an improvement to the method.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reliability? "Repeat with fresh enzyme and substrate and take the mean."
source_files: 11483 - Beatty Answering Planning Questions for Practicals (ans) (edited).pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Expanding a bracket
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying only the first term inside
pitfalls.why_wrong: $2(a + 3b)$ is $2a + 6b$ — writing $2a + 3b$ leaves the second term unmultiplied. The rainbow arcs exist to force one arc per term.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count the arcs: one for every term inside the bracket.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Writing coordinates
pitfalls.wrong_move: Swapping x and y
pitfalls.why_wrong: (2, 3) and (3, 2) are different points. The pair is ordered: horizontal position first, vertical second. Swapping reflects every point across the diagonal and wrecks gradients and areas downstream.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Along first, up second — (x, y).

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Final answer lines after a long generation chain
pitfalls.wrong_move: Copying the collected answers carelessly (or dividing the last value wrongly) without a substitution check
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source itself shows how easy this is: Ex 2e's final line garbles $-150°, -30°, 30°, 150°$ into "$-150°, 30°, 30°, 15°$"; Ex 2c's rounding line swaps a solution for the basic angle; and the Misc Q4 key prints $225°$ for $255°$ ($510° \div 2$). All three had correct working above the slip.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After collecting, substitute one or two answers back into the ORIGINAL equation — ten seconds catches transcription slips.
source_files: AM 16 Trigonometry 03a Simple Trigo Identities and Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: 'Show that the line is a tangent / the roots are real' proof questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Start by writing b²−4ac = 0 (or ≥ 0) and work downwards from it
pitfalls.why_wrong: That assumes the very thing to be shown — circular reasoning that earns no marks. Adrian's note: you cannot just sub a, b, c into b²−4ac = 0; you have to prove it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Start from b²−4ac = (expression), expand and simplify (complete the square if needed) until the sign is undeniable, then conclude with a statement.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Adding or subtracting surds
pitfalls.wrong_move: Combining unlike surds: √2 + √5 = √7, or 2√3 + 3√5 = 5√8
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only 'like' surds (same number inside) collect — the root does not distribute over +. √2 + √5 ≈ 3.65 while √7 ≈ 2.65.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Just add up 'like' terms — same surd inside, add the numbers in front.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Two dice are thrown and you want P(sum of scores is even)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Arguing the sum is either odd or even, so the probability must be 1/2
pitfalls.why_wrong: Odd and even sums are not equally likely outcomes — counting the actual outcome table gives 12/30 = 2/5 here. The n(A)/n(S) shortcut only works over equally likely outcomes.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Build the outcome table and count; never assume two cases are 50-50.
source_files: 13894 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S1, S2 Permutation Combination Probability.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Solving d2y/dx2 = f(x) by integrating twice
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the general solution with a single arbitrary constant
pitfalls.why_wrong: Each integration introduces its own constant; a second order general solution must carry two, and a particular solution needs two conditions
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Add a fresh constant at each integration (Ax + B pattern) and use both given conditions
source_files: 13893 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 9. Differential Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Deciding whether a conductor is ohmic
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calls a component ohmic because its I–V graph is a smooth rising line.
pitfalls.why_wrong: An ohmic conductor gives a STRAIGHT line through the origin: resistance stays constant. A filament lamp's line curves because its resistance rises as it heats up.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Straight and through the origin = ohmic.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Preparing a sodium, potassium or ammonium salt
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adds excess solid to acid and filters.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Compounds of these ions are all soluble, so nothing can be added in excess and filtered off.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sodium, potassium, ammonium salt: titration.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Factorizing or applying the formula to an equation like 2x² = 5x + 18
pitfalls.wrong_move: Working on it without first rearranging to = 0
pitfalls.why_wrong: The zero-product property and the formula's $a, b, c$ only exist for $ax^2+bx+c = 0$. Factorizing $2x^2 = 5x+18$ in place produces nonsense; rearranged, $2x^2-5x-18 = (2x-9)(x+2)$ falls out.
