pitfalls.corrective_cue: Standard form FIRST: sweep every term to one side, keep the x² coefficient positive.
source_files: EM 01 Quadratic Equations 1 Solving Quadratic Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Sliding-ladder questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Recomputing the new position with a new ladder length or the old angle
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the ladder's LENGTH survives the slide — the height and angle both change. 'Slips 0.8 m' updates the wall height (2.477 → 1.677) and the new angle comes from sin⁻¹(1.677/3.062) = 33.2°; keeping 54° or recomputing the length from the new height contradicts the physical setup.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Carry the hypotenuse across the slide; rebuild everything else.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Labelling a drawing of an onion epidermal cell
pitfalls.wrong_move: Labels chloroplasts, mitochondria or "cell sap".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Onion epidermis has no chloroplasts, and mitochondria cannot be seen with a light microscope. The mark scheme rejects these labels.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Label only what you can see: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Kite or string problems
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using tangent with the string length
pitfalls.why_wrong: The taut string IS the hypotenuse, so height = 240 sin 47° ≈ 176 m. Writing 240 tan 47° treats the string as a horizontal ground distance and inflates the kite's height by half as much again.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: String/ladder/slant = hypotenuse → sine or cosine, never tangent.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Drawing the full structural formula of a carboxylic acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes –COOH as a block on the end of the chain.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The marks are for showing C=O and C–O–H drawn out.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Acid group: one carbon, a double bond to O, a single bond to O, then O–H.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Times-up with negatives
pitfalls.wrong_move: Losing a sign when both sides are negative
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\frac{y}{-8} = -\frac{3}{2}$ gives $y = (-8)(-\frac{3}{2}) = +12$ — negative times negative is positive. The printed key's $-12$ keeps a stray minus.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count the minus signs: two minuses multiply to plus.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Planting trees as an answer to rising carbon dioxide
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says planting trees solves the problem.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide much faster than photosynthesis removes it, and trees take years to grow.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compare the two rates: release by burning is far greater than uptake by trees.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Final rounding to 3 significant figures
pitfalls.wrong_move: Truncating instead of rounding (or re-rounding an already rounded number)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $4595.03$ m² to 3sf is $4600$ m² — the assignment key prints "4590 m²" though the identical worked example in the same file concludes 4600. Truncation and double-rounding both shift the third significant figure.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Look at the digit AFTER the cut: 4595 → the 9 rounds the 5 up → 4600.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Reading a and b off a grid diagram
pitfalls.wrong_move: Guessing the components instead of counting squares from tail to head
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice Q2's answer $\sqrt{26}$ only drops out with $\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ — a one-square misread of either arrow changes $2\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}$ and the magnitude entirely. Grid questions are exact, not sketches.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count each arrow's squares across and up, write the column, THEN combine.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Writing column vectors
pitfalls.wrong_move: Putting the y-move on top (or reading a coordinate pair straight into the wrong slots)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The convention is x-direction first, then y: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ means right 1, up 3. Swapping components silently reflects every vector in $y = x$ and wrecks magnitudes' components, gradients and parallels downstream.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Top = across, bottom = up. Say 'x over y' as you write each one.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Choosing values of x to substitute after comparing numerators
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting arbitrary x-values that keep every unknown in play, creating messy simultaneous equations
pitfalls.why_wrong: Each substitution then involves all the unknowns at once; the arithmetic balloons and errors creep in.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sub in values that make some expressions zero (x=1 kills B(x-1)); only when no zeroing value is left, use x=0 or another easy value.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Using the standard results for the sums of r, r^2 or r^3 when the sum starts above r = 1
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting the given limits straight into the standard formula
pitfalls.why_wrong: Those results are stated for a lower limit of 1. A sum from r = n+1 to r = 2n must first be written as (sum from 1 to 2n) minus (sum from 1 to n); using the formula directly counts the wrong block of terms.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rewrite as (sum from 1 to upper) minus (sum from 1 to lower minus 1) before quoting any standard result.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Keying binomial probabilities into the GC
pitfalls.wrong_move: Typing P(X >= a) or P(X < a) straight into binompdf/binomcdf without converting
pitfalls.why_wrong: The GC only computes P(X = x) and P(X <= x); an unconverted inequality returns the probability of the wrong region — off by one term or complemented.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Rewrite before keying: P(X >= a) = 1 - P(X <= a-1) and P(X < a) = P(X <= a-1).
source_files: 13896 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S4 Binomial Distribution.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Constant term or specific coefficient of a PRODUCT of two brackets
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking only one pairing (usually constant × constant) and missing the other routes
pitfalls.why_wrong: Every pair of powers summing to the target contributes: in Example 2b the constant comes from $4(1) + \frac{2}{x}(-14x) + \frac{1}{4x^2}(84x^2) = 4 - 28 + 21$ — taking only the 4 gives a wildly wrong answer. Practice 2 Q1's routes even cancel to exactly 0.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: List the powers available in one factor, then fetch the matching power from the other — one line per route, then add.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Multi-part questions reusing an earlier probability
pitfalls.wrong_move: Rounding an intermediate probability to 3 s.f. and feeding it into a later part
pitfalls.why_wrong: The rounding error propagates — a binomial-within-binomial answer built on a 3 s.f. p is wrong in the third figure. Working values should carry 5 s.f.; only the final answer is 3 s.f.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Keep intermediate probabilities to at least 5 s.f. (or in GC memory); round to 3 s.f. only at the final answer.
source_files: 13896 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S4 Binomial Distribution.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Describing what an alloy is
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the elements in an alloy are chemically combined, or that it conducts because of mobile ions.
pitfalls.why_wrong: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with another element. It conducts because of mobile electrons, like any metal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Alloy = mixture; conducts by mobile electrons.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Computing tax from a salary
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taxing gross income — skipping the reliefs or the times-12
pitfalls.why_wrong: The table runs on CHARGEABLE income: a 5300 monthly salary is 63600 a year carrying 30200 of reliefs, so tax applies to 33400 (giving 319), not to 63600. Percentage donations reduce income too.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Chargeable = 12 × monthly − every relief, before touching the table.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Exponential motion: limits and substitution slips
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking the limiting velocity as t → 0 (or copying e-coefficients carelessly)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Limiting behaviour is $t \to \infty$ where $e^{-kt} \to 0$ (the print in Ex 2a says "$t \to 0$" while its own margin note says ∞, and its substitution line drops the 2 in $2e^{-2}$). Also remember $e^{-kt} > 0$ always — exponential velocities like $8e^{1-2t}$ NEVER hit zero, so no turning.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Limiting value = behaviour at large t; exponentials never vanish; re-derive each coefficient rather than copying.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Reflecting a point P in a line after finding the foot F
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing OP-prime = OF - OP, or 2(OF - OP)
pitfalls.why_wrong: F is the midpoint of PP-prime, so OF = (OP + OP-prime)/2. Rearranging gives OP-prime = 2*OF - OP; the other versions come from doubling the wrong side of the midpoint relation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write the midpoint relation down first, then make OP-prime the subject.
source_files: 13887 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 3. Vectors I.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Choosing a starting substance to react with an acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Picks a nitrate or chloride of the metal to add to the acid.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A soluble salt mixed with an acid just gives a mixture of ions. No reaction removes the unwanted ions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: To react with an acid, choose the metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: What chromatography needs
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the substances must have different colours to be separated.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Separation depends on the substances dissolving in the same solvent and moving by different amounts. Colourless ones are shown with a locating agent.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Condition: all soluble in the solvent used.
source_files: 12656 - ACSBR 9 Methods of Separation - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Copying the expression from line to line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Recopying from memory instead of from the previous line
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source's Ex 2b mutates the question mid-solution ($\frac{1}{5} \to \frac{2}{5}$, $a^4 \to a^3$) and Ex 3a drops a lone $b$ ($16a^2b^9 \to 16a^2b^8$), corrupting the final answers ($\frac{3}{5}a^3b^{-3}$ and $\frac{2b^3}{3a^2}$ are correct). One lost factor invalidates everything after.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: After each line, glance back at the ORIGINAL expression and count the factors of each base.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Drawing the line on a practical graph
pitfalls.wrong_move: Joins the points dot to dot, or bends the line to pass through the origin.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Readings carry scatter. The best-fit line shows the trend, and it need not pass through (0, 0).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One straight ruled line with points balanced on both sides.
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Angles at an intersection of two chords or lines (X, F, G points)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading an angle at the crossing point straight off a circle property
pitfalls.why_wrong: Circle properties live on the circumference and centre — a crossing point like $G$ in Misc Q6 or $X$ in Assignment Q3 obeys only triangle facts: $\angle BGC = \angle BAG + \angle ABG = 70° + 41° = 111°$ (exterior angle of $\triangle ABG$). Guessing 'same segment' at $G$ gives $70°$ or $29°$, both wrong.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: At interior crossing points, switch tools: exterior angle of a triangle (or angle sums), not circle properties.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Multi-step 3D chains
pitfalls.wrong_move: Feeding rounded intermediates into later parts
pitfalls.why_wrong: Ex 1(c) divides $9.270509$ by $85.44003$ — using the rounded $9.27$ and $85.4$ shifts the angle's first decimal. The notes deliberately print full calculator values mid-chain and round only at the end.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Store intermediates in calculator memory; round once, at the final line.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Fraction where the degree of the numerator ≥ degree of the denominator (improper fraction)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Splitting into partial fractions straight away without long division
pitfalls.why_wrong: The standard split forms assume a proper fraction; the polynomial (quotient) part is unaccounted for, so comparing numerators fails or gives wrong constants.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check degrees first: improper → long division to get a quotient and a proper fraction, then split.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Tiered water and electricity rates
pitfalls.wrong_move: Charging the whole consumption at the higher rate
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only the slice above the threshold pays the higher rate: 42.8 cubic metres is $40 \times 1.21 + 2.8 \times 1.52 = 52.66$, not $42.8 \times 1.52 = 65.06$ — a quarter too much.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Split at 40; the 1.52 touches only the 2.8 excess.
source_files: EM 15 Financial Math 5 Personal and Household Finance.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Final gas volume when a more concentrated acid is used and the solid is limiting
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws the new curve ending higher because the acid is stronger.
pitfalls.why_wrong: If the solid runs out, the moles of solid fix the amount of gas. The curve is steeper but ends at the same height.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask first: which reactant runs out? Only its moles set the final volume.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining how a catalyst works
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes that the catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The original route keeps its activation energy. The catalyst opens a different route that needs less energy.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Catalyst? Write: provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
source_files: 21974 - SASS Chem Speed of Rxn AfL Ans.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Predicting the voltage of a simple cell
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expects a bigger voltage from two metals close together in the series.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The voltage comes from the difference in reactivity. Metals further apart give more.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Bigger gap in the reactivity series, bigger voltage.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Per-thousand repayment tables
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying by the loan in dollars (or using years instead of monthly counts)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The table cell is per $\$1000$: a 150000 loan uses $150 \times 7.75$, not $150000 \times 7.75$; totals need months ($240$, $180$), not years. A factor-of-1000 or 12 slip dwarfs the actual interest.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Loan ÷ 1000 × cell = monthly; monthly × (12 × years) = total repaid.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Area between a graph and the y-axis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Integrating y dx with x-limits (or forgetting to make x the subject)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The $y$-axis formula is $\int x\,dy$: rearrange to $x = f(y)$ AND convert the limits to $y$-values. Mixing variables gives dimensionally wrong nonsense that still 'computes'.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say it before integrating: which axis? → which differential? → whose limits?
source_files: AM 18 Integration 2 Area and Definite Integrals.pdf

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Counting intervals in the clap–echo method
pitfalls.wrong_move: Divides the total time by the number of claps.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The intervals between claps are one fewer than the claps: 51 claps make 50 intervals.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Intervals = claps − 1.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: 'More than x' counts from a CF curve
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting CF(x) instead of n − CF(x)
pitfalls.why_wrong: CF(x) counts those AT OR BELOW x. Teachers slower than 40 min = 65 − 58 = 7, not 58; students above 40 marks = 250 − 80 = 170. Using the raw read-off answers the opposite question.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Above → subtract from the total. Below → read directly.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Solving for the hypotenuse from cos θ = adj/hyp
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying instead of dividing when x is in the denominator
pitfalls.why_wrong: cos 52° = 8/x gives x = 8/cos 52° ≈ 13.0, not 8 cos 52° ≈ 4.9. The wrong version produces a 'hypotenuse' shorter than the leg — impossible. When the unknown sits under the fraction, it comes out by division.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Hypotenuse answers must beat every other side; if not, you multiplied when you should have divided.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Comparing surd expressions to find unknowns (a + b√n = c + d√n)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Equating across kinds — matching a rational term against a √ coefficient (e.g. from k − √2 = 2h+1 + (h+1)√2, setting k = h+1)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Rational and irrational parts live in separate worlds: a rational number can never equal an irrational one, so each part must match its own kind. Group into (number) + (number)√n shape BEFORE comparing.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compare rational with rational, √ with √ — group first, then match.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Angle between two legs of a journey at the turning point
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting the two raw bearings
pitfalls.why_wrong: At the turn, the incoming leg is seen BACKWARDS: $\angle PQR$ in Practice 4 is $(35° + 180°) - 75° = 140°$, not $75° - 35° = 40°$. Raw-bearing subtraction only works for two sight-lines from the SAME point (Ex 3: $118° - 38° = 80°$).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Standing at the turn? Back-bearing the leg you arrived on before subtracting.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Setting up elevation/depression angles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Measuring from the vertical (or from the slope) instead of the horizontal
pitfalls.why_wrong: Both angles are defined FROM THE HORIZONTAL at the observer. Measuring from the vertical silently converts $\theta$ to $90° - \theta$; measuring along a slope (the 104 m path instead of the 100 m horizontal in Q3) corrupts every later part.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Draw the dashed horizontal line at the eye first; the angle opens from it.
source_files: EM 08 Trigonometry 4 Angles of Elevation and Depression.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Getting crystals after a titration
pitfalls.wrong_move: Crystallising the solution from the first titration, which still has indicator in it.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The indicator would stain the crystals.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: First run finds the volume. Second run, same volumes, no indicator: crystallise that one.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Spinners/dice/diagrams with printed labels
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assuming a 'nice' labelling (1–9, all distinct) instead of reading the diagram
pitfalls.why_wrong: Practice 3 Q4's spinner is labelled $1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4,5$ — repeats change EVERY count: $P(\text{odd})$ is $\frac{2}{3}$ not $\frac{5}{9}$, prime-at-least-once $\frac{65}{81}$ not $\frac{56}{81}$, equal spins $\frac{19}{81}$ not $\frac{1}{9}$. An assumed labelling can fail every part while looking plausible.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: List the actual labels off the diagram first, repeats and all; only then count.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Linking how easily a carbonate decomposes to the metal's reactivity
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the carbonate that gives the most carbon dioxide belongs to the most reactive metal.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The more reactive the metal, the more stable its carbonate to heat. Easy decomposition means a less reactive metal.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Decomposes easily = less reactive metal. Potassium and sodium carbonates do not decompose in a Bunsen flame.
source_files: 9424 - Chem Practical Planning Questions with Anskey.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Choosing between the BUY and SELL columns
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the rate that favours the customer
pitfalls.why_wrong: The changer always wins: acquiring foreign currency uses the (higher) SELL rate, cashing it in uses the (lower) BUY rate. Swapping them makes 1000 local buy $\frac{1000}{1.2310} = 812.35$ US instead of the correct 801.92.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask who is selling the foreign currency. If the changer sells it to you, SELL rate — and your answer should look slightly worse than mid-rate.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Marble chips with dilute sulfuric acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expects steady effervescence until the marble is used up, as with hydrochloric acid.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Insoluble calcium sulfate forms a layer on the marble and keeps the acid away, so the reaction soon stops.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Calcium carbonate + sulfuric acid: insoluble coating, reaction stops early.
source_files: 21974 - SASS Chem Speed of Rxn AfL Ans.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Expanding (a − bx)^n — any bracket with a negative second term
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the second term as bx and patching signs at the end (or forgetting them entirely)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The second term is $(-bx)$, sign and all, raised to each power: $(-2x)^3 = -8x^3$, $(-2x)^4 = +16x^4$. Patching by memory produces wrong signs on even or odd powers — the source notes themselves misplace one such exponent, printing $(-8x)^3$ for $(-8x^3)$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write $(-bx)^r$ in brackets every single time; odd $r$ keeps the minus, even $r$ removes it.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Combining probabilities in a tree
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding along a path or multiplying across scenarios
pitfalls.why_wrong: Along one path the events all happen → MULTIPLY; across alternative paths only one happens → ADD. Swapping them gives numbers bigger than 1 or absurdly small (three-coin '2H 1T' is $3 \times \frac{1}{8}$, not $\frac{1}{8}^3$ or $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}$).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Multiply ALONG the branches, add ACROSS the paths.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Assigning coordinate signs to quadrants
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing up which coordinate is negative in which quadrant
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source notes themselves slip: in a Q4 example the note reads "1 is positive (because x-coordinate is negative)" — Q4 has POSITIVE $x$. One flipped sign flips every downstream ratio.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Recite the pair per quadrant: Q1 (+,+), Q2 (−,+), Q3 (−,−), Q4 (+,−) — and tie each leg's sign to it explicitly.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Velocity–time graph below the time axis, sloping up towards zero
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the acceleration is negative because the velocity is negative.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The sign of the acceleration comes from the slope. The slope is upward, so the acceleration is positive while the object slows down in the negative direction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sign of acceleration = sign of the slope of the v–t graph.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Drawing a results table for an osmosis experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes the unit after every number in the table.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Units belong in the column heading only. Cells hold numbers alone.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Heading = quantity / unit. Variable you changed goes in the first column.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Reflecting a circle in an axis or a line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Changing the radius, or mangling the centre's coordinates (e.g. reflecting (2,3) in the y-axis to (−1,3))
pitfalls.why_wrong: Reflection moves only the CENTRE and preserves the radius. In the y-axis, exactly the x-coordinate is negated: $(2,3) \to (-2,3)$. The source notes themselves slip to $(-1,3)$ in Example 3c.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Reflect the centre exactly (negate one coordinate for an axis; use the perpendicular-foot midpoint for an oblique line); keep the radius.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Perimeter of a composite or cut-out figure
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counting internal join lines, or forgetting a cut-out's arc
pitfalls.why_wrong: Where a triangle meets its semicircle (QS = 12), the join is inside the figure and adds nothing; but where a semicircle is CUT OUT, its arc becomes new boundary (the V-figure gains 2π for the removed notch).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Walk the outline once; joins don't count, cut arcs do.
source_files: S1 MATH 20A Mensuration 1 Area and Perimeter (RECAP).pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Writing the products when magnesium, zinc or iron reacts with steam
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing the metal hydroxide as the product.
pitfalls.why_wrong: With steam the product is the metal OXIDE and hydrogen. Hydroxides form only with cold water.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cold water: hydroxide + hydrogen. Steam: oxide + hydrogen.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Balancing a chemical equation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Changes a formula to make the atoms match, such as writing CO₃ for carbon dioxide or O for oxygen gas.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A different formula is a different substance, so the equation no longer shows the reaction.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Get every formula right first. After that, only the numbers in front may change.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Computing a percentage change
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the change by the final value instead of the original
pitfalls.why_wrong: The car that went 45 000 → 85 000 rose by 40000/45000 = 88.9%. Dividing by 85 000 gives 47.1% — a different (wrong) statement. The base of a change is always where you started.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Percentage change = change ÷ ORIGINAL × 100%.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Time for half the reactant to be used up
pitfalls.wrong_move: Takes half of the total reaction time.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reaction is faster at the start, so half the product forms well before half the time.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Halve the final volume on the y-axis, then read across to the curve and down to the time.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Two-tail test decided by the p-value
pitfalls.wrong_move: Comparing the single-tail probability P(Z >= |z_calc|) against alpha
pitfalls.why_wrong: A 2-tail p-value covers both tails, so the single-tail probability must be doubled before comparing with alpha.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: For H1: mu not equal to mu0, use p-value = 2P(Z >= |z_calc|).
source_files: 13900 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S7 Hypothesis Testing.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Cosine rule rearranged for an angle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Scrambling which side goes on top (or dropping the minus signs)
pitfalls.why_wrong: $\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$ puts the side OPPOSITE the wanted angle with the minus. A sign slip flips obtuse to acute: Practice 2b(iii) needs $\cos\theta = \frac{-164}{252} \implies 130.6°$; mangled orders give $49.4°$ with no warning. A negative cosine is CORRECT for obtuse — don't 'fix' it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Opposite² is subtracted on top; negative cosine simply means the angle is obtuse.
source_files: EM 08 Trigonometry 2 Sine Rule and Cosine Rule.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Application answers (lengths, ages, positive integers)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting both roots when the context forbids one
pitfalls.why_wrong: x = −19 can't be a positive integer and x = −4/3 can't be a length: reject with 'NA' and a reason. Conversely, when both roots ARE valid (wire cut: x = 4 or 7), keep both — the two squares just swap.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Test each root against the story; reject with a stated reason.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Solvent level in chromatography
pitfalls.wrong_move: Lets the solvent cover the start line.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The spot dissolves into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solvent level below the start line.
source_files: 12656 - ACSBR 9 Methods of Separation - Lesson Package.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Calculator mode with radian angles
pitfalls.wrong_move: Evaluating sin θ in degree mode when θ is in radians
pitfalls.why_wrong: The segment formula $\frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$ needs $\sin 0.8$ = 0.717 (radians), not $\sin 0.8°$ = 0.014 — degree mode inflates the segment area enormously and looks plausible in other problems. The notes flag this explicitly.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Angle written without a ° sign → switch to RAD before touching sin/cos.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 1 Arc Length and Sector Area.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Scaling volumes and capacities of similar solids
pitfalls.wrong_move: Squaring the length ratio (or forgetting to cube it)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Volumes scale by $k^3$. The source's own Ex 1f(c) prints $V_1 = \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times 9.6$ for a CAPACITY — the correct factor is $\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{64}$, giving 4050 cm³ from 9600 cm³, not 5.4.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Say the quantity's dimension aloud: area → square, volume/capacity/mass → cube.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: 'Same speed' vs 'overtakes' in two-mover questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Equating speeds when the question asks about overtaking (or vice versa)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Equal speeds = equal HEIGHTS on the S-T graph; overtaking = equal DISTANCES = equal AREAS. They give different times (P matches Q's speed at 20 s but only overtakes at 45 s). For phase boundaries, check distances at the boundary to know which segment contains $t$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Underline the verb: 'same speed' → heights; 'overtake/meet/catch up' → areas. Boundary check first.
source_files: EM 04 Graphs 3 Applications Distance and Speed Time Graphs.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Copying computed answers into the final line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting a key digit that fails a magnitude check
pitfalls.why_wrong: A 21290 cm² surface for a prism whose wrap is 1050 cm², or a 114 400 cm³ volume from a 440 cm² cross-section 26 cm long, are 10–16× too big — stray digits and extra zeros survive when no one estimates first.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Estimate the order of magnitude before accepting any answer.
source_files: S1 MATH 20C Mensuration 3 Volume and Surface Area Cylinder and Prism.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Forming 'A takes longer than B' equations
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting the bigger time from the smaller
pitfalls.why_wrong: The slower journey/tap has the LARGER time: $\frac{360}{x-10} > \frac{360}{x}$, so the difference is $\frac{360}{x-10} - \frac{360}{x}$. Reversed order gives a negative left side and an impossible equation.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask which quantity is bigger (smaller denominator = bigger fraction) and write bigger − smaller = difference.
source_files: EM 01 Quadratic Equations 2 Quadratic Equations Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Quartiles of a small data set
pitfalls.wrong_move: Marking Q1/Q3 on 'nice' data positions instead of using (n+1)/4 positions
pitfalls.why_wrong: For the 9 seedlings, pointing at the 3rd and 7th values gives $Q_3 = 16$, IQR 3; the $\frac{3}{4}(n+1) = 7.5$ position gives $Q_3 = \frac{16+18}{2} = 17$, IQR 4 — the source prints BOTH. Exams mark the position-formula answer.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Compute the position first ($\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{3}{4}$ of $n+1$), then read (or average) the data.
source_files: EM 13 Statistics 1 Standard Deviation and Interquartile Range.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Reading table problems backwards
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the count when the question asks for the figure number
pitfalls.why_wrong: In the shaded-squares table, $S = 36$ at $x = 6$ — the answer is the DIAGRAM number 6, not 36. Backwards questions solve for n; the given number is already known.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask which column the blank sits in before answering.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Two-centre figures (arcs from different circles)
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using one circle's radius for the other circle's arc or sector
pitfalls.why_wrong: In Q8 the same chord $AB$ belongs to a radius-4 sector at $O$ AND a radius-7 sector at $X$ — each arc, sector and segment must use its own centre's radius and its own angle (1.8 vs 0.928). Q4's arc $BC$ has radius $AB = 2\sqrt{2}$, not 2. The notes warn: "two different centres — hence two different radii".
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Label every arc with its centre before computing; radius = distance from THAT centre.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 1 Arc Length and Sector Area.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Using invNorm to find an unknown bound d in P(a < X < d) = p
pitfalls.wrong_move: Using the CENTER tail option when a and d are not known to be symmetric about the mean
pitfalls.why_wrong: invNorm CENTER assumes both bounds are equidistant from the mean; with one fixed bound that symmetry usually fails
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Convert to a left-tail statement: P(X < d) = p + P(X < a), then use the LEFT tail
source_files: 13898 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - S5 Normal Distribution Lecture Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Obtaining the solid salt from its solution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Heating the solution until all the water is gone.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Many salts lose their water of crystallisation or break down when heated dry, so you get a powder or a different substance.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Heat only until saturated, then cool. Dry the crystals between filter paper, not in a flame.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Deciding whether a simple cell gives a voltage
pitfalls.wrong_move: Expects a reading with two electrodes of the same metal, or with solid sodium chloride or ethanol between them.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Two identical metals give no difference to drive electrons. A solid salt has ions that cannot move, and ethanol has no ions.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: A working cell needs two different metals and a liquid with mobile ions.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Reading a light-intensity graph where the curve levels off
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says light is still the limiting factor on the flat part.
pitfalls.why_wrong: More light gives no more photosynthesis there, so another factor such as carbon dioxide or temperature is holding the rate back.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Flat line: the x-axis factor is no longer limiting. Name another factor.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: What a catalytic converter does
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says the converter removes all pollutants, or cuts carbon dioxide.
pitfalls.why_wrong: It turns carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Carbon dioxide is still given out, and sulfur dioxide is not removed.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Converter: CO and NO in, CO₂ and N₂ out. It makes carbon dioxide.

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Which traveller's time is bigger in a difference equation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Subtracting the times in the wrong order
pitfalls.why_wrong: The slower speed gives the LONGER time: 400/x (slower Albert) exceeds 400/(x+20), so the difference is 400/x − 400/(x+20) = 1. Reversed, the equation has no positive solution — and the printed margin note in this very worksheet cites the wrong fractions from an older edition.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Slower speed → bigger fraction → it goes first.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications (Supplementary Worksheet).pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: "For how long is h ≥ k" inequality questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reporting the boundary times instead of the duration (or forgetting to scale to the full day/two revolutions)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The jetty question wants a total time per DAY: the per-cycle window (4.94 h) must be doubled for two tidal cycles → 9.89 h. The windmill's two-revolution version likewise doubles the single-revolution 2.04 s.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solve the window within one period, take its LENGTH, then multiply by the number of periods in the asked timespan.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Equations of horizontal and vertical lines
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing x = k for a horizontal line (or y = k for a vertical)
pitfalls.why_wrong: y = 2 collects all points WITH y-coordinate 2 — a flat line; x = 2 stands upright. Matching the letter to the axis it cuts: y = k cuts the y-axis, x = k cuts the x-axis.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: The variable in the equation names the axis the line cuts.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Stating the job of limestone in the blast furnace
pitfalls.wrong_move: Calling limestone a reducing agent, or saying it removes basic impurities.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Limestone breaks down to calcium oxide, a BASE, which reacts with the ACIDIC impurity silicon dioxide.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Limestone removes sand as slag: CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Expanding sin(A + B), cos(A − B), etc.
pitfalls.wrong_move: Distributing the function over the bracket: sin(A+B) = sin A + sin B
pitfalls.why_wrong: It is NOT algebraic expansion — Adrian's notes flag this in bold. The addition formulae are the only legal expansion, and cosine's sign FLIPS: $\cos(A+B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Never distribute a trig function; quote the addition formula in full and watch cosine's flipped sign.
source_files: AM 16 Trigonometry 03b Further Trigo Identities and Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Multiplying multiples of surds, e.g. 3√2 × 4√5
pitfalls.wrong_move: Crossing the channels: multiplying a coefficient into the surd or misreading the coefficients (e.g. 20√10 instead of 12√10)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The two channels stay separate: number times number (3 × 4 = 12), surd times surd (√2 × √5 = √10). The printed sheet itself slips to 20√10 here.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Number times number, surd times surd.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Cancelling terms in a telescoping (method of difference) sum
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assuming every term cancels with the row immediately below it
pitfalls.why_wrong: When the general term is f(r) - f(r-2), the cancellation is two rows down, so two terms survive at each end. Cancelling neighbours discards terms that never actually cancel.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Leave the terms unsimplified and use the denominators as a guide. However many survive at the start, the same number survives at the end.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Ring (annulus) perimeter
pitfalls.wrong_move: Counting only the outer circle
pitfalls.why_wrong: The shaded ring between two circles has TWO boundary curves; cutting a 10-radius circle from a 20-radius circle gives perimeter 2π(20) + 2π(10) = 188.52 cm, not 125.7.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: A hole's edge is part of the region's boundary.
source_files: S1 MATH 20A Mensuration 1 Area and Perimeter (RECAP).pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: '25% were above/below the limit' boxplot questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the wrong quartile tail
pitfalls.why_wrong: 25% EXCEEDING the limit means the top quarter, which sits above $Q_3$ — the speed-camera limit is $Q_3 = 80$ km/h. The printed working grabbed $Q_1 = 71$, the bottom quarter. Same number of percent, opposite tail.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Above → Q₃; below → Q₁. Match the tail to the wording before reading the plot.
source_files: EM 13 Statistics 1 Standard Deviation and Interquartile Range.pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Combining constants while solving a DE
pitfalls.wrong_move: Folding an expression that still contains x into a "new arbitrary constant" (e.g. treating C/ln x as a constant)
pitfalls.why_wrong: An arbitrary constant must be a pure number; anything with the variable inside changes with x, so the "solution" no longer satisfies the DE
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Only merge pure constants into A; never absorb any term containing the variable
source_files: 13893 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 9. Differential Equations.pdf

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Drawing a chart to compare separate kinds of plant
pitfalls.wrong_move: Draws the bars touching, like a histogram.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Different crops are separate categories, not a continuous scale. A bar chart has gaps between bars of equal width.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Categories on the x-axis? Bar chart: equal bars, equal gaps, each bar labelled.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: 'Given ∫f, evaluate ∫[f ± polynomial]' definite-integral questions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Treating the polynomial part as unknown too (or losing the sign when limits are swapped)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Only $f$ is unknown; $\int kx\,dx$ you compute yourself. And $\int_2^0 = -\int_0^2$: the assignment's Q2(b) needs BOTH moves ($-16 + 4k = 20$). The key's own Q2(a) slips: $\int_0^2[2f+3]dx = 10+6 = 16$, not the printed 20.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Split into (given ∫f) + (explicit integral you evaluate); fix limit order before substituting.
source_files: AM 18 Integration 2 Area and Definite Integrals.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Matching a lower, flatter curve to a change in conditions
pitfalls.wrong_move: Chooses a lower temperature alone to explain a curve that ends at half the height.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Temperature changes only the steepness. Half the final volume needs half the mass of the limiting reactant.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check both features of the curve: the gradient (rate) and where it levels off (amount).

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Recovering n from one printed angle
pitfalls.wrong_move: Taking the exterior angle as 360° minus the interior
pitfalls.why_wrong: Interior and exterior are supplementary ON A LINE: exterior = 180 − interior (162° interior → 18° exterior → n = 20). Using 360 − 162 = 198 treats the reflex angle as the exterior and n collapses to nonsense.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Interior + exterior = 180, then n = 360 ÷ exterior.
source_files: S1 MATH 17B Polygons and Angles 2 Quadrilaterals and Polygons.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Perpendicular distance from a vertex to a line
pitfalls.wrong_move: Guessing the distance with a ratio instead of equating two area expressions
pitfalls.why_wrong: In Misc Q1(c) the distance from $R$ to $PQ$ comes from $\frac{1}{2}(20)(21) = \frac{1}{2}(29)d \implies d = \frac{420}{29} = 14.5$. There is no single trig ratio that reads it off directly; eyeballed ratios give unverifiable numbers.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Same triangle, two bases: easy-legs area first, then divide by the slanted base.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Starting an enzyme reaction at a chosen temperature
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixes enzyme and substrate at once, then puts the tube in the water bath.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The reaction starts before the mixture reaches the temperature, so the result is not for that temperature.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Leave the tubes in the bath about 5 minutes first, then mix and start timing.
source_files: 11483 - Beatty Answering Planning Questions for Practicals (ans) (edited).pdf

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Area between two curves where part of the region lies below the x-axis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Splitting the region at the x-axis and negating the lower piece
pitfalls.why_wrong: Upper curve minus lower curve is already a positive height everywhere inside the region, so the extra correction is applied twice.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One integral of upper minus lower between the intersection points is enough. Split only where the two curves actually swap over.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Oxidising an alcohol to a carboxylic acid
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives an acid with one carbon more or one fewer than the alcohol.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Oxidation changes the end group only. The number of carbon atoms stays the same.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count the carbons: propanol → propanoic acid.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Stating the magnification of a drawing
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves the magnification out, or divides actual length by drawing length.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Magnification is the drawing length divided by the actual length, written with ×.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Drawing on top, actual below, same unit, answer as ×2.5.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: A question that says "exactly", "algebraically" or "without the use of a calculator"
pitfalls.wrong_move: Reading the answer off the graphing calculator and writing it to 3 significant figures
pitfalls.why_wrong: The instruction forbids it: the marks are for the algebraic working, and a rounded decimal is not an exact answer. A calculator window can also hide roots, so what you see is not always what you should get.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Scan the wording for those keywords first. If any appear, complete the square or factorise and leave the answer in surd, log or fraction form.
source_files: 13889 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 5. Inequalities + APGP.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Sloped-bottom pools
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying length × width × one depth
pitfalls.why_wrong: A pool sloping 0.8 m to 2.2 m is a trapezium-prism: V = ½(0.8 + 2.2) × 50 × 24 = 1800 m³. Using either single depth misses by up to ×2.75 — and the wet bottom uses the slope length 50.02, not 50.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Side view = trapezium; slope length for the wet bottom.
source_files: S1 MATH 20E Mensuration 5 Miscellaneous Area and Volume Questions.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Cross method: choosing the factor split
pitfalls.wrong_move: Accepting the first split without checking the cross-products
pitfalls.why_wrong: The split is only right when the two cross-products ADD to the middle term: for 15x² − 8x − 63, the pair 3x/5x with −7/+9 gives 27x − 35x = −8x ✓; other splits of 15 and 63 give the wrong middle. The check IS the method.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cross-multiply and add — the middle term must come out exactly.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Sharing problems that give a difference
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing the given amount by the TOTAL units
pitfalls.why_wrong: "Betty has $\$24$ more than Andrew" (ratio 3 : 5 : 11) pins 24 to the 2-unit GAP, not the 19-unit total. Dividing 24 by 19 instead of 2 wrecks every share.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Ask what the dollar amount is attached to: a gap, a total, or one share.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Using printed answer keys
pitfalls.wrong_move: Trusting a key fraction that no second route confirms
pitfalls.why_wrong: This file's keys slip twice: $\overrightarrow{YX} = \frac{4}{5}\overrightarrow{SP}$ (actual $\frac{3}{4}$: $\frac{15/4}{5}$) and $\overrightarrow{OM} = \mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b}$ for a midpoint of $PS$ (actual $\mathbf{a} + \frac{3}{2}\mathbf{b}$ — the key's own next part uses $\frac{3}{2}$). A quick re-derivation catches both.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Cross-check key fractions against a neighbouring part or a coordinate sketch before believing them.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Effect of temperature on fermentation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says a temperature well above 37 °C makes fermentation faster.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The enzymes in yeast are denatured at high temperature, so fermentation stops.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Yeast needs about 37 °C. Hotter: enzymes denatured. Colder: too slow.

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Finding when a particle comes to instantaneous rest
pitfalls.wrong_move: Solving a = 0
pitfalls.why_wrong: Instantaneous rest means the velocity is zero, so it is v = ds/dt = 0 that must be solved. Zero acceleration marks maximum or minimum velocity instead.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Solve v = 0 for t, reject any negative t, then substitute that t into s to say where the particle stops.
source_files: 13890 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 6. Differentiation _ Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S2
pitfalls.context: Quadratics with no constant term, e.g. 2x² + 4x = 0
pitfalls.wrong_move: Dividing both sides by x (or forgetting the x = 0 root)
pitfalls.why_wrong: Dividing by x throws away the root x = 0. Factor instead: 2x(x + 2) = 0 gives x = 0 OR x = −2 — the notes' own example misprints the first root as 3; 2x = 0 can only give 0.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Factor out x; the first root is always x = 0.
source_files: S2 MATH 01 Algebra 6A Quadratic Equations and Applications.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Final step after completing the square inside factored brackets, e.g. 2[(x + 5/4)^2 - 17/16]
pitfalls.wrong_move: Multiplying the factored coefficient back into the square term but not the constant (writing 2(x + 5/4)^2 - 17/16)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The coefficient multiplies everything inside the brackets, including the constant; the printed notes themselves slipped at exactly this step once (Example 2g: 2[(x+5)^2 - 26] printed as 2(x+5)^2 - 104 instead of -52)
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Expand/multiply the coefficient back into BOTH terms — square AND constant

pitfalls.subject: JC
pitfalls.context: Evaluating a definite integral using a given substitution
pitfalls.wrong_move: Substituting the integrand into the new variable but keeping the original x-limits
pitfalls.why_wrong: Limits belong to the variable of integration, so u in the integrand with x in the limits evaluates a completely different integral.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Put the substitution to work on the limits too: find the new value at each end before you integrate.
source_files: 13892 - NYJC H2 Mathematics Lecture Notes - 8. Integration _ its Application.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Perimeter of a segment or composite region
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding radii that are not part of the boundary (or forgetting the chord)
pitfalls.why_wrong: A segment's boundary is arc + CHORD ($2r\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$) — radii belong to SECTOR perimeters. In composite figures (Q7: arc + straight piece + arc) each boundary piece must be walked once: the perimeter 20.6 = 7.496 + 3.292 + 9.8 has no radius in it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Trace the outline with a finger; write one term per piece you traced.
source_files: EM 09 Circular Measure 1 Arc Length and Sector Area.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining how a magnesium block stops iron from rusting
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says magnesium forms a coating, or keeps oxygen and water away from the iron.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A block touches only a small part of the iron. It protects because it is more reactive and corrodes in place of the iron.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Attached block = sacrificial. Write: more reactive, corrodes in preference to iron.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Writing f(x) = divisor × Q(x) (+ remainder) before comparing coefficients
pitfalls.wrong_move: Guessing the shape of Q(x) — e.g. writing a linear Q(x) when a quadratic is needed
pitfalls.why_wrong: Degree of quotient = degree of dividend − degree of divisor. A degree-4 polynomial divided by a quadratic needs Q(x) = Ax²+Bx+C; a wrong degree makes coefficient comparison impossible or inconsistent.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Count degrees first: degree of quotient = degree of dividend − degree of divisor, then write Q(x) with exactly that degree.
source_files: notes_inbox/AM/AM 06 Polynomials 1 Remainder and Factor Theorem.pdf

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Bills with service charge plus GST
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adding 10% + 7% as a single 17% surcharge
pitfalls.why_wrong: GST is charged on the price INCLUDING the service charge, so the true multiplier is $1.10 \times 1.07 = 1.177$ — a 17.7% markup. On a 120 meal that is 141.24, not 140.40.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Multiply the factors: ×1.10 then ×1.07 — never add the percentages.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Classifying numbers as prime
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assuming an odd number with no obvious factor is prime
pitfalls.why_wrong: $51 = 3 \times 17$, $57 = 3 \times 19$ and $81 = 3^4$ all look prime but are not — a digit sum divisible by 3 exposes each. And 1 is not prime at all (a prime needs exactly two divisors).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Test small primes in order: 2 (even?), 3 (digit sum), 5 (ends 0/5), 7, 11...
source_files: S1 MATH 01 Numbers 1 Prime Numbers Square and Cube Roots.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Recalling the special ratios (30°, 45°, 60°) under exam pressure
pitfalls.wrong_move: Swapping sin 30° with sin 60°, or writing tan 60° = 1/√3
pitfalls.why_wrong: The values pair up confusably ($\frac{1}{2}$ vs $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ vs $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$). A single swap poisons every no-calculator evaluation in the paper.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: When unsure, redraw the two source triangles (half-equilateral: 1, √3, 2; half-square: 1, 1, √2) and read the ratio — bigger angle sees the bigger opposite side.

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Students joining or leaving a surveyed group
pitfalls.wrong_move: Adjusting the old angle instead of recomputing from the new total
pitfalls.why_wrong: When 4 join a group of 60, America's sector becomes (15 + 2)/64 × 360 ≈ 96° — both numerator and the total changed. Adding 'a bit' to the old 90° or keeping the 60 denominator gives a wrong angle.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: New chart = new count over new total, times 360.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Rate experiment with solid pieces such as marble chips
pitfalls.wrong_move: Keeps the solid the same by using pieces of "the same size".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Pieces of similar size can still differ in mass, so the amount of solid is not controlled.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Weigh out the same mass of solid for every run, as well as keeping the piece size the same.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Making up a solution in a volumetric flask before titration
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses the solution without shaking the flask.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The solution is not evenly mixed, so each pipette portion has a different concentration and the titres do not agree.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Stopper and invert the flask several times before taking any sample.

pitfalls.subject: BIO
pitfalls.context: Explaining why a plant is kept in the dark for two days before a photosynthesis experiment
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says it is to use up the glucose in the leaves.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The starch test detects starch. The dark period is to remove stored starch, so any starch found later was made during the experiment.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Dark for two days? Write: to destarch the leaves.
source_files: 21999 - SASS Bio Nutrition in Plants Notes.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Copper(II) salt solution with copper electrodes
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives oxygen or chlorine at the anode and says the blue colour fades.
pitfalls.why_wrong: A copper anode is not inert. It dissolves to form copper(II) ions as fast as they are removed at the cathode, so the concentration and the colour stay the same.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Check the electrode material first. Copper anode: it dissolves, no gas.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Chlorine with litmus
pitfalls.wrong_move: Says chlorine just turns litmus red.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Chlorine is acidic, but it also bleaches. The litmus ends up colourless.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Chlorine: damp blue litmus turns red, then is bleached.
source_files: 12648 - ACSBR 6 Identification of Ions and Gases - Assignment ANS.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Recording a test in which nothing happens
pitfalls.wrong_move: Leaves the observation blank, or writes "no reaction".
pitfalls.why_wrong: A blank earns nothing, and "no reaction" is a conclusion, not something seen.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write "no visible change".
source_files: 18856 - 2025 Montfort Sec 6092 Revision Guide for Practical.pdf

pitfalls.subject: S1
pitfalls.context: Sequences with growing gaps
pitfalls.wrong_move: Forcing a + (n−1)d onto a quadratic pattern
pitfalls.why_wrong: $1, 19, 49, 91$ has gaps 18, 30, 42 — not constant, so no linear formula fits. The give-away structure ($2 \times (3n^2 - 2) - 1$) comes from comparing with a provided quadratic, not from d.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Gaps changing steadily → think n², compare against a known quadratic.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Writing proof statements
pitfalls.wrong_move: Claiming a fact as 'Given' when it must be derived (or naming the wrong angle pair)
pitfalls.why_wrong: The source's own Ex 1b prints 'OS = OQ (Given)' — never given, and false; the real side pair is $OS = OR$, derived from $PR = QS$ minus the equal parts. It also labels the adjacent pair $\angle SOQ = \angle ROQ$ 'vertically opposite' — the vertical pair is $\angle POS = \angle QOR$. Wrong reasons forfeit the proof marks even when the conclusion is right.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Re-read the givens before writing (Given); vertical pairs sit ACROSS the intersection point, sharing only the vertex.

pitfalls.subject: PHYS
pitfalls.context: Choosing a graph scale
pitfalls.wrong_move: Uses an awkward step such as 3 or 7 units per big square to fill the grid.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Points cannot be plotted or read accurately on such a scale, and the scale mark is lost.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Steps of 1, 2 or 5 only (or these times ten).
source_files: 11535 - Beatty PURE PHYSICS PRACTICAL NOTES 6 Oct 2023.pdf

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Reducing a hot metal oxide with hydrogen
pitfalls.wrong_move: Stops the hydrogen as soon as heating stops.
pitfalls.why_wrong: Air enters the tube and the hot metal reacts with oxygen again, forming the oxide.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Keep the hydrogen flowing until the metal has cooled.

pitfalls.subject: EM
pitfalls.context: Reporting a standard deviation
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writing down the mean (or Σx²/n) instead of finishing the formula
pitfalls.why_wrong: SD $= \sqrt{\frac{\sum x^2}{n} - \bar{x}^2}$ — stopping early or copying the wrong calculator readout gives numbers like 21.9 for marks that only span 17–27 (true SD 3.24). An SD comparable to the data's whole spread is a red flag.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Sanity check: SD should be a small fraction of the data's range. Subtract the mean² BEFORE the square root.
source_files: EM 13 Statistics 1 Standard Deviation and Interquartile Range.pdf

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Calculator mode and time-unit bookkeeping
pitfalls.wrong_move: Mixing radians and degrees, or decimal hours and minutes
pitfalls.why_wrong: Most models here are radian-based ($k = \frac{5\pi}{34}$) but one uses $(480t)°$ — degree mode; and answers like 3.3198 h must become 3 h 19 min → 0319, not "3:31". Each mismatch produces a plausible-looking wrong time.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Fix the angle unit from the formula (π's → radians; ° sign → degrees) and convert decimal hours via ×60 before writing clock times.

pitfalls.subject: AM
pitfalls.context: Solving x^2 >= k (e.g. x^2 >= 16), including discriminant inequalities
pitfalls.wrong_move: Square-rooting both sides: x >= ±4
pitfalls.why_wrong: x >= ±4 is uninterpretable — greater than +4 or greater than -4? It silently loses the whole x <= -4 branch (x = -5 satisfies x^2 >= 16 but not x >= -4… reading it either way fails).
pitfalls.corrective_cue: One side zero, factorize (x-4)(x+4), read the graph: x <= -4 or x >= 4.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Mass of solid remaining when the acid runs out
pitfalls.wrong_move: Gives the mass that reacted when the question asks for the mass that remains.
pitfalls.why_wrong: The mass that reacted is only a step. What remains is the starting mass minus it.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Underline 'remains' or 'left'. Finish with start − reacted.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Comparing a simple cell with electrolysis
pitfalls.wrong_move: Assumes the positive electrode does the same job in both.
pitfalls.why_wrong: In electrolysis, oxidation happens at the positive electrode. In a simple cell, oxidation happens at the negative electrode.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Do not go by the sign. Ask where electrons are lost: that is oxidation.

pitfalls.subject: CHEM
pitfalls.context: Explaining why a simple molecular substance does not conduct electricity
pitfalls.wrong_move: Writes only "it has no free electrons".
pitfalls.why_wrong: Current can be carried by mobile ions or by free electrons. A molecular substance has neither, and both must be ruled out.
pitfalls.corrective_cue: Write: "no mobile ions or free electrons to carry the current".
